docs.title: Vergil Tooling
docs.text: Vergil-tooling is a Python package and script collection providing shared development tooling for all managed repositories. It delivers CLI tools for commits, PRs, releases, and validation alongside bash validators and git hooks -- all consumed via PATH.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Python CLI tools (src/vergil_tooling/): vrg-commit, vrg-submit-pr, vrg-release, vrg-update-deps, vrg-finalize-pr, vrg-validate

Lint tools (installed as vrg-*): vrg-repo-profile, validation drivers

Claude Code hook guard (.claude/hooks/): PreToolUse hook that blocks raw git and gh, routing through vrg-* wrappers

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
• Portability -- scripts run on both macOS and Linux
  • shellcheck clean -- all shell scripts pass shellcheck
  • No repo-specific logic -- every script works in any consuming repository
  • Host-level install -- uv tool install puts vrg-* on PATH; no sibling checkout required

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. vergil-tooling is installed on the developer's host via uv tool install, placing vrg-* scripts in ~/.local/bin/.
  2. vrg-container-run bridges host commands into dev container images where language runtimes and validators live.
  3. Inside the container, vrg-container-run uses a per-branch cached image with vergil-tooling installed at the release line pinned in vergil.toml ([dependencies].vergil), so vrg-* tools run there by bare name too.
  4. Each repo ships a .claude/hooks/guard.sh shim wired via .claude/settings.json, blocking raw git/gh in agent sessions.
  5. Consuming repos call tools by bare name -- no file copying or syncing.
  6. Lima and cloud agent VMs install the signed vergil-tooling package with apt instead of uv. The apt/dnf install guide is the vergil-project/packages README (pinned primary key fingerprint B3A1D804DC03AB036566A4E367861822166ECABE).

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: A quickstart for putting a repository under vergil-tooling. You install the host tools, let vrg-github-repo-init create (or adopt) the repository, and verify the result. For the detailed walkthrough, see Consuming Repo Setup.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install these on your host:

  • Homebrew (macOS) — with the Xcode Command Line Tools, which Homebrew needs (xcode-select --install). Install the host tools below with it.
  • git — brew install git on macOS; vrg-git, vrg-commit and the PR workflow run it on the host
  • Docker — the dev container engine
  • uv — Python package manager (install)
  • gh CLI — GitHub CLI, authenticated as you (gh auth login)
  • macOS or Linux (Bash)

Everything else — language runtimes, linters, test frameworks — lives inside the dev container. The vrg-* tools are installed on the host with uv tool install.

This list is the minimum to get started. On macOS, once vergil-tooling is installed (step 1), vrg-host status is the complete host-dependency check: it reports every tool Vergil needs on the host, including the Command Line Tools, git and the agent-VM tools, and flags anything missing or out of date.

docs.title: 1. Install vergil-tooling on the host
docs.text:
uv tool install --python 3.14 'vergil-tooling @ git+https://github.com/vergil-project/vergil-tooling@v2.1'

This installs all vrg-* console scripts into ~/.local/bin/. uv's official installer already puts that directory on PATH; with a Homebrew-installed uv, run uv tool update-shell once to add it.

which vrg-container-run    # should resolve to ~/.local/bin/vrg-container-run
vrg-container-run --help   # should print usage

On macOS, vrg-host then reports the health of every tool Vergil needs on the host (installed vs. latest, missing tools, health checks) and upgrades them:

vrg-host                   # read-only status report; exit 0 = all OK
vrg-host upgrade --all     # upgrade the tools vrg-host manages

See the vrg-host reference for the dependency list and for pinning a tool that a new release has broken.

On Linux, vergil-tooling is also published as a signed .deb/.rpm package (this is how Lima and cloud agent VMs get it). Follow the vergil-project/packages README to set up the apt or dnf repository. Check the downloaded signing key against the pinned primary fingerprint B3A1D804DC03AB036566A4E367861822166ECABE.

docs.title: 2. Create or adopt the repository
docs.text:
vrg-github-repo-init builds a managed repository that conforms from its first commit. Run it in a human shell: it uses your gh credentials for gh repo create and the GitHub settings, and it refuses to run under an agent identity.

A new repository. Run it from inside the directory named after the GitHub org (or any subdirectory of it), or name the clone's parent directory with --target-dir:

cd ~/dev/projects/<org>
vrg-github-repo-init <org>/<name>

The wizard prompts for the project description, repository type, primary language, branching model, versioning scheme, release model and the other vergil.toml values. Every prompt has a matching flag; --non-interactive runs with no prompts and fails loudly if a required flag is missing (see vrg-github-repo-init --help).

An existing repository. From the root of its clone, on a feature branch:

vrg-github-repo-init --adopt

Adopt overwrites every Vergil-managed file to its canonical state — vergil.toml, CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks/guard.sh, LICENSE, README.md, .gitignore, .github/dependabot.yml, the CI/CD workflows and the docs site config — and applies the GitHub settings, rulesets and labels. It asks for confirmation first. Values already in vergil.toml become the prompt defaults, and hand-written tables such as [package] or [container] are kept. Review the resulting commits and land them through a PR.

Either way, the repository ends up with:

Path What it is vergil.toml The repository profile and tooling config CLAUDE.md Agent guidance, including the canonical consumer section (worktree convention, shell command policy, validation) .claude/settings.json Wires the hook guard, enables the Vergil Claude Code plugin, and turns off Claude Code's AI co-author attribution .claude/hooks/guard.sh Hook-guard shim that blocks raw git/gh in agent sessions .gitignore The vergil-managed ignore block for your language, including .worktrees/ .github/dependabot.yml The canonical report-only Dependabot config: every entry has open-pull-requests-limit: 0, so Dependabot never opens a PR .github/workflows/ ci.yml, ops.yml (nightly config audit, branch sweep and Dependabot alert audit), epic-rollup.yml, and cd.yml when the repo publishes releases or docs

.claude/settings.json is generated from the packaged template claude_settings.json, with the plugin marketplace pinned to ref: "main". Its attribution block is what keeps Claude Code from adding an AI co-author trailer to commits and PRs; AI co-author attribution is not used (#3200):

"attribution": {
  "commit": "",
  "pr": ""
}

docs.title: 3. Verify
docs.text:
# Full validation, inside the dev container
vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate

# Config audit: vergil.toml, CLAUDE.md, .claude/, .gitignore, workflows,
# and the GitHub settings (exit 0 compliant, 1 drift, 2 could not complete)
vrg-github-repo-config audit

vrg-validate includes vrg-repo-profile, which checks vergil.toml. The hook guard fires on Claude Code Bash tool calls; to test it end to end, have Claude Code try a raw git commit in a session in the repository.

docs.text:

  • Identity Setup — the GitHub App identities that AI agents run as.
  • Git Workflow — branching, commit / PR / finalize cycle, two-layer enforcement, worktrees in practice.
  • Worktree convention spec — full rationale for the parallel-agent convention, failure modes, memory-path implications.

docs.title: Identity Setup
docs.text:
This guide walks through creating and configuring the GitHub App identities that VERGIL tooling uses for AI agents. Each contributor registers two GitHub Apps — one per agent role — under their personal account.

For the model these identities serve, see Identity Architecture. For how credentials are selected at runtime, see Credential Management. For repo-level onboarding (installing tools, hooks, CI), see Consuming Repo Setup.

docs.title: The two agent identities
docs.text:
Every AI agent is represented by a GitHub App whose name encodes the human who owns it and the agent's role: <username>-vergil-<role>. The App's installation is the agent's only credential, and the agent's capability is bounded entirely by the App's declared permission shape. There are no agent user accounts and no collaborator grants — the bot identity (<username>-vergil-<role>[bot]) that appears on commits and PRs comes from the App itself.

App Role Shape <username>-vergil-user Daily development (Driver) write code, read PRs <username>-vergil-audit PR review (Officials) read code, write PRs (inverted)

A third role — <username>-vergil-admin — is a reserved slot and is not provisioned. Do not create it.

The two Apps have deliberately inverted permission shapes. The user App can write code but only read PRs; the audit App can only read code but can write (review/comment on) PRs. This split is the core of the permission model — set the permissions exactly as documented.

docs.title: Why GitHub Apps
docs.text:
• No shadow-ban risk — Apps are first-class GitHub citizens
  • Short-lived tokens — 1-hour installation tokens, minted on demand, instead of long-lived PATs
  • Multi-org from one identity — install the same App on every org you manage
  • Server-side merge control — branch protection recognizes the App identity
  • Dynamic token resolution — the tooling acquires tokens per-org at runtime from the App's private key; no static token configuration

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A GitHub account that is an owner of the organizations where the agents will operate
  • A ~/.config/vergil/keys/ directory on your development machine

docs.title: Step 1.1 — Register the App
docs.text:
1. Go to github.com → your profile icon → Settings → Developer settings (bottom of the left sidebar) → GitHub Apps → New GitHub App.

  2. Fill in the registration form:

Field Value GitHub App name <username>-vergil-user Description AI agent identity (user / Driver role) owned by <username>. Daily development agent running in an isolated VM; authenticates via installation tokens for commits, pushes, and issues. Homepage URL your GitHub profile URL Webhook uncheck "Active" (no webhook needed)
  1. Under Repository permissions, set exactly these and leave everything else at No access:
Permission Access Contents Read and write Issues Read and write Pull requests Read-only Actions Read-only Checks Read-only Commit statuses Read-only Repository security advisories Read and write Metadata Read-only (mandatory; usually auto-selected) Workflows No access — leave untouched

!!! note "Repository security advisories is for security records" vrg-security-record creates, reads and updates the private draft advisories in each org's .github that hold security findings, and vrg-intake-route and vrg-queue planning read and retarget them (see Security Records). Each org's automation App (<org>-automation, see Identity Architecture) needs the same Read and write grant for the scheduled sweep, which closes and reopens advisories. The audit App does not get it: it is not in use today, and the decision is deferred until the audit identity is revived. Adding this permission to an existing App changes its permission set, so each installation must accept the change (the org or account owner approves it from the installation's settings page) before the new grant takes effect.

!!! note "Actions, Checks and Commit statuses are for reading CI" vrg-pr-await and pr-watch read a PR's check runs, commit statuses and workflow runs. On a private repo, an App without these grants gets HTTP 403 "Resource not accessible by integration". On a public repo the reads succeed anyway, which hides a missing grant. All three are read-only and grant no ability to trigger, re-run or change CI.

!!! warning "Pull requests is Read-only on purpose" The user agent does not open or comment on PRs. Its workflow ends at "ready for PR"; the human submits the PR from the host. pull_requests: read is the server-side hard gate that makes gh pr create fail for this identity even if the soft gate is bypassed. The agent still needs read to see PR and CI status.

!!! warning "Never grant Workflows" No agent identity may push changes under .github/workflows/. Leaving Workflows at No access is what makes GitHub reject such a push server-side. This is deliberate containment, not an oversight.

  1. Under Where can this GitHub App be installed?, select Any account — this lets you install it on your organizations, not just your personal account.

!!! warning "Cannot change this easily later" If you select "Only on this account", the App can only be installed on your personal account. To change it afterward: App settings → Advanced → Danger zone → Make public. Once public and installed elsewhere, this cannot be reverted.

  1. Click Create GitHub App. You land on the App's settings page, which shows the App ID and Client ID near the top.

docs.title: Step 1.2 — Record the App ID and Client ID
docs.text:
On the General settings page, record both identifiers:

  • App ID — a short number (e.g., 3940487).
  • Client ID — a string beginning with Iv (e.g., Iv23li...).

The tooling authenticates using the App ID today (it becomes the JWT iss claim via VRG_APP_ID). GitHub is gradually migrating GitHub App authentication from the numeric App ID toward the Client ID; that migration is only partially rolled out, so the App ID is still what the tooling uses. Record both now so the eventual switch to Client ID needs no return trip to the GitHub UI.

You do not need installation IDs — the tooling resolves those dynamically at runtime.

docs.title: Step 1.3 — Generate a private key
docs.text:
1. Ensure the keys directory exists:
mkdir -p ~/.config/vergil/keys

  1. On the App settings page, scroll to Private keys → click Generate a private key. Your browser downloads a .pem file.

  2. Move it into the keys directory, keeping the original filename:

mv ~/Downloads/<username>-vergil-user.<YYYY-MM-DD>.private-key.pem \
   ~/.config/vergil/keys/

GitHub names the file <app-name>.<YYYY-MM-DD>.private-key.pem (for example, wphillipmoore-vergil-user.2026-06-02.private-key.pem). Keep the name — the date is useful metadata for key rotation.

No install prompt is expected here

On a freshly created App you may see no "install this App" banner after generating the key. Installation is a separate, deliberate step (next) — do not wait for a prompt.

docs.title: Step 1.4 — Install the App
docs.text:
1. On the App's settings page, left sidebar → Install App.
  2. GitHub lists every account you can install on — your personal account and each organization you own.
  3. Click Install next to each account that owns repositories this agent will operate on. A single App installed on multiple accounts is normal and expected — it works across every org you manage. Without an installation on a given account, the tooling cannot mint a token for that account's repos.
  4. Choose repository access:
  5. All repositories — covers every repo in that account, including ones added later (low friction).
  6. Only select repositories — tighter; you return here to add more.
  7. Click Install. You land on the installation's configuration page (its URL contains an installation ID, which you do not need to record — the tooling resolves it at runtime).

The user App is now fully provisioned. Configuring identities.toml happens in Part 3, after the audit App exists.

docs.title: Part 2 — The audit App (<username>-vergil-audit)
docs.text: The audit App follows the same flow as the user App, with two differences: the name, and an inverted permission shape (it reads code and writes PRs, the mirror of the user App).

docs.title: Step 2.1 — Register the App
docs.text:
Follow Step 1.1, changing:

  • GitHub App name: <username>-vergil-audit
  • Description: AI agent identity (audit / Officials role) owned by <username>. PR-review agent running in an isolated VM; reads code and writes PR reviews/comments via installation tokens.
  • Repository permissions — note these are inverted from the user App:
Permission Access Contents Read-only Issues Read-only Pull requests Read and write Actions Read-only Checks Read-only Commit statuses Read-only Repository security advisories No access (deferred) Metadata Read-only (mandatory) Workflows No access — leave untouched

Actions, Checks and Commit statuses are the same read-only CI grants as the user App (see the note in Step 1.1); they are not inverted. Repository security advisories stays at No access: the audit identity is not in use today, and whether it needs the grant is decided when it is revived.

Everything else (Webhook unchecked, Any account, the "Make public" warning) is identical to Step 1.1.

docs.title: Step 2.2 — Record the App ID and Client ID
docs.text: Same as Step 1.2 — record both for the audit App.

docs.title: Step 2.3 — Generate a private key
docs.text: Same as Step 1.3. The downloaded file is named <username>-vergil-audit.<YYYY-MM-DD>.private-key.pem; move it into ~/.config/vergil/keys/.

docs.title: Step 2.4 — Install the App
docs.text: Same as Step 1.4 — install the audit App on the same set of accounts as the user App.

docs.title: Part 3 — Configure identities.toml
docs.text:
~/.config/vergil/identities.toml is the host-side configuration that tells VM provisioning which App credentials to inject into each agent VM. The dual-identity model uses one stanza per role.

default_identity = "vergil-user"
vergil = "v2.0"        # vergil-tooling version for the human host
vergil-vm = "v2.1"     # VM template tag (from the vergil-vm repo)

[identities.vergil-user]
vm_instance = "vergil-user"
auth_type = "app"
app_id = <user-app-id>
private_key_path = "~/.config/vergil/keys/<username>-vergil-user.<date>.private-key.pem"
vergil = "v2.1"        # pin this VM's vergil-tooling to 2.1 (set once 2.1 is released)
# client_id = "Iv..."  # recorded for the App ID → Client ID migration; not yet read by the tooling

[identities.vergil-audit]
vm_instance = "vergil-audit"
auth_type = "app"
app_id = <audit-app-id>
private_key_path = "~/.config/vergil/keys/<username>-vergil-audit.<date>.private-key.pem"
vergil = "v2.1"
# client_id = "Iv..."

Notes:

  • app_id is the identifier the tooling uses today (it becomes VRG_APP_ID inside the VM). The Client ID is recorded only as a comment until the App ID → Client ID migration lands in the tooling.
  • private_key_path is relative to your home directory when it starts with ~, otherwise absolute.
  • Per-identity vergil pin. Setting vergil = "v2.1" on the agent identities lets the agent VMs run new tooling while the human host stays on a stable v2.0 (the top-level default). Only set the v2.1 pin once 2.1 has been released.
  • VRG_IDENTITY_MODE (user / audit) is derived from the identity's stanza name at provisioning time — a name containing user provisions as user mode, audit as audit mode; a name containing neither (or both) fails provisioning. The mode is written to ~/.config/vergil/identity-mode in the VM and exported from the shell profile. It selects the identity-aware allowlists at runtime; it is a soft-gate ergonomic, not the security boundary (the App credential is).
  • Query identity with vrg-whoami, never a single environment variable. VRG_IDENTITY_MODE is only the first of five fallback steps (env var → mode file → app.pem → VRG_APP_ID → human); an unset value means "fall through," not "default to human." Ask the authoritative resolver instead: vrg-whoami prints the resolved role, vrg-whoami --mode emits a single token for scripting (export VRG_IDENTITY_MODE="$(vrg-whoami --mode)"), and vrg-whoami --explain reports which signal resolved and warns when signals disagree.

docs.title: Verification checklist
docs.text:
After both Apps are registered, installed, and configured:

  • [ ] Two private key files exist in ~/.config/vergil/keys/ (one per App), with their generation dates in the filenames
  • [ ] identities.toml has a vergil-user and a vergil-audit stanza, each with the correct App ID and key path
  • [ ] Each App shows the correct inverted repository permissions (user: contents/issues write, PRs read; audit: contents/issues read, PRs write; both hold Actions, Checks and Commit statuses read-only; neither holds Workflows)
  • [ ] The user App holds Repository security advisories: Read and write, the audit App does not, and every installation has accepted the change
  • [ ] Each org's automation App (<org>-automation) holds Repository security advisories: Read and write, and its installation has accepted the change
  • [ ] Both Apps are installed on every account that owns repos the agents will operate on
  • [ ] The reserved <username>-vergil-admin App was not created

Full end-to-end verification requires the agent VMs to be provisioned (vergil-vm) and vergil-tooling 2.1 to be released and pinned.

docs.text:

  • Credential Management — how installation tokens are minted and selected at runtime
