docs.title: Agent VM .claude Share Set
docs.text:
This guide explains which parts of the host's ~/.claude directory are shared into agent VMs, how conversation resume survives a VM rebuild, and why plugins and the session roster are deliberately kept VM-local. The wiring lives in src/vergil_tooling/lib/lima.py (create_vm, link_claude_dirs, copy_claude_config); the vergil-vm template only declares the static projects mount.

The share set below describes local (Lima) VMs. Cloud VMs cannot share the host store live, so they receive canonical agent data as a read-only cached projection instead — see Cloud VMs: read-only memory projection.

docs.title: The share set
docs.text:
Subdir How it is shared Writable Why projects/ virtiofs mount + symlink yes Durable conversation transcripts; must survive rebuilds. skills/ virtiofs mount + symlink no Read-only reference. sessions/ not shared (VM-local) n/a Disposable per-VM roster; sharing breaks atomic writes (EXDEV). plugins/ not shared (VM-local) n/a Installed/refreshed in-VM from GitHub marketplaces.

copy_claude_config additionally copies CLAUDE.md and settings.json into each VM on create and on every start.

docs.title: Why resume survives a rebuild
docs.text: Conversation transcripts are written as append-only *.jsonl files under ~/.claude/projects/<slug>/. That directory is a symlink onto the path-preserved host mount, so the transcripts live on the host and are untouched when a VM is destroyed and recreated. Resuming a conversation reads those transcripts — not the sessions/ roster — so a rebuild never loses history.

docs.title: Why sessions/ is VM-local
docs.text:
~/.claude/sessions/ holds a small roster of pid -> session files that Claude writes atomically: it writes a temp file in the VM-local tmpdir and then rename()s it onto the target. Renaming across filesystems (VM-local ext4 to the virtiofs host mount) fails with EXDEV, so the write would silently fail and no roster file would ever appear. The roster is also per-machine (pids only mean anything on the owning host), so there is no value in sharing it. Session detection reads each VM's local roster in-guest over limactl shell. See vergil-tooling #1301 and vergil-vm #73.

A host ~/.claude/sessions mount used to exist (mounts[3]) but the VM never read it once the roster was made VM-local; it was removed as dead weight (#1603).

docs.title: Why plugins are VM-local, not shared
docs.text: Plugins are declared in the host settings.json (enabledPlugins and extraKnownMarketplaces), which is copied into each VM. The marketplaces are GitHub repositories, so each VM installs the enabled plugins itself on first launch and keeps them current with an in-VM refresh — the same model used for vergil-tooling. The host's materialized ~/.claude/plugins checkout is never shared: doing so would cross the macOS/Linux boundary (fragile if any plugin ships a binary) and hit the same EXDEV write problem as the roster. Instead, update_plugins refreshes the marketplaces (claude plugin marketplace update) and then updates each enabled plugin to its latest version with the plugin's own scope (claude plugin update <id> --scope <user|project> — there is no bulk-update form), all inside the VM. It is driven by vrg-vm update and a warn-mode stage on VM start/rebuild.

docs.title: Cloud VMs: read-only memory projection
docs.text:
The share set above works because local (Lima) VMs path-preserve the project mount and symlink ~/.claude/{projects,skills} onto the host's live directories, so a memory write in a local-VM session flows straight through to the durable host disk. Cloud VMs — off-platform x86 boxes backed by the ephemeral /vergil data disk — cannot do that. Their disk is nuked and rebuilt freely, and the checkout lives at a different path, so a memory write there would either be lost on the next rebuild or land under a slug no other environment reads. The corrosive part is that the loss is silent: the harness advertises the memory directory as persistent, an agent writes memory believing it durable, and the write quietly evaporates.

To keep the physical host the single source of truth, a cloud VM receives canonical agent data — the per-repo memory/ subtree and the global CLAUDE.md — as a read-only cached projection that never flows back automatically. See epic vergil-project/.github#156 and its spec for the full rationale, trust model, and failure modes.

docs.title: The three platforms
docs.text:
A single platform-awareness signal distinguishes three states along two axes — sandbox (in a VM) vs. host (not a VM), and cloud vs. local:

Platform Sandbox? Credentials Canonical store physical-host no human live and writable (source of truth) local-vm yes agent (GitHub App) shared live via path-preserved mounts (durable) cloud-vm yes agent (GitHub App) read-only copy on ephemeral disk

physical-host names the property that matters — physical, not a VM — not the operating system; it is macOS today only because that is the hardware in use. The read-only memory control activates only on cloud-vm: local-vm writes already reach the live host store, and physical-host is the store.

docs.title: The platform resolver (vrg-whoami --platform)
docs.text:
vrg-whoami --platform reports the platform as a single token, parallel to the existing --mode; vrg-whoami --explain reports the resolving signal and warns on disagreement. The resolver is empirical — it derives the platform from heuristics (a /vergil mount ⇒ in a VM; a reachable cloud metadata endpoint ⇒ cloud; host OS and resolved identity as corroboration), with no written marker file.

It fails closed for the memory control: if a VM signal is present but the box cannot be positively confirmed as local-vm, it is treated as cloud-vm (locked), never as physical-host. Fail-open — silently deciding "host" and re-enabling futile writes — is the exact failure this model exists to kill, and is prohibited.

docs.title: Read-only projection, refreshed at session start
docs.text:
Projection is coupled to vrg-vm cloud-session start, not build: a cloud VM is not used until a session opens, so the first session on a freshly built box performs the initial projection and every subsequent session refreshes it. Before opening the session, vrg-vm:

  1. aligns the guest working directory to the host project path (via a symlink onto the /vergil checkout) so Claude derives the same memory slug as the host and finds the projected memory;
  2. copies that repo's memory/ + MEMORY.md and the global CLAUDE.md from the host over the established transport idiom (the same cat > <file> mechanism copy_claude_config uses — there is no rsync over the transport);
  3. re-applies surgical read-only permissions — locking memory/, MEMORY.md, and CLAUDE.md while leaving the session-transcript .jsonl files writable (a blanket chmod of projects/<slug>/ would break session logging);
  4. verifies that the host path resolves in the guest and the slug memory directory is non-empty, failing loudly otherwise — a broken indirection would otherwise degrade silently to empty memory.

Steps 2–4 run only when the invocation names a session (--label, --resume, --fresh) or overrides the command (-- bash). A bare vrg-vm session <workspace> only lists the workspace's sessions and exits, so it skips the projection; the reconnect that names a session performs it.

The read-only permissions are the hard backstop: a write attempt in the cloud fails with EACCES — loudly, so a futile write can no longer succeed-then-vanish.

docs.title: The policy clause (soft control)
docs.text: The hard read-only permissions are paired with a soft control: a condition-gated clause in the canonical ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md that stops an agent from attempting a cloud memory write in the first place. Its substance: when vrg-whoami --platform reports cloud-vm, memory and copied config are a read-only cache; never write memory — the write would fail (EACCES) and would be futile anyway — and when memory needs to change, file it via /vergil:intake-capture for implementation on the host. Because that file is the developer's personal, global config, the clause is authored once on the host and rides the copied file into every environment; its condition is simply almost never true outside cloud-vm. Keeping the clause part of the canonical file also keeps CLAUDE.md byte-identical across environments, so it stays lockable.

docs.title: Issue-driven writeback
docs.text:
Canonical data never flows back automatically. When a cloud session determines that memory or config must change, it files an issue through the existing /vergil:intake-capture flow, producing an intake issue under the org's intake epic in .github. The change is later implemented on the physical host against the live store and re-projected on the next cloud session or rebuild. Given how infrequently this data changes, this issue-driven, human-executed writeback is sufficient — no automated two-way sync.

See also: Identity Architecture.

docs.title: CI Architecture
docs.text: This guide explains the continuous integration model used by every Vergil-managed repository, and how a repository gets it.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Overview
  • Tier 1: Local pre-commit
  • Tier 2: PR CI
  • Architecture
  • Implementation guide
  • CI gates
  • Dev container images

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Testing is split into two tiers with increasing scope, cost, and feedback latency:

Tier Trigger Time Security 1 Manual (before commit) Seconds to minutes No 2 Pull request Minutes Yes
  • Tier 1: Single version, full local validation, dockerized
  • Tier 2: Full version matrix, all checks, security uploads

The goal is fast local feedback for the developer and comprehensive gated checks on the PR itself. Tier 1 is a discipline, not a gate: vrg-commit checks the branch and commit context but does not run validation, so run Tier 1 yourself before each commit. If you do, the PR should already be green when it opens.

Historical: three-tier CI

Earlier versions of this guide documented a third tier — push-CI — as a thin workflow_call wrapper that ran a subset of checks on every push to a feature branch. That tier was removed once vrg-validate matched the checks push-CI ran; the push-CI workflow added no coverage that PR-CI didn't already provide and created a concurrency-group deadlock with ci.yml. Integration-test coverage at push-time was deliberately dropped and is tracked separately as future work on local integration testing. See vergil-project/vergil-actions#176 for the parity audit and removal rationale. Since epic vergil-project/.github#488 the repository's custom validator also runs in PR CI (as quality / custom), so every Tier 1 stage now has a PR-CI job. The "parity with PR-CI" framing is precise only for the single-interpreter checks Tier 1 runs — see the coverage-parity caveat under Tier 2: PR CI below for the one deliberate gap.

docs.title: Tier 1: Local pre-commit
docs.text:
Run in a dev container on the developer's machine. Docker is the only host prerequisite.

vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate

This is the single Tier 1 command. vrg-container-run starts one container and runs vrg-validate inside it, with the repository bind-mounted. The image is ghcr.io/vergil-project/<prefix>-<language>:<version>: the prefix is prod unless you pass --prefix dev, the language comes from [project].primary-language, and the version is the resolver's primary version: [ci].primary-version when it is set, otherwise the newest resolved version (see Version resolution). C++ and TypeScript carry a family in the image name instead (see Dev container images), and a repository with no language uses the base image. On top of that image, vrg-container-run builds a per-branch cached image with vergil-tooling installed. Set DOCKER_DEV_IMAGE to use a different image.

vrg-validate first runs the common checks: vrg-repo-profile, markdownlint, shellcheck, yamllint, hadolint, actionlint, and ansible-lint when the repository has Ansible content. It then runs the language's lint, typecheck, test and audit commands, and last the repository's custom validator when it has one. To run one stage, pass --check common, lint, typecheck, test, audit or custom. The Validation Matrix lists every check and where it runs.

A repository can change the in-container command with [validation].container-command in vergil.toml. vergil-tooling uses this to run its own unreleased code (uv run vrg-validate).

Python tests run in parallel by default

For Python repos the validation gate's test stage runs in parallel via pytest-xdist's work-stealing scheduler — the shared command appends -n <workers> --dist worksteal to the coverage-gate argv when pytest-xdist is installed in the project's test environment. This is the fleet-wide default and materially cuts test-stage wall-clock — roughly 3.2× on this repo's own suite (epic vergil-project/.github#333). The worker count defaults to auto and is tunable per validation context (ci, local-vm, …) with [test].workers and [test.<context>]. A repo with an order-dependent suite opts out with [test].parallel = false in its vergil.toml; see Test Config ([test]) for the knobs and how the flag is computed. Parallelism changes only how fast the suite runs — the --cov-branch --cov-fail-under=100 gate is present in every computed command, serial or parallel, and measures the identical set.

Two adjacent levers were evaluated for this epic and dropped: the sys.monitoring coverage backend (COVERAGE_CORE=sysmon) is inert under --cov-branch — coverage.py silently falls back to the C tracer — and --import-mode=importlib gave no measured speedup and was not fleet-safe. Neither ships; parallelism is the one universal win. See epics/333-python-test-perf/evidence/baseline.md for the measured evidence.

docs.title: Tier 2: PR CI
docs.text:
Triggers on pull_request events. Runs the full validation suite.

What runs (each item is one job in ci.yml, calling one vergil-actions reusable workflow):

  • audit (ci-audit.yml): dependency audit across the full version matrix, for languages that have an audit command
  • quality (ci-quality.yml): the common checks once (vrg-validate --check common), the repository's custom validator once (vrg-validate --check custom, as quality / custom), then lint and typecheck across the full version matrix. The custom job's transcript is quality-custom.log, and quality / evidence needs the job, so a failing custom validator fails that gate
  • security (ci-security.yml): CodeQL, Trivy and Semgrep
  • test (ci-test.yml): the language's test command across the full version matrix
  • version (ci-version-bump.yml): fails when the PR's version equals the version on main. It is a no-op before the first release, and it passes when [project].release-model is none
  • docs (ci-docs.yml): builds the docs site, only in repos with [publish].docs enabled
  • package: binary package build and install-test (ci-package.yml, only in repos whose vergil.toml has [package]). Feature PRs run the reduced tier: every build cell, but one install-test cell per format (the oldest selected release, amd64 first). Release PRs (release/* into main) and non-PR events run the full matrix. See Tiers: full and reduced.

The workflow file is .github/workflows/ci.yml. It runs on pull_request and is also exposed through workflow_call (see Thin-caller pattern).

Local validate is not full coverage parity

Tier 1 runs one dev container on a single Python interpreter (currently 3.15, the newest window version), so its --cov-fail-under=100 gate proves 100% coverage on that one interpreter only. PR-CI re-runs the test-and-coverage gate independently in a separate container per resolved matrix version (currently 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 and 3.15: this repo is a library with no [ci].versions pin, so it tests the whole version window). Because branch coverage (--cov-branch) can legitimately differ across CPython versions — a branch reachable on one version may be dead on another, or a version-guarded code path may only execute on some interpreters — code that measures 100% locally can still fall below 100% on a 3.12, 3.13 or 3.14 leg and fail CI. The default local validate covers a single interpreter, trading the matrix away for speed. For Python, vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate --all-versions closes the gap on demand: inside the same one container it runs the gate on every resolved version, each on a uv-managed interpreter (see All versions). For other languages the multi-version matrix stays a PR-CI-only gate.

docs.title: Thin-caller pattern
docs.text:
A consuming repo's ci.yml is a thin caller: each job simply uses: a vergil-actions reusable workflow (ci-audit, ci-quality, ci-security, ci-test, ci-version-bump, ci-docs, ci-package) pinned to the repo's vergil series tag (for example @v2.1; vrg-github-repo-init uses the vX.Y series of the installed vergil-tooling). Apart from the scope inputs below, it passes only language: and container-suffix:, and ci-docs and ci-package take no inputs. It does not pass a version matrix or a container tag — the reusable workflows run vrg-ci-resolve against the repo's vergil.toml at run time and take both the matrix and the primary-version container from it (epics vergil-project/.github#338 and vergil-project/.github#407). A window change or a [ci].versions change therefore takes effect with no edit to ci.yml.

ci.yml also declares workflow_call with one boolean input, run-security, defaulting to true. On a pull_request run the input is empty, so the generated ci.yml compares it with != 'false' and it stays on. run-security is forwarded to ci-security.yml. The security job passes no container-suffix:, because ci-security.yml ignores it. The generated ci.yml no longer declares or forwards run-release: the version gate in ci-version-bump.yml follows [project].release-model instead.

docs.title: Shared security workflow
docs.text:
The security scanners live in the reusable workflow vergil-project/vergil-actions/.github/workflows/ci-security.yml. It runs three scanner jobs and one aggregate. Because the caller's job is named security, the checks report as:

  • security / codeql
  • security / trivy
  • security / semgrep
  • security / evidence

vergil-tooling's own ci.yml calls it like this:

security:
  uses: vergil-project/vergil-actions/.github/workflows/ci-security.yml@v2.1
  permissions:
    contents: read
    security-events: write
    actions: read
  with:
    language: python
    run-security: ${{ inputs.run-security != 'false' }}
    container-suffix: python

CodeQL is skipped when run-codeql is false (set for languages CodeQL does not support) or when upload-sarif is false (set for private repositories without GitHub Advanced Security). container-suffix is a deprecated no-op here, and the old standards-compliance job is gone: PR issue linkage is now checked by vrg-submit-pr when it builds the PR body.

Semgrep rulesets

vrg-semgrep-scan maps the language to a registry ruleset: python, java and rust map to p/<language>, and go maps to p/golang. It adds p/dockerfile when the repository has Dockerfiles and p/github-actions when it has workflows. ci-security.yml adds p/c for cpp and p/typescript for typescript.

docs.title: Fleet-excluded semgrep rules
docs.text:
The semgrep scanner (vrg-semgrep-scan, backed by src/vergil_tooling/lib/semgrep.py) always excludes a small set of fleet-default rules — DEFAULT_EXCLUDED_RULES — via semgrep's --exclude-rule. Callers can add further exclusions with the repeatable --exclude-rule <RULE_ID> flag; those are added on top of the fleet defaults, never in place of them.

The one fleet default today is github-actions-mutable-action-tag, which flags every uses: …@vN action reference. It is exempted fleet-wide pending backlog vergil-project/.github#194 (pin third-party action SHAs once pin-advancement tooling exists). Our own vergil-project/vergil-actions@v2.1 references are a permanent exception — they are our release line, not a mutable third-party tag. Every other semgrep rule stays enforced.

docs.title: Suppressing a reviewed finding in source
docs.text:
The SARIF gate (vrg-sarif-evaluate, and the vrg-semgrep-scan / vrg-trivy-scan wrappers, all backed by src/vergil_tooling/lib/sarif.py) honors SARIF result suppressions. A result does not fail the gate when its suppressions array holds an entry with:

  • kind of inSource (an in-code comment) or external (an out-of-band record), and
  • status absent or accepted.

Every other case fails closed and still counts against the gate: a status of underReview or rejected, an unknown or missing kind, or an empty or malformed suppressions array.

Suppressed findings are reported, not hidden. They are listed in a separate "suppressed finding(s)" table in the job summary (rule, level, file, line, suppression kind, and justification). The scan wrappers also emit a suppressed_count step output next to finding_count.

GitHub code scanning does not apply the same rule: it raises an alert for every SARIF result, suppressed or not. So the SARIF that is uploaded to code scanning omits accepted-suppressed results, while the CI-evidence bundle keeps the full, unfiltered SARIF. The filtered copy comes from vrg-sarif-filter:

vrg-sarif-filter INPUT OUTPUT

It drops every result whose suppression is in effect by exactly the rule above (the same effective_suppression() logic as the gate), from every run and at any severity. Everything else is kept: the tool, rules, invocations, and every unsuppressed or fail-closed result. It prints vrg-sarif-filter: removed N suppressed result(s) from INPUT -> OUTPUT. INPUT and OUTPUT may be the same path, because the output is written atomically. Unreadable or invalid SARIF (bad JSON, or no runs list) is a hard error with exit code 1.

For semgrep, write the suppression as a nosemgrep comment that names the exact rule ID, and put the justification and a tracking reference in the same comment, after the rule ID:

    secrets: inherit  # nosemgrep: yaml.github-actions.security.secrets-inherit.secrets-inherit -- reusable workflow needs the release token; reviewed in #123

Semgrep also accepts the comment on the line above the finding:

# nosemgrep: python.lang.security.audit.subprocess-shell-true.subprocess-shell-true -- fixed command string, no user input; see #456
subprocess.call(CMD, shell=True)

Semgrep emits both forms in SARIF as "suppressions": [{"kind": "inSource"}]. It does not carry the comment text into SARIF, so the summary's justification column stays empty for semgrep. The justification lives in the code, where review sees it. Rules for writing a suppression:

  • Always name the rule ID. A bare # nosemgrep silences every rule on the line, including ones nobody reviewed.
  • Always give a reason and a tracking issue. An unexplained suppression is not a reviewed exception.
  • Treat suppressions as reviewable code. A suppression is visible in the diff and in the scan summary, so reviewers can challenge it like any other change.

Other analyzers are honored as long as their SARIF carries a suppressions entry. Trivy's .trivyignore works differently: it drops the finding before SARIF is written, so ignored findings never appear in the summary at all.

docs.title: CD: release-publishing secrets
docs.text:
The release-publishing workflow generated into a consuming repo's cd.yml (by repo_init) forwards explicit, least-privilege secrets to the reusable cd-release workflow per ecosystem — never a blanket secrets: inherit (epic vergil-project/.github#189). The map lives in _cd_release_secrets() (src/vergil_tooling/lib/repo_init.py) and mirrors exactly what each publisher reads:

Ecosystem Secrets forwarded python none — PyPI OIDC trusted publishing go none — no publish token rust CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN java CENTRAL_USERNAME, CENTRAL_TOKEN, GPG_PRIVATE_KEY, GPG_PASSPHRASE

A language that needs no secret (python, go, or any non-publishing language) gets no secrets: block at all, not secrets: inherit. References to our own vergil-actions@v2.1 reusable workflows are unaffected — they are trusted first-party refs.

Exception: repos with [package]. A repo whose vergil.toml has a [package] section MUST call cd-release with secrets: inherit, suppressed inline:

    secrets: inherit  # nosemgrep: yaml.github-actions.security.secrets-inherit.secrets-inherit

Its package-sign job reads PACKAGE_SIGNING_KEY and PACKAGE_SIGNING_PASSPHRASE from the caller's package-signing environment. Environment secrets reach a job in a cross-repo reusable workflow only through inherit: an explicit secrets map leaves package-sign with an empty key (proven by the probe in vergil-project/packages#6). The callee is first-party, so the blanket form is an accepted, reviewed exception. vrg-repo-init generates this caller for [package] repos (vergil-project/vergil-tooling#3144). See the CD section of the package config reference for the full caller.

docs.title: Version resolution
docs.text:
The matrix is not embedded in the workflow or passed as an input. The supported versions of each language live in one place: the version manifest in vergil-containers, which publishes them as docker/versions/window.json at every Vergil ref (the version window). The lifecycle job in vergil-containers adds versions to the window and drops them from it as they enter and leave support; consuming repos do not edit anything when the window moves.

One resolver (src/vergil_tooling/lib/versions/resolve.py) turns a repo's vergil.toml and the window into the versions it builds. It reads the window at the repo's [dependencies].vergil ref (for example v2.1), so a window change reaches the repo without a tooling release. The dev container, vrg-validate, the required-check computation and the CI setup step (through vrg-ci-resolve) all call it. The rules:

  • [project].repository-type = "library" resolves as a library and builds every window version. Every other type resolves as an app and builds one version, the newest in the window.
  • [ci].versions is an optional pin. Every pinned version must be in the window, and an app pin must name exactly one version; either violation is an error. C++ and TypeScript versions carry a family (clang-20, node-24), so those repos must pin.
  • The primary version is [ci].primary-version when it is set (it must name a resolved version), otherwise the newest resolved version.

Each matrixed reusable workflow (ci-audit, ci-quality, ci-test) fans out over the resolved versions. Single-container jobs (ci-security, ci-version-bump, ci-docs) run on the primary version. Nothing is hand-maintained in ci.yml, so the matrix cannot drift from the window. Set VRG_VERSION_WINDOW=<path> to resolve against a local window.json for deliberate offline work; a window that cannot be fetched is an error, never a silent default.

docs.title: Implementation guide
docs.text:
A repository does not write its CI by hand. vrg-github-repo-init generates it, for a new repository or for an existing one with --adopt:

  • ci.yml is rendered as the thin caller described above. Its jobs follow the language: audit only when the language has an audit command, test only when it has a test command or [ci].integration-tests is on, docs only when [publish].docs is on, version only when [project].release-model is not none, and package only when vergil.toml has [package].
  • The CI gates ruleset is applied to main and develop with the required checks listed in CI gates. Before it is applied, the tool checks that the generated ci.yml produces every required check and fails if it does not.

After that, vrg-github-repo-config keeps the repository in line: audit reports drift, diff shows it, and apply reconciles the GitHub side, including the ruleset. vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate is the local command. Nothing else needs to be added to the repository.

docs.title: CI gates
docs.text:
The CI gates ruleset requires these checks. The list is computed from vergil.toml:

Check Required when quality / evidence Always security / trivy, security / semgrep Always docs / docs [publish].docs is on audit / evidence The language has an audit command test / evidence The language has a unit test command version / version-bump [project].release-model is not none package / evidence vergil.toml has [package] security / codeql, CodeQL GHAS is available and CodeQL supports the language Trivy, Semgrep OSS GHAS is available test / integration / <version> [ci].integration-tests is on (one per resolved version)

GHAS (GitHub Advanced Security) is taken from [project].ghas when it is set. Otherwise it counts as available for any repository that is not private. The bare CodeQL, Trivy and Semgrep OSS checks come from GitHub code scanning, not from a workflow job. Without GHAS those checks never report, so they are not required.

docs.title: Every check that runs is a gate
docs.text:
There is no tier of checks that runs on a PR but does not block it. The required set above is pinned by a test so it cannot drift silently.

For the matrixed kinds — audit, quality, and unit tests — the required check is the stable, version-agnostic <kind> / evidence aggregate each reusable workflow emits (audit / evidence, quality / evidence, test / evidence), not the per-version legs (audit / dependencies / 3.12, quality / lint / 3.13, …). Each evidence job needs the whole version matrix, so a single required context covers every version. Because the required-check names no longer carry a version, a matrix change — including a reduction — merges through the same gate. This closes the old deadlock, where branch protection required a per-version leg that a reduced matrix could never produce, leaving the PR "expected, never reported" and permanently blocked with no --admin escape (epic vergil-project/.github#338). quality / evidence also aggregates the non-matrixed quality / common and quality / custom jobs: it needs common, custom, lint and typecheck and fails if any of them did not succeed. That holds in every repo, whatever its language, so quality / evidence is required everywhere and quality / common, which still runs, is not required on its own. A failing custom validator therefore blocks the merge even in a repo with no primary language. The other non-matrixed checks (the security scanners, the version-bump gate, docs / docs) keep their fixed, version-free names. A repo whose vergil.toml has a [package] section also requires package / evidence, the one stable gate ci-package.yml emits over its whole target matrix; repos without [package] neither call ci-package.yml nor require the gate.

vrg-github-repo-config audit hard-fails on required-set drift: if a repo's configured required checks diverge from the desired set, the audit fails rather than reporting a warning. vrg-release gates on that audit, so a repo whose required-check set has drifted cannot release until the set is reconciled.

docs.title: Dev container images
docs.text: Published to ghcr.io/vergil-project/<prefix>-<language>:<version> from the vergil-containers repository. The dev- images are built from its develop branch and the prod- images from main. vrg-container-run and the CI workflows use prod- by default.

docs.title: Available images
docs.text:
This page does not repeat the published versions of each image. The generated version table in the vergil-containers README is the single source of truth.

dev-python : Base: python:<v>-slim. Includes git, curl, uv.

dev-java : Base: eclipse-temurin:<v>-jdk. Includes git, curl.

dev-go : Base: golang:<v>. Includes golangci-lint, govulncheck, go-licenses, gocyclo.

dev-cpp-clang : Base: debian:trixie-slim + apt.llvm.org. Includes clang, clang-tidy, clang-format, lld, llvm (llvm-cov), the sanitizer runtime, CMake, Conan 2, cppcheck, and gcovr.

dev-cpp-gcc : Base: debian:trixie-slim. Includes g++, gcov, CMake, Conan 2, cppcheck, and gcovr.

dev-ts-node : Base: debian:trixie-slim + prebuilt Node from NodeSource (never built from source). Includes Node.js, npm, TypeScript (tsc), ESLint + typescript-eslint, Prettier, Vitest, @vitest/coverage-v8, and license-checker. The runtime family rides the ts-node image suffix and the Node major is the tag (node-24 → prod-ts-node:24); node-24 is the primary, node-22 the second (epic vergil-project/.github#284).

C++ is the one language with a compiler-family axis: it ships two image families (dev-cpp-clang / dev-cpp-gcc, and matching prod- images) so TYPECHECK and TEST run per compiler and per version. The family rides the [ci].versions tag prefix (clang-20, gcc-14), so a C++ repo must pin [ci].versions. Only a library can pin more than one entry; an app builds exactly one.

docs.title: Building locally
docs.text:
cd ../vergil-containers
docker/build.sh

This builds all images. Individual images can be built with:

docker/generate.sh python
docker build --build-arg PYTHON_VERSION=3.14 \
  -t dev-python:3.14 docker/python/

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text: Images are published automatically on push to develop (dev-) or main (prod-) in the vergil-containers repository: its cd.yml calls the reusable .github/workflows/cd-docker-publish.yml workflow.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
• Thin images — language runtime + package manager + git/curl
  • Project-managed dependencies — tools come from lockfiles at container startup (e.g., uv sync, go install)
  • No host requirements — Docker is the only prerequisite for local development

docs.title: Repo-specific system packages
docs.text:
The shared base images stay language-generic on purpose — a system dependency is treated as a property of the language, not the repo, which is what keeps the image cache sound. A repo that genuinely needs a Debian binary its language image does not carry (for example a repo whose render/e2e tests shell out to LilyPond) declares it once in vergil.toml, without touching the shared base image:

[container]
system-packages = ["lilypond"]

The full key reference — trust model, the names-only surface, cache-key behaviour, and the fail-closed error — lives in Container Config Reference → system-packages. Two things matter for the CI/container model here:

  • Two paths, one declaration. Locally the packages are baked into the per-branch cached dev image, so they are present for every check in that one image. In CI they are installed per run by a composite setup step (vergil-actions#807) on the base-image container, before the tests. The two paths agree on what is installed (the same names, from the same Debian sources) even though they differ on when — baked once locally vs installed per run in CI.
  • Test-runtime contract. In CI the install runs only on the jobs that execute the repo's tests, never on lint or typecheck — these binaries are needed at test time only. Locally the single cached image carries them for every check as a convenience of the one-image model, but that does not license depending on a system package during lint or typecheck. If a package has no install candidate for the build architecture, the build (local) and the CI step both fail closed, naming the package and the architecture — no silent skip.

docs.title: Repo-specific build steps
docs.text:
For a dependency that is not an apt package — a JS library a test driver consumes at runtime, say — a repo declares a build-command (with optional build-cache-files) instead of system-packages:

[container]
build-command = "npm install -g @coderline/alphatab"
build-cache-files = ["package-lock.json"]

The full key reference — the out-of-workspace contract, the NODE_PATH handling for baked npm libraries, the trust model, and the cache-key behaviour — lives in Container Config Reference → build-command. It follows the same two-paths, one-declaration shape as system-packages:

  • Two paths, one declaration. Locally the command is baked into the per-branch cached dev image, so its artifact is present for every check in that one image. In CI the command is run per job on the test jobs — the job obtains it with vrg-container-build-command --script and runs it against the base-image container before the tests. The two paths agree on what is provisioned (the same command string) even though they differ on when — baked once locally vs run per test job in CI.
  • Fail-closed. A non-zero exit from the command fails the build (local) and the CI step, rather than producing an image whose missing dependency only surfaces mysteriously inside a test.

docs.title: CI Evidence Convention
docs.text:
This guide is the contract for the CI evidence archival mechanism: the naming convention, file schemas, and bundle format that any release-publishing repo — or any future CI gate — conforms to. It is the authoritative reference for the ci-evidence-<gate> artifact, the evidence.json fragment, the evidence-producing gate set, and the manifest.json bundle index.

For the motivation, the determinism analysis, and the full architecture, see epic vergil-project/.github#140. This page documents the wire format only.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Overview
  • Producer side: the ci-evidence-<gate> artifact
  • The evidence.json fragment schema
  • The evidence-producing gate set
  • Producer prerequisite: real report files
  • The bundle tree
  • The manifest.json schema (v1.0)
  • Verification: how a downstream auditor checks the bundle
  • Deployment lifecycle

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
CI evidence archival makes each release's gate output durable, complete, and machine-verifiable. At publish time the release harvests every CI gate's full report, bundles it into a compressed, self-describing archive, cryptographically attests the archive to the pipeline and the exact released commit, and attaches it to the GitHub Release — where it lives permanently, independent of Actions retention.

The evidence step is an enforcing gate: a release does not publish without complete, attested evidence for every required gate. Incomplete or failed evidence hard-fails the release before anything is attached (see the deployment lifecycle).

The mechanism has two sides coupled only by a naming convention — no direct calls — which is what keeps the harvester language-agnostic and the whole mechanism fleet-wide:

  • Producer side (CI gates in vergil-actions). Each gate reusable workflow uploads its full report(s) as a workflow-run artifact named ci-evidence-<gate>, alongside a small evidence.json fragment.
  • Consumer side (publish-time harvest in vergil-tooling). A single language-agnostic command, vrg-ci-evidence, downloads every ci-evidence-* artifact, validates completeness, assembles the bundle tree plus a manifest.json index with per-file sha256, and produces v{version}-ci-evidence.tar.gz.

The only cross-repo coupling is the ci-evidence-* artifact name and the evidence.json shape. Everything else is derived. Adding a future gate requires no harvester change: it emits the convention and is picked up automatically.

Scope boundary

The evidence step lives inside cd-release, so it applies to — and only to — repos that publish releases through cd-release. Repos that do not cut package releases (vergil-project/.github, docs-only repos) never invoke it. "Fleet-wide" here means "every release-publishing repo," not literally every repository.

docs.title: Producer side: the ci-evidence-<gate> artifact
docs.text:
Each evidence-producing gate uploads exactly one workflow-run artifact:

  • Artifact name: ci-evidence-<gate> — for example ci-evidence-security, ci-evidence-test, ci-evidence-audit, ci-evidence-quality, ci-evidence-package.
  • Contents: the gate's full report files (SARIF, coverage XML, JUnit XML, audit/license JSON, SBOM, …), plus an evidence.json fragment at the artifact root describing what the gate ran and found.

docs.title: One uniform evidence source — always artifacts
docs.text:
Every gate — including the security scanners — uploads its report(s) as a ci-evidence-<gate> artifact unconditionally, decoupled from any code-scanning upload. Under GitHub Advanced Security, CodeQL still drops its SARIF as an artifact alongside its code-scanning upload; Trivy and Semgrep do the same regardless of GHAS availability.

The harvester therefore reads artifacts only and never touches the code-scanning API — one code path, no GHAS branching, one fewer external dependency that can fail. Severity metrics come from each gate's evidence.json fragment (computed from its own SARIF at gate time), never from a server API.

docs.title: The evidence.json fragment schema
docs.text:
The evidence.json fragment sits at the root of each ci-evidence-<gate> artifact. It is the gate's self-description:

{
  "gate": "security",
  "tools": [{ "name": "codeql", "version": "..." }],
  "metrics": { "findings_by_severity": { "critical": 0, "high": 0 } },
  "files": ["python.sarif", "trivy-results.sarif", "semgrep-results.sarif"]
}
Field Type Meaning gate string The gate name — matches the <gate> in the artifact name. tools array of objects Each tool that ran, with name and version. metrics object Gate-specific summary (e.g. findings_by_severity, coverage_pct, tests). files array of strings The report file names present in the artifact.

Current limitations (shipped state). The tools and metrics values above show the intended shape, not what every bundle carries today. Verified against the v2.1.195 bundle:

  • The security gate's tools array currently ships empty ([]) — the scanners run and emit their SARIF, but the fragment does not yet enumerate them. (The test, audit, and quality gates do populate tools.)
  • metrics currently ships empty ({}) for every gate; the findings_by_severity / coverage_pct / tests summaries are the target shape, not yet populated.

These are producer-side gaps, not schema changes: the fields exist and the consumer reads them; they populate as producers are updated.

If the fragment is absent, the harvester still bundles the raw files and records the gate's conclusion from the check-runs API — but for a required gate an absent fragment or an absent artifact counts against completeness (see the deployment lifecycle).

Completeness requires the report payload, not merely the artifact or the evidence.json envelope. A required gate whose artifact carries only an evidence.json and no report file fails completeness — the empty-payload guard (#2812) rejects an envelope with no attested report behind it. An empty report is not evidence, so it does not satisfy the gate.

docs.title: The evidence-producing gate set
docs.text:
The set of gates that MUST emit evidence is not a hand-maintained list. It is derived from the same source of truth that drives branch protection: lib/github_config.py:desired_ci_gates_ruleset() computes a repo's required status checks from its VergilConfig (language, resolved versions, GHAS availability, and whether a [package] section is present). The evidence layer consumes that same computation, so the gates that are enforced to merge and the gates that are required to have evidence are provably the same set, with no drift.

This is the load-bearing invariant: management of the required gates and collection of their auditing evidence come from common configuration code.

docs.title: Classification by check-name prefix
docs.text:
Required status checks are grouped into evidence gates by their check-name prefix:

Check name / prefix Evidence gate Evidence-producing? security / …, plus GHAS Trivy / Semgrep OSS / CodeQL security Yes test / … test Yes audit / … audit Yes quality / … (common, custom, lint, typecheck) quality Yes package / … (only with [package]) package Yes version / … — No (non-blocking) docs — No (low-signal)

The guiding principle: any gate that can block the build is evidence worth keeping. Quality (common checks, custom validator, lint and typecheck) sits alongside security, test, and audit as first-class evidence, and every repo requires the quality / evidence gate, whatever its language. A repo whose vergil.toml has a [package] section also requires the package / evidence gate (the ci-package.yml aggregate over its whole target matrix), so the harvest pulls ci-evidence-package for it; a repo without [package] never calls ci-package.yml and is never asked for it. version/ is a sanity check on version state, not substantive evidence, and docs is low-signal; the absence of either does not fail the release.

docs.title: Per-repo correctness for free
docs.text:
Because the set is derived, a repo with a different real profile — no GHAS (CodeQL not required), a non-Python stack, or a gate legitimately disabled — demands evidence for exactly the gates it actually gates on. It cannot spuriously fail for a gate it never ran. Adding a future required gate automatically pulls it into the evidence set via the shared config; the harvester never changes.

The config the set is derived from is always the release repo's own vergil.toml, read at the release PR's validated head through the GitHub contents API (Contents: read) — the same commit whose CI run is being evidenced. vrg-ci-evidence harvest (and bundle) never read the vergil.toml in the current directory, so the command gives the same result from any directory and can never judge one repo's checks against another repo's config. A vergil.toml that is absent or unparseable at that commit fails the harvest with an actionable error; there is no fallback.

docs.title: Producer prerequisite: real report files
docs.text:
The evidence layer only has value if the gates emit machine-readable report files with real data. A bundle whose test / audit / quality entries carry only an evidence.json envelope and no report is an empty report — and there is no point publishing empty reports.

Producers must therefore emit real report files at the workspace-root paths the producer composite globs for:

The test and audit report files and the quality lint and typecheck reports are emitted once per resolved version (<ver> ∈ 3.12 / 3.13 / 3.14 / 3.15 for this repo today). The quality transcripts and the security SARIF are not per-version:

Gate Required report file(s) test coverage-<ver>.xml, junit-<ver>.xml audit pip-audit-<ver>.json, licenses-<ver>.json quality quality-common.log, quality-custom.log, quality-ruff-<ver>.json, quality-mypy-<ver>.xml security python.sarif, trivy-results.sarif, semgrep-results.sarif

quality-common.log is the transcript of vrg-validate --check common and quality-custom.log the transcript of vrg-validate --check custom, each captured once per run by the quality / common and quality / custom jobs. Every repository emits both, so even a language-less repository's quality gate carries real reports. A repository with no custom validator still ships quality-custom.log, holding the one "no custom validator" line.

Producers emit these files today: the check registry runs pytest --cov … --cov-report=xml --junitxml=…, pip-audit / license checks write --output JSON, and ruff / mypy write their machine-readable reports — each per Python version. The empty-payload guard enforces the prerequisite at harvest time: no bundle is attached until its reports carry real data, so a gate that emitted only an evidence.json envelope hard-fails rather than shipping an empty report. (An earlier registry ran the checks pass/fail only — pytest with no --cov-report=xml / --junitxml, pip-audit with no --output — and persisted no report; that gap is closed.)

docs.title: The bundle tree
docs.text:
The harvester assembles a single compressed archive, v{version}-ci-evidence.tar.gz, designed to be consumed by a machine auditor — self-describing and verifiable:

v{version}-ci-evidence.tar.gz
└─ evidence/
   ├─ manifest.json          # top-level machine index (see below)
   ├─ checks.json            # raw check-runs snapshot (name, conclusion, timing, log URL)
   ├─ gates/
   │   ├─ security/          # python.sarif, trivy-results.sarif, semgrep-results.sarif, evidence.json
   │   ├─ test/              # coverage-<ver>.xml, junit-<ver>.xml (per Python version), evidence.json
   │   ├─ audit/             # pip-audit-<ver>.json, licenses-<ver>.json (per Python version), evidence.json
   │   ├─ quality/           # quality-common.log, quality-custom.log, quality-ruff-<ver>.json, quality-mypy-<ver>.xml (per Python version), evidence.json
   │   └─ sbom/              # sbom.cdx.json
   └─ README.md              # human orientation for the archive
  • manifest.json is the curated, per-gate machine index (schema below).
  • checks.json is the raw check-run snapshot — distinct from the manifest's curated view — capturing every check's name, conclusion, timing, and log URL.
  • gates/sbom/ is populated by copying the SBOM already built during publish (also a standalone Release asset) into the bundle at harvest time, so the archive stays fully self-contained.
  • README.md is a fixed human orientation for the archive.

A standalone copy of manifest.json is also attached as a small, separate Release asset, so a tool can read the summary without downloading the full tarball.

docs.title: The manifest.json schema (v1.0)
docs.text:
manifest.json is the top-level machine index. It records the release identity, the provenance anchor, and a per-gate summary with per-file sha256:

{
  "schema_version": "1.0",
  "repo": "vergil-project/vergil-tooling",
  "release": {
    "version": "2.1.129",
    "tag": "v2.1.129",
    "released_commit": "<main merge SHA>"
  },
  "provenance": {
    "release_pr": 2281,
    "validated_head_sha": "<PR head SHA>",
    "ci_run_urls": ["https://github.com/.../actions/runs/123"]
  },
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601, injected by CD>",
  "gates": [
    {
      "name": "security",
      "conclusion": "success",
      "tools": [{ "name": "codeql", "version": "..." }],
      "metrics": { "findings_by_severity": { "critical": 0, "high": 0 } },
      "files": [{ "path": "gates/security/python.sarif", "sha256": "..." }]
    },
    {
      "name": "test",
      "conclusion": "success",
      "metrics": { "coverage_pct": 100, "tests": 1423 },
      "files": [{ "path": "gates/test/coverage-3.14.xml", "sha256": "..." }]
    }
  ],
  "missing_gates": []
}
Field Meaning schema_version Manifest schema version. This document specifies "1.0". repo owner/name of the release-publishing repo. release The released version, git tag, and released_commit (the main merge SHA). provenance The evidence anchor: the release_pr, its validated_head_sha, and the ci_run_urls the evidence was harvested from. generated_at ISO-8601 timestamp, injected by the CD environment. gates Per-gate record: name, conclusion, tools, metrics, and files (each with path and sha256). missing_gates Names of required gates that produced no evidence — recorded as data, never silently dropped.

Current limitations (shipped state). As with the evidence.json fragment, the metrics and (for security) tools values shown are the intended shape. In the v2.1.195 bundle the manifest ships metrics: {} for every gate and an empty tools: [] for the security gate. The fields are present and read by auditors; they populate as producers are updated.

Two trust properties are load-bearing:

  1. Every file carries a sha256. An auditor can prove the archive is intact and unmodified.
  2. missing_gates is explicit. A required gate that produced no evidence is recorded as data, never silently dropped.

docs.title: Why the provenance anchor is the release PR, not the released commit
docs.text: develop → main promotion uses a merge commit, and the security/audit/test gates run on pull requests, not on pushes to main. The final main merge-commit SHA therefore has no gate check-runs anchored to it. The gates do run on the release PR, whose validated tree is identical to what lands on main. Evidence is thus anchored to provenance.validated_head_sha (the release PR head) and harvested at publish time while the PR's runs and artifacts are still fresh. released_commit records what shipped; validated_head_sha records what was validated — they name the same tree.

docs.title: Verification: how a downstream auditor checks the bundle
docs.text:
An auditor who pulls a release months later verifies the bundle in two steps:

1. Verify the attestation (chain of custody). After the bundle is assembled, the pipeline produces a build-provenance attestation over the bundle's digest (actions/attest-build-provenance), binding the archive to this repository's workflow and the released commit. Verify it with:

gh attestation verify v2.1.129-ci-evidence.tar.gz \
  --repo vergil-project/vergil-tooling

A successful verification turns "here is a tarball" into "here is a tarball cryptographically proven to be the genuine output of this pipeline for this commit." This is the chain-of-custody core of the mechanism.

2. Verify every file's integrity. Unpack the archive and confirm each file's sha256 matches its manifest.json entry:

tar -xzf v2.1.129-ci-evidence.tar.gz
cd evidence
# For each gate file listed in manifest.json:
sha256sum gates/security/python.sarif
# compare against manifest.json → gates[].files[].sha256

Every file listed in the manifest carries a sha256, so an automated auditor can confirm the archive is intact, then read gates[].conclusion and gates[].metrics to confirm what ran, with what result, against which commit — and that missing_gates is empty.

docs.title: Deployment lifecycle
docs.text:
The evidence step is a hard, enforcing gate today. evidence-enforce defaults to true (as of vergil-actions v2.1.27), so evidence-first ordering is in force: the step harvests, validates completeness, bundles, attests, and attaches — and substantive incompleteness or any failure is terminal. Incomplete or failed evidence hard-fails the release before publish; nothing is published without complete, attested evidence for every required gate.

The gate reached enforcing mode through a completed warning → enforcing lifecycle, now behind us:

  • Warning mode (historical, initial rollout). The step ran the full path — harvest → bundle → attest → attach — but on any failure it emitted a loud warning and let the release proceed with whatever evidence it had gathered. It was timeout-bounded and never aborted a release. This was always a temporary deployment state of a hard gate — not a permanent soft gate.
  • Enforcing mode (current state). After baking ~4 weeks in warning mode and proving reliable, the gate was promoted by a single, global, human-gated flag flip (evidence-enforce → true). That promotion is complete: the gate now enforces on every release.

A permanent soft/report-only gate was never on the table and remains rejected. For the full lifecycle history, the bake-in window, and the human-gated flip, see epic vergil-project/.github#140 (§9.2, §14.1).

This safety property is load-bearing on the all-hard-gates model: bundling everything onto a public Release asset is safe precisely because every gate is a hard gate, so a bundle by definition reflects a passing scan with no unremediated findings to expose. For why every check that matters is a hard, asserting gate — and there are no report-only/warning gates — see the all-hard-gates principle in the vergil-actions documentation.

docs.title: Consuming Repo Setup
docs.text: This is the full walkthrough for putting a repository under vergil-tooling. For the one-screen quickstart, see Getting Started. For how the workflow unfolds once you're set up, see Git Workflow.

docs.title: Mental model — what you're installing
docs.text:
Vergil-tooling is delivered through three coordinated surfaces:

Surface What it is How you consume it Host tools vrg-container-run, vrg-commit, vrg-submit-pr, vrg-github-repo-init and the other vrg-* CLI tools. uv tool install from the vergil-tooling git URL; scripts land in ~/.local/bin/. Dev container ghcr.io/vergil-project/prod-* images (dev-* with vrg-container-run --prefix dev) with the language runtimes and validators. Pulled by vrg-container-run, which builds a per-branch cached image with vergil-tooling installed; nothing to install manually. Claude Code plugin vergil-claude-plugin — hooks, skills, agents and slash commands that enforce the workflow at the Claude Code tool level. Declared in .claude/settings.json; Claude Code loads it on session start.

Every managed repository also carries files that are not installed as packages but checked in:

  • vergil.toml — the repository profile and tooling config.
  • Claude Code hook guard — a .claude/hooks/guard.sh shim, wired in .claude/settings.json as a PreToolUse hook.
  • GitHub workflows — a thin ci.yml that calls the reusable workflows in vergil-project/vergil-actions, plus ops.yml, epic-rollup.yml and, when the repo publishes, cd.yml.

vrg-github-repo-init generates all of them (Step 3). See Git Workflow → Two enforcement layers for how the hook guard and vrg-commit fit together.

docs.title: Step 1: Host prerequisites
docs.text:
Install on your host (macOS or Linux):

Docker — the container engine. Docker Desktop on macOS is fine; Docker Engine on Linux works too.

uv — Python package manager. Used to install vergil-tooling on the host and (inside the container) to manage Python dependencies. On macOS, install it with Homebrew (brew install uv), which is how vrg-host reads and upgrades it. On Linux, use the official installer.

gh — GitHub CLI, logged in as you (gh auth login). Your own credentials drive vrg-github-repo-init, vrg-submit-pr, vrg-finalize-pr and vrg-release. AI agents do not use gh auth; they run as GitHub Apps — see Identity Setup and Credential Management.

Git and Bash — standard on Linux. On macOS, install the Xcode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install; Homebrew needs them) and then Homebrew's git and bash (brew install git bash). Apple's /bin/bash is 3.2 and is never updated, and the Homebrew copies are what vrg-host tracks and upgrades.

You do not need to install language runtimes, linters, test frameworks, markdownlint, or shellcheck on the host. All of those live inside the container.

Once vergil-tooling is installed (Step 2), vrg-host on macOS checks these prerequisites — and the agent-VM tools vrg-vm needs — for you; see Keeping up to date.

docs.title: Step 2: Install vergil-tooling
docs.text:
uv tool install --python 3.14 'vergil-tooling @ git+https://github.com/vergil-project/vergil-tooling@v2.1'

This installs all vrg-* console scripts into ~/.local/bin/. uv's official installer already puts that directory on PATH; with a Homebrew-installed uv, run uv tool update-shell once to add it.

Verify:

which vrg-container-run    # should resolve to ~/.local/bin/vrg-container-run
vrg-container-run --help   # should print usage

Dev-tree override for vergil-tooling development

If you are developing vergil-tooling itself and want to test unreleased code on the host, use the single-.venv dev-tree override described in the vergil-tooling CLAUDE.md (uv sync --group dev, then prepend .venv/bin to PATH). A single .venv is safe because the dev container masks the host .venv with an anonymous volume, so host and container never clobber each other's environment. This does not apply to consuming repos.

docs.title: Step 3: Bootstrap with vrg-github-repo-init
docs.text:
vrg-github-repo-init is the entry point for every managed repo. It writes each managed file in its canonical form, so a repo it creates passes vrg-validate and the config audit from its first commit.

Run it in a human shell. It uses your gh credentials for gh repo create and the org-level settings, and it refuses to run under an agent identity.

docs.title: A new repository
docs.text:
cd ~/dev/projects/<org>        # or any subdirectory of the <org> directory
vrg-github-repo-init <org>/<name>

Managed repos live at <projects>/<org>/<name>, so the clone goes next to the org's other repos: the wizard walks up from the current directory to the first one named <org>. Pass --target-dir <parent> to name the clone's parent directory explicitly. The clone uses SSH (git@github.com:<org>/<name>.git).

The wizard runs ten steps, each committed as chore(init): step N - … so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped:

  1. Create the GitHub repository (--visibility, default public).
  2. Clone it.
  3. Generate vergil.toml from your answers (see Step 4).
  4. Scaffold VERSION, CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks/guard.sh, README.md, .gitignore and LICENSE.
  5. Scaffold the language skeleton, where the language has one.
  6. Generate the workflows under .github/workflows/ (see Step 6).
  7. Scaffold the MkDocs site under docs/site/ (when docs publishing is on).
  8. Create and push develop and main, and make develop the default branch.
  9. Apply the GitHub settings, rulesets and labels.
  10. Configure GitHub Pages (when docs publishing is on).

Every prompt has a matching flag (--description, --repository-type, --language, --branching-model, --versioning-scheme, --release-model, --versions, --license and others). --non-interactive runs with no prompts and fails loudly if a required flag is missing; run vrg-github-repo-init --help for the full list. The CLI Tools Overview covers the born-green language skeleton.

docs.title: An existing repository
docs.text:
From the root of the repo's clone, on a feature branch:

vrg-github-repo-init --adopt

Adopt is an idempotent "make it canonical" run. It overwrites every Vergil-managed file — vergil.toml, CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks/guard.sh, LICENSE, README.md, .gitignore, the CI/CD workflows and the docs site config — and applies the GitHub settings, rulesets and labels. It asks for confirmation first (--non-interactive accepts it). Values in an existing vergil.toml become the prompt defaults, and any table the wizard does not own ([package], [container], [validation], …) is kept verbatim.

Adopt commits its file changes to the branch you have checked out. Review them — especially README.md and LICENSE — and land them through a PR. Re-run adopt whenever you want to bring the managed files back to canonical, for example after adding a [package] table.

docs.title: Step 4: vergil.toml — the repository profile
docs.text:
vergil.toml at the repo root is the primary configuration surface for the tooling. vrg-github-repo-init writes this shape:

[project]
repository-type = "library"
versioning-scheme = "semver"
branching-model = "library-release"
release-model = "tagged-release"
primary-language = "python"

[ci]
integration-tests = false

[publish]
release = true
docs = true

[dependencies]
vergil = "v2.1"

The wizard writes no [ci].versions line unless you pass --versions (a comma-separated pin), so a new repo follows the version window.

Required keys and accepted values:

Key Values Notes [project].repository-type application, documentation, infrastructure, library, tooling Required. A library builds every version in the version window; every other type resolves as an app and builds one version, the newest in the window. [project].versioning-scheme application, library, none, semver Required. [project].branching-model application-promotion, docs-single-branch, library-release Required. Determines which branch prefixes vrg-commit allows. [project].release-model artifact-publishing, environment-promotion, none, tagged-release Required. [project].primary-language cpp, go, java, python, rust, typescript Optional. Omit it for a repo with no primary language; it selects the per-language checks, container image and .gitignore fragment. [ci].versions non-empty list of strings Optional pin. Omit it to follow the version window. Every pinned version must be in the window, and an app may pin only one version; either violation is an error. C++ and TypeScript repos must pin. [dependencies].vergil vX.Y Required. The vergil release line; new repos get the line of the vergil-tooling that created them.

[publish] (release, default false; docs, default true) and [ci].integration-tests (default false) are optional. Optional tables have their own references: [container], [test], [package], [dependency-update] and [vm].

vrg-repo-profile validates vergil.toml (required keys and enum values) and the README.md structure; vrg-validate runs it as part of its common checks. See the repo-profile reference.

docs.title: Step 5: Claude Code hook guard and settings
Hook guard
docs.text:
.claude/hooks/guard.sh blocks raw git and gh commands in Claude Code agent sessions. It delegates to vrg-hook-guard when vergil-tooling is installed and otherwise falls back to a jq-based hard deny. vrg-github-repo-init writes it, executable, from the packaged template hook_guard_shim.sh. No per-clone configuration is required.

All branch/context checks (detached HEAD, protected branches, branch prefix, issue number) live in vrg-commit itself. See the Claude Code Hook Guard reference.

docs.title: .claude/settings.json
docs.text:
vrg-github-repo-init writes .claude/settings.json from the packaged template claude_settings.json and pins the plugin marketplace to ref: "main", the plugin's single released channel. It has four parts:

Key Purpose permissions.allow Allows Bash(vrg-*), so the vrg-* tools run without a permission prompt. hooks.PreToolUse Runs ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/guard.sh on every Bash tool call. extraKnownMarketplaces / enabledPlugins Declares the vergil-marketplace marketplace (vergil-project/vergil-claude-plugin, ref: "main") and enables vergil@vergil-marketplace. attribution Turns off Claude Code's AI co-author trailer on commits and PRs.

AI co-author attribution is not used (#3200). The attribution block uses empty strings, which work on every Claude Code version:

"attribution": {
  "commit": "",
  "pr": ""
}

Commit the file. Any Claude Code session opened in the repo then loads the hook guard and the plugin. vrg-github-repo-config audit checks the marketplace entry, its ref, the enabled plugin and the attribution block against the template.

The plugin adds these hooks:

  • PreToolUse on Bash — blocks raw git commit, raw gh pr create, commits from the main tree once the worktree convention is adopted (on main/develop otherwise), heredoc syntax, bash associative arrays, host/container tool misrouting, auto-close linkage keywords, agent PR merges and GitHub Contents API writes.
  • PreToolUse on Write/Edit — blocks writes to the main worktree once the worktree convention is adopted, and limits the audit identity to writing its own artifacts.
  • PostToolUse on Bash — surfaces deprecation warnings in command output.

See the plugin's own Hooks reference for the details.

docs.title: Worktree convention
docs.text:
Every managed repo adopts the worktree convention so multiple Claude Code agents can work in parallel without colliding. The generated files already carry both halves:

  • .worktrees/ is in the base fragment of the managed .gitignore block (see Step 7). The plugin's worktree hooks activate on that line.
  • The CLAUDE.md consumer section includes "Parallel AI agent development", the local on-ramp to the canonical worktree convention spec.

The managed block already ignores your validation/build output

Validation and build artifacts (coverage reports, compiled output, cache dirs, temporary venvs) are part of the composed managed block in your .gitignore. Keeping them ignored matters: un-gitignored output dirties a worktree, and a merged worktree left dirty is one vrg-finalize-pr cannot auto-remove — it surfaces as needs-attention in vrg-worktree-status and requires the opt-in --clean-dirty (or a manual clean) to clear. Carrying the managed block means merged worktrees sweep automatically.

For how to use worktrees during development, see Git Workflow → Parallel work with worktrees.

docs.title: Step 6: CI workflow
docs.text:
vrg-github-repo-init generates .github/workflows/ci.yml as a thin caller of the reusable workflows in vergil-project/vergil-actions, pinned to the [dependencies].vergil line. It passes only language: and container-suffix:; the reusable workflows read the version matrix from vrg-ci-resolve themselves (see Version resolution). Depending on the profile, it calls ci-audit, ci-quality, ci-security, ci-docs, ci-test, ci-version-bump and ci-package. Step 9 of the wizard creates the CI-gates ruleset that requires the checks these jobs report, and refuses to apply one that requires a check ci.yml never produces.

Alongside it:

  • ops.yml — runs the config audit on a daily, per-repo staggered cron schedule (see Step 7).
  • epic-rollup.yml — on any issue close, closes the parent epic once all of its tasks are closed.
  • cd.yml — the release and docs publishing workflow, generated when [publish] enables either.

To regenerate them after a vergil.toml change, re-run vrg-github-repo-init --adopt. See the CI Architecture guide for the CI tiers.

docs.title: Optional: OS packages
docs.text:
To ship signed .deb/.rpm packages from releases:

  1. Add a [package] table to vergil.toml (see Package configuration).
  2. Re-run vrg-github-repo-init --adopt from the repo root. It keeps [package] (and any other hand-written table) and regenerates the workflows: ci.yml gains a package job calling ci-package.yml, and the cd.yml release job switches to secrets: inherit. The GitHub config step then makes package / evidence a required check.
  3. Create a package-signing environment, restricted to main, holding PACKAGE_SIGNING_KEY and PACKAGE_SIGNING_PASSPHRASE.
  4. Make sure the org's GitHub App can dispatch to <org>/packages, which indexes each released package.

docs.title: Optional: dependency-update hook
docs.text:
Every vrg-release ends by updating the repo's dependencies (see Dependency updates). The built-in updaters cover Python (uv.lock), vergil ecosystem refs, the packaged runtime, and container image tags. If the repo has other dependencies to keep current, such as binary tool versions or provider pins, add a hook to vergil.toml:

[dependency-update]
hook = "scripts/dev/update-deps.sh"

The hook runs in the dev container after the built-in updaters. It edits files but never commits, and it reports anything it holds back as JSON lines in $VRG_DEPS_REPORT. The full contract is in the dependency-update reference.

Dependency-update PRs carry the dependency-update label. The update creates the label the first time it needs it, but provisioning the full label set up front keeps the repo in line with the registry:

vrg-ensure-label --sync --repo <owner>/<repo>

docs.title: Step 7: Managed .gitignore block and config audit
docs.text:
Every managed repo owes two things to the fleet's self-policing config audit, and both are checked nightly:

  1. Your .gitignore must carry the vergil-managed block. The fleet's ignore vocabulary is composed — a language-agnostic base fragment plus the fragment for your repo's [project].primary-language — into a fenced managed block: a # >>> vergil-managed: base + <language> … begin marker, the composed pattern lines (editors, OS, secrets, Vergil internals, all build/validation output, and your language's artifacts), and a # <<< vergil-managed <<< end marker. The audit requires that block to be present and to match the composed block for your language exactly, with no managed pattern left loose outside the fence. A language with no fragment of its own — or a repo that declares none — gets the base-only block. Genuinely repo-local entries live outside the fence and are never touched; run vrg-gitignore-sync to write or refresh the block.

  2. Your repo must carry a scheduled ops.yml wired to the config audit. .github/workflows/ops.yml must call the reusable ops-github-config.yml workflow on a cron schedule. That scheduled job is what runs the audit each night.

Both are fatal in the nightly audit: any drift returns exit 1 and turns the scheduled ops.yml run red. vrg-github-repo-init writes both, so a new or adopted repo starts conforming.

You never bump a pin to receive fragment changes: every repo tracks the rolling vergil-tooling@vX.Y tag, so an updated fragment released under that line is picked up on the next vrg-gitignore-sync run — and the nightly audit flags the drift until you run it.

Repos also carry a canonical, report-only .github/dependabot.yml (epic vergil-project/.github#420): Dependabot alerts stay on, but every updates entry sets open-pull-requests-limit: 0, so Dependabot never opens a PR. The file is an exact match of the render for your [project].primary-language — no local additions. vrg-github-repo-init writes it, and vrg-dependabot-sync --write writes or refreshes it. vrg-validate rejects any dependabot.yml entry whose open-pull-requests-limit is missing (Dependabot then defaults to 5) or not 0, and the nightly audit flags a missing or non-canonical file until you run vrg-dependabot-sync --write.

The same nightly run also fails while the repo has any open Dependabot alert: its dependabot-audit job runs vrg-dependabot-audit, which exits 1 on an open alert and 2 when it cannot read the alerts. Fix the dependency or dismiss the alert on GitHub to clear it. See the Dependabot Alert Audit reference.

The audit also checks vergil.toml, CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks/guard.sh, the reusable-workflow pins and the GitHub settings. Check your repo locally before relying on the nightly run:

vrg-github-repo-config audit   # exit 0 compliant, 1 drift, 2 could-not-complete

See the GitHub Config Audit reference for the full check list and the managed-block propagation model.

docs.title: Step 8: Verify end-to-end
docs.text:
Once the repo is bootstrapped, sanity-check each layer:

# 1. Host tools — should print vrg-container-run help
vrg-container-run --help

# 2. Full validation inside the dev container, including
#    vrg-repo-profile against vergil.toml
vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate

# 3. Config audit — local files and GitHub settings
vrg-github-repo-config audit

# 4. Hook guard (requires a Claude Code session) — in a Claude
#    Code session in this repo, have Claude try to run a raw
#    `git commit`. The hook guard should block it.

If any step fails, check the corresponding section above, then re-run. Common causes: uv tool install not run, .claude/settings.json not committed to the branch your Claude Code session loaded, or a managed file edited by hand (re-run vrg-github-repo-init --adopt).

docs.title: Keeping up to date
docs.text:
After each vergil-tooling release, upgrade the host tools:

uv tool upgrade vergil-tooling

uv tool upgrade re-resolves the git reference, pulls the current tip of the rolling minor tag, and rebuilds the isolated tool venv. No need to repeat the full git URL.

On macOS, vrg-host covers vergil-tooling and the other host prerequisites together (uv, gh, Docker, and the vrg-vm tools such as Lima, gcloud and OpenTofu):

vrg-host                   # report drift, missing tools and failed health checks
vrg-host upgrade --all     # upgrade every auto-managed tool, respecting pins

vrg-host upgrade vergil-tooling runs the same uv tool upgrade. Docker Desktop and macOS itself are reported but never upgraded by vrg-host. When a new release of a host tool breaks your workflow, pin it with vrg-host pin rather than skipping upgrades — see the vrg-host reference.

vrg-container-run pulls the base dev image on every run and rebuilds its per-branch cached image when the base image, the language lockfile or vergil.toml changes, so there is nothing to refresh by hand. vrg-container-cache status shows the cache state for the current branch.

After a plugin release, refresh the Claude Code plugin from inside Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace update vergil-marketplace
/reload-plugins

See the plugin README's Update section for what each step does.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• vrg-container-run: command not found — uv tool install has not been run, or ~/.local/bin is not on PATH. Re-run the install command from Step 2 and confirm which vrg-container-run resolves.
  • vrg-github-repo-init refuses to run — it is human-credential only; run it in a human shell, not an agent session. For a new repo, run it from inside the <org> directory or pass --target-dir.
  • Plugin hooks don't fire — check that .claude/settings.json is present, committed, and syntactically valid JSON. Restart Claude Code; the plugin is loaded at session start. If still stuck, refresh the plugin per "Keeping up to date" above.
  • Commits blocked with "originate from inside .worktrees/" — intentional. This repo has adopted the worktree convention. Create a worktree for your work; see Git Workflow → Parallel work with worktrees.
  • "raw git/gh blocked" — the Claude Code hook guard is working as intended. Use vrg-commit instead of raw git commit, and vrg-git/vrg-gh instead of raw git/gh.

For a broader troubleshooting index see Git Workflow → Troubleshooting.
