docs.title: Credential Management
docs.text:
VERGIL agents authenticate as GitHub Apps. There are no stored tokens, no classic PATs, and no gh auth account juggling in the agent path. The tooling holds an App's private key, mints a short-lived installation token on demand, and discards it. Each operation runs under the App identity whose permission shape bounds what it can do.

For App registration and initial setup, see Account Setup. For the identity model that credentials serve, see Identity Architecture.

docs.title: The credential is the App
docs.text:
An agent's only credential is its GitHub App private key, recorded in identities.toml as private_key_path. From that key the tooling derives everything else at runtime:

  • No static tokens. Installation tokens live ~1 hour and are minted per operation. There is nothing long-lived to leak or rotate beyond the private key itself.
  • No gh auth dependency in the agent path. The agent does not rely on a logged-in account or a -vergil suffix. The App ID and private key are injected into the agent VM by provisioning.
  • Permission shape is the boundary. The token a given App mints can only do what that App's declared permissions allow. The user App's token cannot write PRs; the audit App's token cannot write code. See Identity Architecture for the inverted shapes.

docs.title: How a token is minted
docs.text:
The implementation lives in src/vergil_tooling/lib/github.py. The flow is:

  1. Read the App config. VRG_APP_ID and VRG_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH identify the App and locate its private key. In an agent VM these come from the identity's app_id and private_key_path in identities.toml.
  2. Generate a JWT. A short-lived JWT is signed with the private key, using the App ID as the iss claim (iat backdated 60s, exp 10 minutes out).
  3. Resolve the installation. The JWT authenticates a call to GET /app/installations; the tooling matches the installation for the target org.
  4. Mint an installation token. The matched installation yields a ~1-hour token, which is injected as GH_TOKEN into the gh subprocess environment for that operation.

The token is never written to disk and never persisted across operations. Parallel sessions each mint their own token independently — no shared state, no lock contention.

App ID, not Client ID — for now

The tooling authenticates using the numeric App ID today (it becomes the JWT iss claim via VRG_APP_ID). GitHub is gradually migrating GitHub App authentication toward the Client ID, but that migration is only partially rolled out. Record the Client ID during setup so the eventual switch needs no return trip to the GitHub UI, but the App ID is what the tooling uses until the migration lands.

docs.title: The tool selects the credential, not the caller
docs.text: There is no flag, no env var override, no way for the caller to choose a different identity. Which App a VM authenticates as is fixed by provisioning (VRG_APP_ID / VRG_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH for that VM). The user VM is the user App; the audit VM is the audit App.

docs.title: The permission shape decides what succeeds
docs.text:
Because each App's token is bounded by its declared permissions, the identity boundary is enforced server-side, not by the wrapper:

  • The user App can push code and read PRs, but cannot open, comment on, approve, or merge PRs — its token holds pull_requests: read.
  • The audit App can write PR reviews, but cannot write code or merge — its token holds contents: read, and merging through the API requires contents: write.

The vrg-gh/vrg-git wrappers add a soft ergonomic layer (clear errors, allowlists) on top of this hard gate, but the App permission shape is the real boundary.

docs.title: Graceful degradation
docs.text:
If App config is absent (no VRG_APP_ID / VRG_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH), the token-minting path returns nothing and the gh subprocess inherits the parent environment. This lets the tooling run in CI environments where credentials are provided through other mechanisms (for example, an Actions-provided token).

Degradation applies only when App config is absent. When App config is present, these two cases stop the command rather than fall back to ambient gh/git auth:

  • No target org. The target org comes from an explicit owner (-R owner/repo for vrg-gh, a command's own target argument such as --repo owner/repo, or a vrg-git clone URL) or else from the current repo's GitHub origin remote. If neither yields an org (for example, vrg-gh without -R run outside a repo), the command stops with GitHub App mode is configured ... but no target org could be determined and exits non-zero. Run it inside a repo whose origin is on GitHub, or name the target explicitly.
  • Minting fails. A broken or rotated key stops the command with GitHub App authentication failed for owner '<owner>' (see Rotating an App private key).

Ambient auth may be a human's gh login. Falling back to it would let an agent act under a different identity without any sign.

One case still falls back: the org is known, but the App has no installation on it, and the command did not name that owner explicitly. The tooling logs a warning naming the owner, then uses ambient auth for it. Some human-run commands and anonymous fetches of public repos rely on this. A command that names the owner explicitly fails with the GitHub App has no installation for owner instead.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
Credential security does not rest on token scope. Defense in depth, in priority order:

  1. App permission shape — the installation token can only perform what the App declares. This is the primary, server-side boundary. A user-App token physically cannot merge a PR.
  2. Branch protection — rulesets prevent merging without review, prevent direct pushes to protected branches, and require CI to pass.
  3. vrg-gh / vrg-git wrappers — gate which operations an agent may attempt and surface clear errors. A soft ergonomic layer, bypassable by root, not the security boundary.
  4. Short-lived tokens — ~1-hour installation tokens minted on demand, with no long-lived secret beyond the private key.

docs.title: Multi-org support
docs.text: A single App installed on multiple accounts works across every org the contributor operates in. Installation tokens are minted per-org from the same private key, so adding a new org requires only installing the existing App on it — no new keys, no credential reconfiguration.

docs.title: Rotating an App private key
docs.text:
Routine rotation replaces an agent App's private key while the old key is still trusted. The user App (<username>-vergil-user) and the audit App (<username>-vergil-audit) each have their own key, so rotate them one at a time with the steps below. If a key is known or suspected to be exposed, do not use this procedure. Follow Responding to a compromised credential instead, which deletes the old key first.

A GitHub App can hold more than one active private key at a time. Rotation relies on that: you add the new key, switch the agent VM to it, prove it works, and only then delete the old one. The agent is never left without a working credential.

No rotation cadence is set for these keys. The date in each key's filename (see Account Setup, Step 1.3) records when it was generated.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Generate a new key. On the App's settings page, go to Private keys and click Generate a private key, as in Account Setup, Step 1.3 (user App) or Step 2.3 (audit App). Leave the existing key in place for now.

  2. Store it next to the old key. Move the downloaded file into ~/.config/vergil/keys/ and keep GitHub's filename, which carries the generation date:

mv ~/Downloads/<username>-vergil-<role>.<YYYY-MM-DD>.private-key.pem \
   ~/.config/vergil/keys/

  1. Point identities.toml at the new key. In ~/.config/vergil/identities.toml, set the identity's private_key_path to the new file. The app_id, the App's permissions, and its installations do not change.

  2. Re-inject the key into the agent VM. Provisioning copies the key into the VM as ~/.config/vergil/app.pem, and it does so only when the VM is created, started, restarted, or rebuilt. A running VM keeps using the old key until one of those happens:

  3. Lima: vrg-vm restart --identity <identity> stops and starts the VM, then re-injects credentials. This ends any session running in the VM, so do it between sessions.

  4. Off-platform: vrg-vm rebuild --identity <identity>. Off-platform VMs do not support restart, so the rebuild destroys the VM and creates it again. Its persistent volume is reattached.

Do this for every VM provisioned from the identity, including any dedicated workspace VM (pass its <org>/<repo> after the command, for example vrg-vm restart --identity <identity> <org>/<repo>).

  1. Verify the new key. Inside the VM, run a read that has to mint an installation token, for example:
vrg-gh pr list --repo <owner>/<repo>

pr list is allowed for both the user and the audit identity. Use a repository on an account the App is installed on. The check passes when the command lists PRs. If the key cannot mint a token, vrg-gh stops before running gh, prints GitHub App authentication failed for owner '<owner>' with the App ID, the key path, and GitHub's error, and exits non-zero. It never falls back to another login, so a broken key cannot pass the check by acting as someone else. Every other vrg-* command fails the same way while the key is broken.

vrg-whoami --explain is not a key check. It reports which identity the VM resolves to, from the injected files, but it does not use the key to authenticate.

  1. Delete the old key on GitHub. Back on the App's Private keys list, delete the old key. Each key is listed with its creation date and a SHA-256 fingerprint. To match a local file to a fingerprint, run:
openssl rsa -in <key-file>.pem -pubout -outform DER \
  | openssl sha256 -binary | openssl base64

Do not delete the old key before step 5 passes. Until it is deleted, a copy of it can still mint tokens.

  1. Delete the old key file. Remove the old .pem from ~/.config/vergil/keys/.

Repeat the steps for the other App.

The org automation Apps (<org>-automation) are not covered by these steps. Their keys are consumed by the APP_PRIVATE_KEY Actions secret, not by an agent VM. The CI publishing secrets are not covered either. For both, see Org automation Apps and CI publishing secrets under the compromise procedure below.

docs.title: Responding to a compromised credential
docs.text: Use this procedure when a credential is known or suspected to be exposed: a private key copied off its host, a secret printed in a log, a lost or untrusted machine. Act on suspicion. Revoking a credential that turns out to be safe costs a few minutes of re-provisioning. Leaving a leaked one live can cost far more.

docs.title: The response, in order
docs.text:
1. Contain. Revoke or suspend the credential so it cannot be used again. The per-credential steps are below.
  2. Halt dependent work. Stop the operations that use the credential, such as agent sessions, releases, and publishing workflows, until a replacement is in place. If the agent VM is the suspected source of the leak, stop it (vrg-vm stop on Lima) or destroy it (vrg-vm destroy off-platform, where stop is not supported). An off-platform VM's injected credentials live on its ephemeral boot disk and are deleted with it.
  3. Review activity. Check what the identity did during the window of suspected exposure (see Reviewing activity).
  4. Restore. Issue a replacement credential and re-provision whatever consumed the old one.
  5. Retrospect. Find out how the credential was exposed, and decide what process or tooling change stops it from happening again.

docs.title: Agent App private key (user or audit App)
docs.text:
The private key in private_key_path is the agent's only long-lived credential. Installation tokens are derived from it and expire after about an hour.

Blast radius. The holder of the key can mint tokens for every account the App is installed on. Each token can reach the repositories that installation covers. The token is limited to the App's declared permissions, as listed in Account Setup:

<username>-vergil-user key <username>-vergil-audit key Contents Read and write. Can push branches and read all code in covered repos, private repos included. Read-only. Can read all code in covered repos, private repos included. Issues Read and write. Can create, edit, and comment on issues. Read-only Pull requests Read-only Read and write. Can write PR reviews and comments. Repository security advisories Read and write. Can read, create and edit the draft advisories in each covered org's .github, which hold security findings. No access Workflows No access. Cannot push under .github/workflows/. No access. Cannot push under .github/workflows/. Merge Cannot open, approve, or merge PRs. Cannot merge, because merging needs contents: write.

Branch protection still limits a leaked user-App key. It cannot push directly to a protected branch or merge without review. It can still push malicious content to feature branches, and it can read every private repo its installations cover. Because both Apps can read code, treat a leak of either key as exposure of that code.

Contain.

  • Delete the compromised key. Open the App's settings page and go to Private keys. Delete the compromised key so that no new tokens can be minted from it. A token minted before the deletion stays valid until it expires (about an hour).
  • Suspend the installations to cut off access immediately, before the outstanding tokens expire. In the settings of each account the App is installed on, open the App's installation and suspend it. Unsuspend it after the replacement key is in place.

Restore. Generate a new private key for the same App as in Account Setup, Step 1.3 or 2.3. Point private_key_path in identities.toml at the new file and delete the old .pem from ~/.config/vergil/keys/. Then re-inject the key into the agent VM. Credentials are injected when a VM is created, started, restarted, or rebuilt, so run vrg-vm restart on Lima or vrg-vm rebuild off-platform. The App ID, permissions, and installations do not change. Verify the new key as described in Rotating an App private key, step 5. For routine, non-emergency key rotation, use that procedure instead.

docs.title: The human account
docs.text:
Blast radius. This is the most severe case. The human account holds the authority that the agent Apps lack: review, approval, merge, and administration (see Identity Architecture). It is also an owner of the orgs the agents work in, and it owns both agent Apps, which are registered under its Developer settings. Anyone in control of the human account can therefore generate fresh keys for both agent Apps.

Contain and restore. Secure the GitHub account itself, then treat both agent App keys as compromised and work through the App-key procedure above for each one. Review the account's recent merge and administrative activity in addition to the agent activity.

docs.title: Org automation Apps
docs.text:
Each org has its own automation App, owned by the org: vergil-project-automation, logical-minds-foundry-automation and mnemosys-project-automation (see Identity Architecture). CI reaches an org's App through the APP_CLIENT_ID and APP_PRIVATE_KEY Actions secrets. The nightly ops workflow uses them for the config audit, the branch sweep and the dependabot-audit job. The epic-rollup and epic-sweep workflows use them to close epics and tasks. The cd-release workflow uses them to dispatch to the org's packages repository (see Package config).

Blast radius. Each App is installed on its org with access to all repositories, not per contributor, so a leaked key reaches every repo in that org. It does not reach the other orgs, which have their own Apps and keys. Its permission set is not listed in the Account Setup tables. Read the exact permissions from the App's settings page before you assess the impact. Its Administration permission is read-only, so the key cannot change repo settings or rulesets. With Dependabot alerts: Read, the key can read a repo's open alerts, including on a private repo. With Repository security advisories: Read and write, it can read and change the draft advisories in the org's .github, which hold the details of unfixed security findings (see Security Records).

Contain and restore. Follow the same steps as for an agent App key: delete the key, suspend the installation if access must stop at once, and generate a new key. Then update the APP_PRIVATE_KEY secret wherever it is stored. Until you do, the workflows that depend on it (ops, epic roll-up and sweep, package-index dispatch) will fail.

docs.title: CI publishing secrets
docs.text:
The release workflow forwards per-ecosystem secrets to cd-release (see CI Architecture):

Secret Blast radius CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN, CENTRAL_USERNAME/CENTRAL_TOKEN Can publish to that registry under the project's account GPG_PRIVATE_KEY/GPG_PASSPHRASE (java) Can sign artifacts as the project PACKAGE_SIGNING_KEY/PACKAGE_SIGNING_PASSPHRASE Can sign .deb/.rpm packages that apt/dnf clients will trust, because clients trust the org signing key

Python publishing uses PyPI OIDC trusted publishing, so there is no stored PyPI token to leak.

Contain. Revoke the token or key at its issuer, such as the registry account or the GPG key, so that a leaked copy stops working. Changing only the GitHub secret leaves the leaked copy valid. Halt releases until a replacement is in place.

Restore. Issue a replacement at the issuer. Then update the repository, organization, or environment secret that held it. PACKAGE_SIGNING_* live in the package-signing environment. The package signing key is more involved to replace than the others, because clients pin it. Its primary fingerprint is pinned in vergil-tooling, checked by vrg-vm, published in Getting Started, and shipped in the vergil-archive-keyring package (see VM spec). Replacing it means changing all of those together.

docs.title: Reviewing activity
docs.text:
• Org audit log. In the organization's settings, open Audit log and filter by the compromised identity across the window of suspected exposure. For an agent App, that identity is the <username>-vergil-<role>[bot] actor. Repeat for every org the App is installed on.
  • Repository history. Every commit, PR, review, and comment made through an App carries its bot identity, so the App's work stands out in branch, PR, and issue history. Look for unexpected branches, pushes, PRs, reviews, and issue edits.
  • Release artifacts. For a publishing secret, check the registry or package index for versions you did not release.

docs.title: Epic home visibility flips
docs.text:
Epic homes are derived from repository visibility (see the epic/task convention and epics.resolve_epic_home):

.github member repo epic home public public <org>/.github public private the member repo itself private (any) <org>/.github absent (e.g. a personal account) private the member repo itself

So a repo's epic home is stable only while its visibility is stable. Visibility changes are supported in one direction only:

  • Private → public is supported. Making a repo public discloses nothing new. Its resolved home moves to <org>/.github, and its existing epics must be relocated to match. This is a rare, corner-case operation; this guide is the runbook for when it happens.
  • Public → private is not supported. See Public to private is unsupported.

docs.title: What moves, and what does not
docs.text:
• Epics move. A private→public flip moves the repo's self-homed epics from the repo into <org>/.github. The epic issue is transferred (not re-created), so its history and comments follow it. It gets a new number in the destination repo.
  • Tasks do not move. A task always lives in its member repo (1:1 with its PR), independent of visibility. Only the epic issue relocates.
  • The intake, planning and deferred queues move themselves. A private repo self-homes its own Epic (intake): <repo>, Epic (planning): <repo> and Epic (deferred): <repo>. Once the repo is public, the daily vrg-epic-audit --close sweep re-links every open item under the org's .github queue epic of the same kind (the items stay in their repo) and closes the emptied self-homed queue epics. No manual step is needed; a read-only vrg-epic-audit lists the queue epics it will move.

There is no dedicated relocation wrapper for epics — the procedure composes vrg-gh issue transfer (an intra-org issue move) with vrg-epic-link.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
Do the following once per epic that the flipped repo owns.

  1. Confirm the new home. Run vrg-epic-create --repo <org>/<repo> (or check the table above) — it echoes the resolved home and its visibility, e.g. -> epic home: <org>/<repo> [PRIVATE].

  2. Transfer the epic into its new home. An intra-org issue transfer moves the epic between repos under the same org, carrying its history with it:

vrg-gh issue transfer <n> <org>/.github -R <org>/<src-repo>

Always pin the source with -R. The -R/--repo owner selects the GitHub App installation and names the source repo unambiguously; <n> is the epic's number in that source repo and the trailing <org>/.github is the destination. The transfer is intra-org — one installation token cannot reach two owners. GitHub assigns the epic a new number in the destination.

  1. Relink reflink-only children. Children linked as native sub-issues ride the transfer — their parent link is preserved automatically. Children linked only by a portable Parent: body reflink still point at the epic's old location, so re-point each with:
vrg-epic-link --epic <org>/.github#<NEW> --task <org>/<repo>#<TASK>
  1. Verify. Run vrg-epic-audit and confirm no invariant violation remains — no epic outside .github for a public repo, no stray .github issue, no closed epic with an open child.

docs.title: Public to private is unsupported
docs.text:
Once a repo has been public, its contents — and anything about it in the public .github, including epic bodies, specs, and plans — may already have been cloned and redistributed. Making it private cannot undo that, and relocating its epics would only give false assurance. So decide at repo creation whether something is private; if it is public, it stays public.

To take public work private, create a new repository that starts life private and migrate the code into it. The new repo self-homes its epics and its intake, planning and deferred queues from day one; the public original is left as it was (archived if appropriate).

If a repo is flipped to private anyway, vrg-epic-audit reports every issue in a private repo that is parented under a public .github epic as a likely unsupported flip, for a human to resolve. Tooling never migrates or retracts anything in that direction.

docs.title: Cross-visibility linkage
docs.text:
A task may hard-link to an epic only if it is no more publicly visible than the epic's home, so vrg-epic-link refuses a public task under a private epic (it would leak the private repo's name into a public issue and break cross-boundary roll-up). Express such a dependency as a soft Blocked-by: reference from the private epic's body instead:

Blocked-by: <owner>/<public-repo>#<TASK>

See the epic/task convention for the asymmetric linkage rule.

docs.title: Git Workflow
docs.text:
This is the single entry point for how we do git across every managed repository. It covers the overall shape of the workflow, the two enforcement layers that back it up, and the per-change cycle you walk through from branching to finalization.

For per-tool detail, each vrg-* command has its own reference page. For the rationale behind the worktree convention, see the worktree convention spec.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
new issue  →  branch  →  commit  →  PR  →  (human review)  →  merge  →  finalize
                  │         │        │                                      │
                  ▼         ▼        ▼                                      ▼
            feature/<N>  vrg-commit  vrg-submit-pr                    vrg-finalize-pr
  • One issue per branch. Branch name encodes the issue number.
  • vrg-commit builds standards-compliant commit messages. Raw git commit is blocked.
  • vrg-submit-pr creates the PR with issue linkage. Raw gh pr create is blocked.
  • Merging is manual. Auto-merge is disabled org-wide as of 2026-04-22.
  • After merge, vrg-finalize-pr pulls develop, deletes the merged branch and its worktree, and prunes remote refs.

For parallel work on multiple issues, use the worktree convention (below) — every session starts at the project root, each concurrent agent gets its own worktree under .worktrees/.

docs.title: Branching model
docs.text:
Every repository's branching model is declared in vergil.toml as [project].branching-model. Three models are supported:

Model Prefixes allowed Typical use library-release feature/*, bugfix/*, hotfix/*, chore/*, release/* Libraries / packages that cut versioned releases application-promotion feature/*, bugfix/*, hotfix/*, chore/*, promotion/* Apps that promote through environments docs-single-branch feature/*, bugfix/*, chore/* Docs-only repos

Protected branches — main, develop, and (for library-release) release — do not accept direct commits. All changes go through PRs against the appropriate integration branch (typically develop).

Work branches must include the issue number in the name:

feature/42-add-caching
bugfix/101-fix-null-pointer
chore/256-bump-dependency-versions

Pattern: ^(feature|bugfix|hotfix|chore)/[0-9]+-[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.-]*$. vrg-git applies it when the branch is created (worktree add -b, checkout -b, switch -c, branch <name>, and a branch -c/-m copy or rename to an issue-branch name) and vrg-commit applies it again at commit time. Listing, deleting and upstream forms of vrg-git branch are not checked.

At creation, vrg-git also reads issue <N> from the current repo. It refuses the branch when the issue is closed, or is an epic or archive (an umbrella is never closed by a PR). It also refuses when the issue cannot be read, so check vrg-gh issue view <N> works and retry.

The release/* and promotion/* prefixes are created by automated workflows and are exempt from the issue-number rule.

deps/update-<version> is the branch vrg-update-deps (and the vrg-release update-deps stage) creates for a dependency update. It is not one of the branching-model prefixes, so vrg-commit refuses to commit on it. That is deliberate: only the driver commits there, and it runs git commit itself rather than going through vrg-commit. Any manual change goes on a fix branch, described next.

When a dependency update fails, its fix task's branch follows the issue-number rule but starts from the failed update: chore/<fix-issue>-dep-update-<version>, cut from origin/deps/update-<version>. See When the dependency update fails.

docs.title: Two enforcement layers
docs.text:
The branching, commit, and PR rules are enforced by two distinct mechanisms. Both exist; they complement each other.

Layer Where it runs Catches Claude Code hook guard .claude/hooks/guard.sh checked into each repo; wired via .claude/settings.json as a PreToolUse hook on the Bash matcher. Delegates to vrg-hook-guard (regex-based detection of raw git/gh commands). The five branch/context checks live in vrg-commit itself. Raw git commands blocked • raw gh commands blocked • vrg-commit additionally checks: detached HEAD, protected branches, branch prefix, issue number Plugin PreToolUse hooks Delivered by the vergil-claude-plugin. Fires on Claude Code's Bash/Write/Edit tool invocations. Raw git commit (forces vrg-commit) • Raw gh pr create (forces vrg-submit-pr) • commits originating from outside .worktrees/* on repos that have adopted the worktree convention • heredoc syntax in CLI args • associative-array bashisms

Why both? The hook guard catches all raw git/gh commands at the Claude Code tool level. The plugin catches additional patterns (heredocs, worktree convention enforcement) that the hook guard does not cover. Together they close the loop.

For the hook guard detail, see the Claude Code Hook Guard reference. For every check and where it runs, see the Validation Matrix. For the plugin hook detail, see vergil-claude-plugin/docs → Hooks.

docs.title: Developing a change
docs.text: Every change follows this path, whether or not other work is running in parallel.

docs.title: 1. Create a worktree on a new branch
docs.text:
From the project root:

vrg-git fetch origin
vrg-git worktree add -b feature/42-add-caching \
  .worktrees/issue-42-add-caching origin/develop
cd .worktrees/issue-42-add-caching

vrg-git checks the branch name and the worktree directory when it creates them, so name both correctly now. The directory must be .worktrees/issue-<N>-<slug>, matching the branch <type>/<N>-<slug>. See Parallel work with worktrees for why every change gets its own worktree.

docs.title: 2. Commit with vrg-commit
docs.text:
vrg-commit \
  --type feat \
  --scope cache \
  --message "cache computed results" \
  --body "Adds an LRU cache to the computation pipeline..."

vrg-commit:

  • Validates the commit type against conventional-commit standards (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore, ci, build).
  • Adds no AI Co-Authored-By trailer: AI co-author attribution is not used, and Claude Code's own attribution is turned off in .claude/settings.json (#3200).
  • Invokes git commit under the hood after all checks pass.

Multi-line bodies go in a file, not a heredoc. The plugin blocks heredocs in CLI args because they cause escaping bugs:

vrg-commit --type feat --scope cache --message "…" --body "$(cat /tmp/body.txt)"

See the vrg-commit reference for the full flag list.

docs.title: 3. Submit the PR with vrg-submit-pr
docs.text:
vrg-submit-pr \
  --issue 42 \
  --summary "Add LRU cache to pipeline" \
  --notes "$(cat /tmp/pr-notes.txt)"

vrg-submit-pr:

  • Pushes the current branch to origin.
  • Constructs a standards-compliant PR body with issue linkage, auto-selecting Closes #42 for a managed task (so it closes on merge) or Ref #42 for a legacy issue. Fixes/Resolves are not accepted.
  • Creates the PR via gh pr create under the hood.

See the vrg-submit-pr reference.

Agent handoff and the post-report-ready freeze

In an agent session, submission is a human action. The agent runs vrg-pr-workflow report-ready, which pushes the branch to origin (setting upstream) and then records the PR metadata in .vergil/pr-workflow.json, and stops; the human runs vrg-submit-pr. No separate push is needed. When the delta touches .github/workflows/** GitHub refuses the agent push; report-ready says so, records the state anyway, and the human's vrg-submit-pr pushes the branch instead. Any other push failure fails report-ready with nothing recorded. Recording ready freezes the branch: vrg-commit and the vrg-git push path refuse further commits/pushes on it, because a task is exactly one PR and more work is a new follow-up issue. One push stays allowed: an explicit push of the branch while HEAD is still exactly the reported commit, which publishes it without advancing it. Correcting the PR prose (re-running report-ready) is still allowed — its push is a no-op while the branch is on origin at the reported commit, and it refuses a HEAD that has drifted past that commit; deliberately reopening the branch needs vrg-pr-workflow unfreeze. See the tool's entry in the CLI Tools Overview.

Cloud (off-platform) agents: same handoff, over GitHub

A cloud x86 VM shares no disk with the Mac, so report-ready always also mirrors the ready-state onto the reserved relay ref refs/vergil/pr-workflow/<branch>. A cloud agent therefore does PR-development end-to-end — implement, push the branch, report-ready — exactly like a Lima agent, and the human submits from the Mac worktree-free with vrg-submit-pr <branch> [<branch> …] (see the reference). The relay ref is world-readable on a public repo, so keep secrets out of the report-ready title/summary/notes.

docs.title: 4. Wait for review, merge manually
docs.text: Once CI is green and a reviewer approves, merge through the GitHub UI (squash merge for feature PRs). No automated merge will happen.

docs.title: 5. Finalize with vrg-finalize-pr
docs.text:
vrg-finalize-pr            # cleanup only, after merging in the UI
vrg-finalize-pr <PR>       # provenance check, merge, then cleanup

This:

  • Switches back to the integration branch (develop).
  • Pulls the latest.
  • Deletes the merged local feature branch and removes its worktree, along with the branch's PR-workflow relay ref (refs/vergil/pr-workflow/<branch>).
  • Prunes stale remote-tracking refs and sweeps any orphaned relay ref whose branch is gone.
  • Runs post-merge validation via vrg-container-run to catch any regression introduced by the merge.

Run this immediately after the PR merges. A Stop hook in the plugin will remind you if you try to end the session with an unsubmitted or unfinalized PR still dangling.

A merged worktree the sweep cannot remove (a dirty tree, or a reused branch name with unmerged commits) is not deleted silently — vrg-finalize-pr surfaces it prominently after the pipeline so it is impossible to miss, and vrg-worktree-status counts it under needs-attention rather than hiding it as active. When the only dirt is un-gitignored build/validation output, --clean-dirty clears it after confirmation; better still, gitignore that output so the worktree sweeps automatically.

See the vrg-finalize-pr reference.

docs.title: Parallel work with worktrees
docs.text:
The main worktree at the project root stays on develop and is read-only. Every change happens in its own worktree under .worktrees/, on its own branch. This lets several agents work in the same repository at once, and lets you start a second issue before the first is merged.

For the full spec (rationale, trust model, failure modes, memory-path implications), see the worktree convention. This section is the user-level "how to."

docs.title: What enforces it
docs.text:
Once .worktrees/ exists in the project root:

  • vrg-git checkout and vrg-git switch refuse to move the main worktree onto a work branch.
  • vrg-commit refuses a work-branch commit made from the main worktree.
  • vrg-git worktree add refuses a worktree outside .worktrees/, or one whose directory name does not match its branch.

vrg-github-repo-init adds .worktrees/ to the managed .gitignore block, so worktrees never show up as untracked files.

docs.title: Creating a worktree for an issue
docs.text:
From the project root:

vrg-git fetch origin
vrg-git worktree add -b feature/42-add-caching \
  .worktrees/issue-42-add-caching origin/develop

Directory layout:

<project-root>/                           ← session starts here
  .git/
  CLAUDE.md, src/, docs/, …               ← main worktree (develop)
  .worktrees/                             ← gitignored, local-only
    issue-42-add-caching/                 ← your worktree, on feature/42-…
    issue-101-fix-npe/                    ← another agent's worktree

docs.title: Launching a session with a worktree assignment
docs.text:
Always start the Claude Code session at the project root, not inside the worktree. The session's initial CWD determines the memory slug; starting inside a worktree creates a separate memory silo and loses shared project context.

Then give the agent the canonical prompt. The template lives in each repo's CLAUDE.md under "Parallel AI agent development → Agent prompt contract"; filled in, it reads:

You are working on issue #42: Add LRU cache to pipeline.

Your worktree is: <project-root>/.worktrees/issue-42-add-caching/
Your branch is:   feature/42-add-caching

Rules for this session:
- Do all git operations from inside your worktree:
    cd <absolute-worktree-path> && vrg-git <command>
- For Read / Edit / Write tools, use the absolute worktree path.
- For Bash commands that touch files, cd into the worktree first
  or use absolute paths.
- Do not edit files at the project root. The main worktree is
  read-only — all changes flow through your worktree on your
  feature branch.
- When you need to run validation, run it from inside your worktree
  (vrg-container-run mounts the current directory).

docs.title: Cleanup after merge
docs.text:
vrg-finalize-pr removes the finalized branch's worktree when it lives under the canonical .worktrees/ directory, so cleanup is normally automatic. To remove one by hand, from the project root:

vrg-git worktree remove .worktrees/issue-42-add-caching
vrg-git branch -D feature/42-add-caching   # usually already deleted
vrg-git fetch --prune                      # usually already pruned

vrg-git branch -D deletes a branch only when its upstream is gone or is an integration branch, and never deletes a protected branch.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Release flow is covered in its own guide: Releasing.

High-level summary:

  1. Accumulate feature PRs on develop.
  2. Run vrg-release from the root checkout. It creates the tracking issue and the release/<version> branch, generates the changelog, merges the release PR to main, waits for CD to tag and publish, merges the version bump back to develop, and cleans up.
  3. As its last step, vrg-release runs the dependency update on the new develop version and opens a dependency-update PR when anything changed. If its validation or merge fails, the PR stays open with a fix task, and the next release refuses to start until it is dealt with.

docs.title: Adoption for a new repo
docs.text:
vrg-github-repo-init creates a new managed repository, or adopts an existing one with --adopt, and writes every managed file in its canonical form: vergil.toml, CLAUDE.md (including the Parallel-AI-agent-development section), .claude/settings.json, .claude/hooks/guard.sh, the managed .gitignore block (including .worktrees/) and the GitHub workflows. Two guides cover it:

  • Getting Started — the quickstart.
  • Consuming Repo Setup — full walkthrough with rationale, CI configuration, plugin details, and troubleshooting.

docs.title: A hook blocked me. Which one, and why?
docs.text:
The hook that fired will print a reason. Common signals:

Message fragment Source What to do "Raw git commit is blocked. Use vrg-commit" plugin Use vrg-commit with the appropriate flags "Raw gh pr create is blocked. Use vrg-submit-pr" plugin Use vrg-submit-pr "Heredoc syntax (<<EOF) is blocked" plugin Write your multi-line content to a /tmp/… file, pass it via $(cat <file>) or --body-file "Commits must originate from inside .worktrees/<name>/" plugin (on repos that have adopted the worktree convention) Create a worktree for your work and cd into it "Commits on protected branch \"develop\" are blocked" plugin or vrg-commit Create a feature branch with the issue number in its name "direct commits to protected branches are forbidden" vrg-commit Same — you're on develop/release/main directly "branch name must use {prefixes}" vrg-commit Rename the branch to feature/42-<slug> or similar "branch name must include a repo issue number" vrg-commit Add the issue number to the branch name "detached HEAD is not allowed for commits" vrg-commit Create a named branch before committing

docs.title: My plugin cache is stale
docs.text:
If you're running an old version of a hook, refresh the plugin from inside Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace update vergil-marketplace
/reload-plugins

See the plugin README's Update section for what each step does.

docs.title: Identity Architecture
docs.text:
VERGIL enforces a hard separation between human and AI agent identity at the GitHub App level. This page describes the identity model, the naming conventions that make it work, and how it extends to adversarial testing.

For the step-by-step App creation process, see Account Setup. For how credentials are minted and selected at runtime, see Credential Management.

docs.title: The identities
docs.text:
Every contributor operates with a human account and a set of AI agent identities. Each agent identity is a GitHub App, not a user account:

Identity Role Backed by <username> Human — review, approval, merge, admin (Chief Steward) The human's own GitHub account <username>-vergil-user Daily development (Driver) GitHub App, write-shaped permissions <username>-vergil-audit PR review (Officials) GitHub App, read-shaped permissions (inverted) <username>-vergil-admin Reserved — not provisioned — <org>-automation CI automation: nightly ops, epic roll-up, package-index dispatch GitHub App owned by the org, one per org

The human account owns the decision-making authority: code review, PR approval, merge, and administrative operations. The two agent Apps do the bounded work — the user App writes code, the audit App reviews PRs. Each org's automation App runs scheduled and event-driven CI work that needs neither human judgment nor a per-contributor identity (see The org automation Apps).

A third agent role — <username>-vergil-admin — is a reserved slot and is not created. Do not provision it.

docs.title: Every agent is a GitHub App
docs.text:
There are no agent user accounts. There are no classic PATs. There are no collaborator grants. An AI agent's entire identity and capability is its GitHub App:

  • The App installation is the only credential. The tooling authenticates as the App (App ID as the JWT iss claim), finds the App's installation on the target org, and mints a short-lived installation token on demand. There is no static token to leak or rotate.
  • Capability is bounded by the App's permission shape. What an agent can do is exactly what its App declares — nothing more. The permission shape is the security boundary.
  • Attribution is clean and automatic. Commits and PRs made through the App carry the bot identity <username>-vergil-<role>[bot]. Anyone reading the history can see at a glance what the human did versus what that human's agents did — and which role did it.
  • It scales. The model is <username>-vergil-<role>, so any number of engineers can each own their own user and audit Apps without naming collisions or shared credentials.

docs.title: The <username>-vergil-<role> convention
docs.text: Every agent App's name encodes two things: the human who owns it and the role it plays. jdoe-vergil-user is jdoe's development agent; jdoe-vergil-audit is jdoe's PR-review agent. The bot identity that appears on commits (jdoe-vergil-user[bot]) comes directly from the App — there is nothing else to configure.

docs.title: Inverted permission shapes
docs.text:
The user and audit Apps have deliberately inverted repository permission shapes. This split is the core of the model:

Permission <username>-vergil-user <username>-vergil-audit Contents Read and write Read-only Issues Read and write Read-only Pull requests Read-only Read and write Metadata Read-only Read-only Workflows No access No access

The user App can write code but only read PRs. The audit App can only read code but can write (review/comment on) PRs. Neither holds Workflows access, so neither can push changes under .github/workflows/.

docs.title: What the user agent can do
docs.text:
• Commit and push to feature branches (contents: write)
  • Create and comment on issues (issues: write)
  • Read PR and CI status (pull_requests: read, plus checks: read, statuses: read and actions: read)
  • Record PR metadata in .vergil/pr-workflow.json (via vrg-pr-workflow) to stage a PR for the human

docs.title: What the user agent cannot do
docs.text:
• Open, edit, comment on, approve, or merge PRs — its App holds pull_requests: read. Its workflow ends at "ready for PR"; the human submits the PR from the host.
  • Push changes under .github/workflows/ — no Workflows access, so GitHub rejects such a push server-side.
  • Access admin settings or manage org membership.

docs.title: What the audit agent can do
docs.text:
• Read code and issues (contents: read, issues: read)
  • Write PR reviews and comments (pull_requests: write)
  • Read CI status (checks: read, statuses: read, actions: read)

docs.title: What the audit agent cannot do
docs.text:
• Write code — contents: read.
  • Merge a PR — merging through the API requires contents: write, which the audit App does not hold. This is a server-side hard gate, not a tooling convention.
  • Push changes under .github/workflows/.

These restrictions are enforced primarily by the App permission shapes (a server-side hard gate) and branch protection, with the vrg-gh/vrg-git wrappers as a soft ergonomic layer on top. See Permission Model for the full defense-in-depth architecture. Where GitHub's permission shapes are coarser than the role model wants, the gap is recorded in Security Boundaries.

Note (2026-06-25, #1872): The local interactive USER/AUDIT loop (where a running AUDIT agent reviewed code in a shared worktree before PR submission) was removed. The audit identity — the vergil-audit GitHub App, its inverted permission shape, and the audit mode in VRG_IDENTITY_MODE — is retained as dormant infrastructure for a future API-driven review phase. The identity model described above remains current and accurate.

docs.title: One App, all orgs
docs.text: A single App is installed on every account the contributor operates in — their personal account and each org they own. Installation tokens are minted per-org at runtime from the App's private key, so one App covers vergil-project, vergils-nemesis, and any future orgs. Adding a new org requires only installing the existing App on it — no new Apps, no new keys, no credential reconfiguration.

docs.title: Harness independence
docs.text: The agent App identity captures AI-driven development work regardless of which AI tool produced it — Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, or any future harness. The specific tool is not recorded at the identity level, and commits carry no AI co-author trailer (#3200). The App represents "AI operating under VERGIL discipline in a given role," not "Claude Code specifically."

docs.title: The -mimir convention
docs.text:
Mimir is the adversarial testing counterpart to Vergil. Where Vergil represents AI operating with discipline, Mimir represents AI's failure modes — hallucination, false confidence, sycophancy, and the tendency to work around constraints rather than within them.

A <username>-mimir identity is the credential that attack tooling presents when attempting to breach Vergil-managed repos. It has no integration with the Vergil tooling — no App, no credential selection. It authenticates with raw gh, raw git, and direct API calls, deliberately bypassing vrg-gh and vrg-commit. It operates against the tooling, not within it.

docs.title: The Vergils-Nemesis org
docs.text:
vergils-nemesis is the GitHub org for adversarial testing. It contains two kinds of repositories:

  • Attack tooling repos — code that implements breach attempts against Vergil-managed targets. These repos are themselves managed by Vergil tooling (built with discipline, used for destruction).
  • Target repos — dummy repositories configured with Vergil protections, serving as test beds for the attack tooling.

The main output is attack reports documenting the success and failure of each breach attempt — demonstrating whether Vergil's guardrails hold under adversarial pressure.

docs.title: The org automation Apps
docs.text:
Each org has its own automation GitHub App, named <org>-automation. The App is owned by the org (registered under the org's Developer settings), and its installation covers all repositories in that org:

Org App vergil-project vergil-project-automation logical-minds-foundry logical-minds-foundry-automation mnemosys-project mnemosys-project-automation

These Apps are an automation identity, not a per-contributor one, and they are separate from the agent Apps above. Workflows reach an org's App through the APP_CLIENT_ID and APP_PRIVATE_KEY Actions secrets and mint a short-lived installation token with actions/create-github-app-token. The vergil-actions reusable workflows use it for:

  • Nightly ops (ops-github-config.yml): the vrg-github-repo-config audit, the branch sweep, and the vrg-dependabot-audit open-alert gate. Each of these jobs mints a token scoped to the calling repo.
  • Epic roll-up and sweep (ops-epic-rollup.yml, ops-epic-sweep.yml): closing epics and tasks across the org.
  • Package-index dispatch (cd-release.yml): sending package-released to the org's packages repo after a packaged release.

Three of the App's permissions matter to the tooling in this repo:

  • Dependabot alerts: Read. vrg-dependabot-audit needs it to list a repo's open alerts (epic vergil-project/.github#420). Without it, or until an installation accepts it, the nightly dependabot-audit job exits 2 ("could not check").
  • Administration: Read-only. The Apps run only the read-only vrg-github-repo-config audit. vrg-github-repo-config apply is a human action that runs as the human's own gh login, because the tooling uses App credentials only when it finds an App key (VRG_APP_ID or ~/.config/vergil/app.pem). Read-only is the correct least privilege.
  • Repository security advisories: Read and write. The scheduled sweep (vrg-epic-audit --close in ops-epic-sweep.yml) lists the draft advisories in the org's .github and closes or reopens each one to follow its issues (see Security Records, epic vergil-project/.github#517). The user App holds the same grant (see Account Setup). Each installation must accept the change before the grant takes effect.

Release PRs are not opened by an App. vrg-release runs on the human's host under the human's own gh login.

docs.title: Permission Model
docs.text:
VERGIL constrains AI agents to a validated set of operations through layered enforcement. Every system interaction flows through wrapper tools that validate, constrain, and log what happens. Raw shell access to git and gh is denied mechanically — not by convention, not by instruction, but by the permission system itself.

For the identity model that permissions protect, see Identity Architecture. For how credentials are selected per-operation, see Credential Management.

docs.title: Base Permission Mode
docs.text: bypassPermissions is the standard mode — but only because the agent runs inside a sandboxed, ephemeral VM (see The VM Sandbox Boundary). Inside that sandbox the agent reads, edits, and runs shell commands without per-action prompts, which is what makes it usable for real work.

docs.title: Why not acceptEdits
docs.text:
acceptEdits was the original target: auto-approve file edits, prompt on any shell command not in the allowlist. It proved impractical for the work VERGIL actually does. An agent doing infrastructure work runs a constant stream of shell commands — container builds, cloud CLIs, system inspection, ad-hoc scripts — and under acceptEdits every non-allowlisted one stops for human approval. The prompts never end, and autonomous work becomes impossible. Chasing an ever-growing bash allowlist was a losing race.

So VERGIL moved the boundary outward instead of inward: rather than constrain which commands the agent may run, sandbox the whole agent in a disposable VM and let it run in bypassPermissions there. The blast radius is the VM, which is ephemeral and reproducible.

docs.title: Bypass is not "no enforcement"
docs.text: bypassPermissions removes the prompts, not the guardrails. The vrg-* wrappers, the deny rules, and the hook guard all still apply — a hook hard-block (exit code 2) overrides even bypass mode — and the server-side GitHub App permission shapes remain the ultimate boundary (see The Actual Security Boundary). Bypass changes the agent's experience inside the sandbox; it does not widen what the agent can do to the outside world.

docs.title: vrg-git Wrapper
docs.text: A Python CLI tool that validates subcommands and flags before executing git. Arguments arrive as a Python argv list — no shell expansion, no pipes, no redirection.

docs.title: Subcommand Allowlist
docs.text: Subcommand Denied Flags Notes status — Read-only log — Read-only diff — Read-only show — Read-only branch --force; -D conditional -d allowed; -D allowed when upstream is [gone] ls-remote — Read-only rev-parse — Read-only annotate — Read-only — line-level authorship blame — Read-only — line-level authorship cat-file — Read-only — object type/size/content cherry — Read-only — commits not yet upstream count-objects — Read-only — repo object stats describe — Read-only — nearest reachable tag diff-files — Read-only — plumbing diff diff-index — Read-only — plumbing diff diff-tree — Read-only — plumbing diff for-each-ref — Read-only — enumerate refs grep — Read-only — search tracked content ls-files — Read-only — list tracked files ls-tree — Read-only — list a tree's contents merge-base — Read-only — common-ancestor lookup name-rev — Read-only — symbolic names for commits reflog expire, delete Read-only show/exists allowed; mutating sub-ops denied rev-list — Read-only — list commits shortlog — Read-only — summarized log show-branch — Read-only — compare branches show-ref — Read-only — list refs var — Read-only — logical git variables verify-commit — Read-only — signature verification verify-tag — Read-only — signature verification whatchanged — Read-only — log with file changes worktree add — Parallel agent work worktree list — Read-only worktree remove — Cleanup after merge add — Staging files push --force, -f; --force-with-lease conditional --force-with-lease allowed on non-protected branches fetch — Read-only pull — Fast-forward updates checkout -- ., -- * Specific-file restore allowed switch — Branch switching stash — All stash subcommands allowed merge — Branch updates cherry-pick — Selective commit application rebase -i, --interactive Non-interactive only

docs.title: Denied Subcommands
docs.text:
Anything not on the allowlist is rejected. Notable denials:

  • commit — all commits flow through vrg-commit
  • reset — too dangerous in all forms
  • clean — file deletion
  • config — modifying git configuration
  • remote — modifying remote configuration
  • filter-branch, replace — history rewriting

docs.title: Escape Hatch
docs.text: None in the wrapper. If the agent genuinely needs a denied operation, it explains the situation to the human, who runs the raw command via ! git <command> in the Claude Code prompt.

docs.title: vrg-gh Wrapper
docs.text: Same architecture as vrg-git. Validates the top-level and second-level subcommands as a pair.

docs.title: Subcommand Allowlist
docs.text:
The allowlist depends on the identity mode (resolved by vrg-whoami). The human and user identities share one allowlist (_ALLOWED), from which the user agent loses the agent-denied pairs below. The audit identity has its own, much narrower allowlist (_ALLOWED_AUDIT). Any pair not listed is rejected as not recognized.

Subcommand human user audit Notes issue view yes yes — Read-only issue list yes yes — Read-only issue edit yes yes — Updating metadata issue comment yes yes — Adding comments issue close yes yes — Closing is mechanical and reversible issue reopen yes yes — Non-destructive; an errant reopen is re-closed issue transfer yes yes — Intra-org issue move (finite-epic relocation) pr view yes yes yes Read-only pr checks yes yes yes CI status pr list yes yes yes Read-only pr diff yes yes yes Read-only pr comment yes yes yes Review context pr review yes yes yes --approve is refused for user pr update-branch yes yes — Server-side update onto the base (--rebase allowed) pr edit yes — — Agents do not edit PRs pr merge yes — — Human only, and a PR number or URL is required run list yes yes — CI status run view yes yes — CI status run watch yes yes — Blocking wait for CI run rerun yes yes — Retry a failed CI job (--failed allowed) workflow list yes yes yes Read-only CI configuration workflow view yes yes yes Read-only CI configuration cache list yes yes yes Read-only CI state repo view yes yes — Read-only repo list yes yes — Read-only release list yes yes — Read-only release facts release view yes yes — Read-only release facts label list yes yes — Read-only label create yes yes — Used by vrg-ensure-label search code / commits / issues / prs / repos yes yes — Read-only, cross-org search api full — GET only See gh api

The audit identity is a read/review reviewer, so it gets the PR read and review actions plus the read-only workflow list, workflow view and cache list, which only read CI configuration and state a reviewer may need to judge a PR's checks. Every write (run rerun, pr update-branch, the issue actions) stays off its allowlist.

docs.title: Denied Subcommands
docs.text:
These pairs are refused with an explanatory message rather than a bare "not recognized":

Subcommand Denied for Reason issue create every identity Use vrg-issue-create, vrg-epic-create or vrg-intake-create, which force the issue's linkage pr close every identity Agents do not close PRs repo edit every identity Admin operation repo create every identity Admin operation repo delete every identity Destructive workflow run every identity Dispatching a workflow can start CD or a release, which is a human action auth every identity Credential management pr create every identity Agents are told PR creation needs a human; a human is pointed to vrg-submit-pr pr edit user, audit PR edit requires a human maintainer pr merge user, audit PR merge requires a human maintainer pr review --approve user Approval is restricted to the audit identity or a human api user Broad, write-capable escape hatch api (non-GET) audit Restricted to read-only GET calls

Other write actions of allowed top-level commands (release create, workflow enable/disable, cache delete and so on) are rejected by the allowlist's deny-by-default.

docs.title: gh api by Identity
docs.text:
gh api can perform any GitHub API operation — create repos, delete branches, modify settings, push code via the Contents API. It has no fixed sub-actions, so the wrapper gates it by identity instead of by pair:

  • human — full access.
  • audit — read-only GET calls only. A call is treated as a write when it passes -X/--method with anything but GET, or passes a field flag (-f, -F, --field, --raw-field, --input) without an explicit GET.
  • user — denied entirely, which closes the escape hatch that individual hook-based blocks cannot fully cover.

docs.title: Credential Selection
docs.text: vrg-gh is responsible for choosing which account's token to use per-command. See Credential Management for the selection logic.

docs.title: VRG Tools That Bypass the Wrapper
docs.text: Mechanized VRG tools (vrg-submit-pr, vrg-release, vrg-update-deps, vrg-ensure-label, vrg-github-repo-config, vrg-finalize-pr) call gh directly in their Python code. They bypass the wrapper because they are already validated — the wrapper only constrains agent-initiated gh calls via the Bash tool.

docs.title: Project Settings (.claude/settings.json)
docs.text:
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(vrg-*)"
    ]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.claude/hooks/guard.sh"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

The project layer allowlists all VRG tools via a single wildcard and wires the Claude Code hook guard (guard.sh) as a PreToolUse hook on every Bash tool invocation. The hook guard delegates to vrg-hook-guard, which uses regex matching to block raw git and gh commands while allowing vrg-git/vrg-gh wrappers through.

This configuration applies to everyone who clones the repo — no per-developer setup needed.

docs.title: Global User Settings (~/.claude/settings.json)
docs.text:
{
  "permissions": {
    "defaultMode": "bypassPermissions"
  }
}

This is the operator's per-host setting. vrg-vm copies it into every identity VM — Lima and off-platform alike — via copy_claude_config, so the agent boots straight into bypass inside the sandbox. The mode is independent of the deny rules: raw git/gh are blocked regardless, because the hook guard hard-blocks them even under bypass.

docs.title: Local Settings (.claude/settings.local.json)
docs.text:
Gitignored, per-developer. Houses temporary read-only bash exceptions:

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(grep *)",
      "Bash(find *)",
      "Bash(ls *)",
      "Bash(diff *)",
      "Bash(cat *)",
      "Bash(head *)",
      "Bash(tail *)",
      "Bash(wc *)",
      "Bash(which *)",
      "Bash(sort *)",
      "Bash(uniq *)",
      "Bash(stat *)",
      "Bash(du *)",
      "Bash(file *)"
    ]
  }
}

These are documented as candidates for removal as alternatives are found (Explore subagent, native Read tool, future vrg-search).

docs.title: What This Means in Practice
docs.text: Command Result vrg-commit No prompt (project allow) vrg-git status No prompt (project allow) grep -r "foo" src/ No prompt (local allow) git push Blocked (hook guard) curl https://... Runs (bypass; contained to the sandbox VM) rm -rf . Runs (bypass; the disposable VM is the containment) vrg-gh pr merge No Claude Code prompt, but wrapper rejects it

docs.title: The Vergil Assumption
docs.text:
Every client-side enforcement layer in this model assumes the agent is cooperative — that it is operating as Vergil, not Mimir. An agent with file write access (which bypassPermissions grants) can dismantle the entire client-side stack:

  1. Delete or edit .claude/settings.json — Layer 1 gone
  2. Run raw git and gh — Layer 2 bypassed (the wrappers are never invoked)
  3. Remove plugin hook configuration — Layer 3 weakened
  4. Delete .claude/hooks/guard.sh or remove the hooks wiring from .claude/settings.json — Layer 4 gone

After those four steps, the agent has unrestricted local access. This is not a theoretical attack — it is trivial for any model that decides to do it.

Client-side layers are behavioral constraints, not security boundaries. They keep a well-intentioned agent on the rails. They prevent mistakes, enforce consistency, and provide an audit trail. They do not stop an adversary.

The two boundaries an agent cannot edit its way out of are not client-side: the VM sandbox that contains it locally, and the server-side GitHub App permission shape that bounds what reaches GitHub.

docs.title: The VM Sandbox Boundary
docs.text:
Agents run inside a per-identity Vergil VM — never on the host. This is what makes bypassPermissions acceptable: the agent has full rein inside the VM, but the VM is the wall.

  • Containment. The agent reaches only what the VM can reach. The host filesystem, other identities' VMs, and the operator's wider environment are outside the sandbox.
  • Disposability. The VM is ephemeral and reproducible from its declared profile, so a bad outcome inside it (an rm -rf, a wedged toolchain) is recovered by a rebuild, not a forensic cleanup. On the off-platform backend, irreplaceable state lives on a separate persistent volume; injected credentials stay on the ephemeral boot disk and die with the VM.
  • Credential bounding. Even with full local control, the agent can only reach GitHub through its injected App token — which the server-side boundary below constrains regardless of what happens in the sandbox.

The sandbox is why VERGIL runs bypassPermissions rather than chasing a per-command allowlist: move the boundary to the edge of a disposable VM, and the prompts inside it stop being the thing that protects you.

docs.title: The Actual Security Boundary
docs.text:
At the GitHub layer, the enforcement an agent cannot edit its way out of is server-side: the GitHub App's installation permission shape and branch protection rulesets.

  • Each agent is a GitHub App whose installation token is bounded by its declared permission shape. The user App holds pull_requests: read, so it physically cannot open, approve, or merge a PR; the audit App holds contents: read, so it cannot write code or merge (merging through the API requires contents: write). Neither App holds Workflows access, so neither can push under .github/workflows/. GitHub rejects the API call regardless of what happens locally.
  • Branch protection rulesets require review approval from a different identity before merging. No client-side manipulation changes this.
  • An App can only act on accounts it is installed on and repos that installation covers.

This and the VM sandbox are the real security model. Everything else is convenience.

Where these boundaries meet other systems, their guarantees do not always line up. Known gaps of that kind are recorded in Security Boundaries.

docs.title: Why Client-Side Layers Still Matter
docs.text:
If server-side enforcement is the only real boundary, why bother with four client-side layers?

  • Mistake prevention. Most failures are not adversarial. An agent that accidentally runs git reset --hard is not trying to subvert the tooling — it made a mistake. The wrappers catch this.
  • Consistency. Routing all operations through vrg-* tools ensures commits have the right format, PRs have the right metadata, and branches follow the naming convention.
  • Audit trail. Wrapper logging records what the agent did and when. Even if a layer is bypassed, the gap in the log is itself a signal.
  • Friction. An agent that has to actively dismantle four layers is doing something visibly wrong. That visibility is the value — not the strength of any individual gate.

The Mimir project exists specifically to test this boundary — to verify that server-side controls hold when every client-side layer is deliberately bypassed.

docs.title: Client-Side Layers
docs.text:
Four layers, each catching mistakes the layer above misses. Redundancy is intentional — no single layer is trusted, and none are sufficient against adversarial behavior.

Layer 1 — Claude Code Permissions (outermost). The allowlist/deny configuration. Denied commands are blocked without prompt. Unknown commands prompt the human.

Layer 2 — VRG Wrappers. vrg-git and vrg-gh validate subcommands and flags before executing the underlying tool. Even if vrg-git reset --hard passes the permission layer (it is allowlisted as vrg-*), the wrapper rejects it.

Layer 3 — Vergil Plugin Hooks. The existing hook system remains as a backstop. Hooks exit code 2 (hard block) overrides even bypass mode. Hooks that become redundant with layers 1-2 are retained — they catch regressions if a higher layer is misconfigured.

Layer 4 — Claude Code Hook Guard (.claude/hooks/guard.sh). The innermost layer. A PreToolUse hook wired in .claude/settings.json that delegates to vrg-hook-guard, blocking all raw git and gh commands via regex matching. With layers 1-3 in place, agents cannot reach this layer through normal operation.

docs.title: Layer Interaction Matrix
docs.text:
Operation L1 Permissions L2 Wrapper L3 Plugin Hook L4 Hook Guard Server-Side vrg-commit allowed n/a n/a allows push accepted vrg-git push allowed validates: no --force n/a n/a push accepted git push denied n/a blocked n/a push accepted (if layers bypassed) vrg-gh pr merge allowed rejected blocked n/a API rejected (no merge permission) gh pr create denied n/a blocked n/a PR created (if layers bypassed) gh pr merge (raw) denied n/a blocked n/a API rejected (no merge permission) rm -rf . prompts human n/a n/a n/a n/a vrg-git reset --hard allowed rejected n/a n/a n/a

The rightmost column is the only one that holds against Mimir.

docs.title: History: the acceptEdits direction, and why it was dropped
docs.text:
The original plan phased toward a tight acceptEdits + allowlist model — acceptEdits as the default mode, then progressively shrinking the bash allowlist until Bash(vrg *) was the only allowed pattern and everything else required human approval.

That direction was not adopted. In practice, prompting on every non-allowlisted shell command made the agent unusable for the infrastructure work VERGIL actually does, where running many varied commands is the job. The allowlist could never keep up, and the operator spent sessions approving commands instead of getting work done.

VERGIL resolved this by changing where the boundary sits rather than how tight the allowlist is: the agent runs in bypassPermissions inside a disposable, sandboxed VM (see Base Permission Mode and The VM Sandbox Boundary). The vrg-* wrappers, deny rules, and hooks remain — as consistency and mistake-prevention guardrails, and as hard blocks on raw git/gh that hold even under bypass — but they are no longer what makes autonomy safe. The VM sandbox and the server-side App permissions are.

The earlier acceptEdits design spec (docs/specs/2026-05-14-permission-model-design.md) is retained as historical context; it does not describe the model in use.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
This guide covers the release workflow for vergil-tooling, including how patch, minor, and major versions affect both the release author (producer) and downstream consumers.

The model: vergil-tooling is distributed as a host-level developer tool plus a dev-container pre-bake (see host-level-tool spec). Three deployment targets — developer host, Python project .venv, and dev container image — each track the rolling minor tag (e.g. v1.3), which is force-updated by tag-and-release on every patch release. The dev container images rebuild automatically on each vergil-tooling release via a repository_dispatch trigger.

docs.title: Tag scheme — what's user-facing, what isn't
docs.text:
Two parallel tag families exist in the repo. Consumers only see and use the first; the second is internal scaffolding for the changelog flow.

Tag pattern Where Purpose User-facing? v1.3.0 main Release tag Yes — pin in install commands v1.3 main Rolling minor tag (force-updated each patch) Yes — what consumers actually pin to develop-v1.3.0 develop Boundary marker for git-cliff's next-changelog scoping No — internal

The develop- prefix is invisible to install / consumption; never pin to a develop-v* tag.

docs.title: Patch release — the common path
docs.text: A patch release fixes a bug or refines an existing feature without adding new public surface. Versions: v1.3.0 → v1.3.1.

docs.title: Producer steps
docs.text:
1. Land all the patch's changes via normal feature PRs to develop.
  2. From the root checkout, on a clean develop that matches origin/develop, run the release:
vrg-release

vrg-release is a human-only command: it refuses to run under an agent identity. It needs git-cliff on PATH and an authenticated gh. It drives the whole release through the stages listed in The vrg-release pipeline below, in a managed worktree, so the root checkout is never switched off develop. See the vrg-release reference for every flag. 3. While vrg-release waits on CD, the post-merge automation runs: - CD on main creates the release tag (v1.3.1). - The rolling minor tag (v1.3) is force-updated to point at the new release. - The boundary tag (develop-v1.3.1) is created on develop. - repository_dispatch fires a vergil-tooling-released event at vergil-containers, which rebuilds the dev images against the now-current v1.3 tag. - The Documentation workflow publishes the new release notes to the docs site under releases/v1.3.1. - Repos with [package] (vergil-tooling is one) also publish signed .deb/.rpm packages, all before the tag exists: cd-release builds every package build cell, then a separate package-sign job signs each .rpm and attests every artifact. Any package failure stops the release before tagging. The signed packages and packages-manifest.json are attached to the GitHub Release. - After tagging, cd-release dispatches package-released to the org's packages repository. Its publish-index workflow verifies every artifact's build attestation (signer workflow cd-release.yml, source ref refs/heads/main) and every .rpm signature, then rebuilds and signs the apt/dnf index. A failed dispatch does not fail the release; the index's weekly reconcile picks the release up. - vrg-release's package-index stage then polls the published index (up to 20 minutes, every 30 seconds) until the new version is visible, so the consumer refresh never races the index. With several [[package]] entries it waits for every package, each at its own full version, and succeeds only once all of them are listed. While it waits, it streams the Publish package index run in <org>/packages that covers the release and prints a heartbeat line on each poll otherwise; the index poll alone decides success. A miss (timeout or polling error) does not undo the release. It is recorded as a deferred publish failure: the tracking issue stays open with a deferral comment, the consumer-refresh stage holds (it prints a warning not to advertise the version instead of the refresh commands), the stage error tells you to re-run the publish-index workflow in <org>/packages, and vrg-release exits 1. See the package config reference. 4. Act on the consumer-refresh commands vrg-release prints at the end (or pass --install to have it run them after a clean release). 5. Check the end of the run for the update-deps result. A failed dependency update does not fail the release, but it leaves an open PR that blocks the next one; see Dependency updates.

docs.title: The vrg-release pipeline
docs.text:
vrg-release runs these stages in order. A fail-fast stage stops the run when it fails. A deferred stage records its failure and lets the later stages run; the run then exits 1 with a summary. Every tracked stage posts a completion or failure comment on the release tracking issue and ticks its box in the issue's stage checklist.

Stage Mode What it does audit fail-fast Runs vrg-github-repo-config audit on the repo. --skip-audit skips it preflight fail-fast Checks the host prerequisites, gh auth, vergil.toml, and that the root checkout is a clean develop matching origin/develop. On a fresh start it also runs the main/develop divergence check, checks the version is not tagged, that no tracking issue exists for it, runs the package re-publish check, and runs the dependency-update gate. Creates the release/<version> managed worktree prepare fail-fast Creates the release: <version> tracking issue, generates the changelog and release notes, and opens the release PR to main merge-release fail-fast Waits for the release PR's checks and merges it. If the PR conflicts with main, it merges main into the release branch and pushes it. A conflict in CHANGELOG.md alone is resolved by keeping the release branch's generated changelog; any other conflict aborts the merge and stops with the commands to resolve it by hand confirm-main fail-fast Watches CD on main. The release job must succeed; other failed publish jobs are recorded as deferred publish failures (see Stale job records) back-merge-bump fail-fast Creates release/post-<version> from main, bumps the version, and merges it to develop. Records the back-merge's merge commit teardown-worktree deferred Removes the release worktree and returns to the root checkout confirm-develop deferred Watches the CD run on develop for the back-merge's merge commit; a failed docs publish is deferred promote deferred Moves the rolling vX.Y tag to the new release (skipped with --no-promote) package-index deferred For repos with [package], waits for the new version in the package index. A miss is a deferred publish failure, not a halted stage close-finalize deferred Closes the tracking issue with a summary and runs vrg-finalize-pr --cleanup-only --no-wait-cd consumer-refresh deferred Prints the [publish].consumer-refresh commands update-deps deferred Runs the dependency update on the new develop version (skipped with --without-deps); see Dependency updates publish-status deferred Repeats any deferred publish failure, and any dependency-update failure, so neither is lost

close-finalize leaves the tracking issue open, and skips the cleanup, when an earlier stage has failed, so the release can be resumed with vrg-release --resume. A deferred publish failure also leaves the issue open, with a comment that says how to finish each deferred item, but the release itself is complete: re-run the CD publish (or the publish-index workflow, for a package-index miss) rather than resuming.

confirm-develop checks the CD run for the back-merge's merge commit, not for the current tip of develop. On vrg-release --resume, other PRs (a dependency update or a feature) may have merged to develop since the back-merge. The tip's CD run then says nothing about the release. A resume re-runs back-merge-bump, which adopts the existing back-merge PR and records its merge commit again. If the merge commit can't be found, confirm-develop fails. It never falls back to the tip.

close-finalize passes --no-wait-cd to vrg-finalize-pr. Without a merge of its own, finalize's CD check would watch the tip of develop, which has the same problem. confirm-develop has already checked the right run, and close-finalize runs vrg-finalize-pr only when every earlier stage passed. A second wait would add nothing. It would also fail the stage on a docs publish failure that confirm-develop has already deferred.

docs.title: Stale job records
docs.text:
The confirm stages wait a bounded time for every CD job to reach completed in the GitHub jobs API, because a job's record can lag the run's. A job that is still not completed after that wait has no conclusion to judge:

  • If the run itself concluded success, GitHub has confirmed that every job succeeded or was skipped, so the record is stale. The stage shows a warning, stale job record: <job>, and nothing is deferred. No CD re-run is needed.
  • Under any other run conclusion the job may really have failed, so it is deferred as <job> (never settled).

A failed job in the release job's own family, such as release / package-sign, is reported by its full name rather than as release, so the message is never mistaken for the release itself failing.

docs.title: Consumer steps
docs.text:
For most consumers, no action is required: the rolling v1.3 tag they're already pinned to now points at the patch release. They get the fix on the next normal action:

Consumer When the patch lands Developer host Manual uv tool upgrade vergil-tooling (or vrg-host upgrade vergil-tooling on macOS) Python repo .venv uv lock --upgrade-package vergil-tooling (typically batched with other dep bumps) Dev container image Already rebuilt by repository_dispatch; new pulls of dev-base etc. carry the patch within the rebuild window (minutes) Agent VM (Lima/cloud) vrg-vm update: an apt upgrade of the packaged install within its pin, once the patch is in the package index. A vX.Y line pin picks the patch up; an exact vX.Y.Z pin stays put

docs.title: Minor release — opt-in for new features
docs.text: A minor release adds backwards-compatible new features. Versions: v1.3.x → v1.4.0.

docs.title: Producer steps
docs.text:
Same steps as patch, with one important addition: the rolling minor tag changes from v1.3 to v1.4. The image's pin in vergil-containers and any per-repo dev-dep declarations must be bumped manually — the rolling-tag mechanism only handles patches within a minor.

  1. Run vrg-release minor. It bumps the version to the next minor (1.4.0) on the release branch instead of releasing the current develop version. Everything else matches a patch release.
  2. Bump vergil-containers's pin in docker/common/vergil-tooling-uv.dockerfile:
ARG ST_TOOLING_TAG=v1.4   # was v1.3

Open a small PR in vergil-containers, merge it, and the next image rebuild (whether triggered by your release or a subsequent push there) carries the new minor. 3. Coordinate consumer bumps. Each Python repo that has [tool.uv.sources] pinning to v1.3 needs its pyproject.toml updated to v1.4.
