This is a per-repo decision — consumers who prefer to stay on v1.3 can keep doing so until they're ready. 4. Update the canonical install command in getting-started.md (and anywhere else the documentation pins a minor) to the new tag.

docs.title: Consumer steps
docs.text:
Minor bumps are deliberate opt-in at every deployment target:

Consumer What changes Developer host uv tool install --reinstall 'vergil-tooling @ git+...@v1.4' (or update the pinned tag in their notes / shell history) Python repo .venv Edit pyproject.toml [tool.uv.sources] to tag = "v1.4", then uv lock --upgrade-package vergil-tooling Dev container image Wait for vergil-containers to land the ARG bump, then pull the rebuilt image Agent VM (Lima/cloud) Set the identity's vergil version (in identities.toml) to v1.4, then vrg-vm rebuild, which installs and records the new line. A plain vrg-vm update keeps upgrading within the line recorded at install time, and vrg-vm update --tag v1.4 is a one-off override that is not remembered (see VM spec)

The release author should announce the minor bump in the GitHub Release notes, calling out any new features and the v1.4 pin update.

docs.title: Major release — explicit migration
docs.text: A major release contains breaking changes. Versions: v1.x.x → v2.0.0.

docs.title: Producer steps
docs.text:
A major release is a minor release plus a deliberate breaking-change communication and migration window:

  1. Document the breaking changes BEFORE cutting the release. A docs/specs/v2-migration.md (or similar) describing what breaks, what to update, and how to recover from common issues.
  2. Run vrg-release major to release v2.0.0. The release notes prominently call out the breaking-change list and link to the migration guide.
  3. Bump vergil-containers's ARG ST_TOOLING_TAG= to v2 in a separate PR — coordinate so consumers can opt in on their own schedule.
  4. Notify consumer maintainers (e.g., update vergil-tooling's release tracking issue / project board with a callout). The release notes alone are not sufficient for major bumps; consumers should be primed.

docs.title: Consumer steps
docs.text:
Same as a minor release in mechanics — every deployment target edits its v1.x pin to v2 deliberately. The difference is timing and risk awareness:

  • Read the migration guide before bumping.
  • Stage the bump in a feature branch, run validation, fix any breakages from removed APIs / changed behaviors.
  • Merge the bump PR per the consumer's normal review flow.

docs.title: Dependency updates
docs.text:
Every release ends by updating the repo's dependencies to the newest versions their declared bounds allow. This is the update-deps stage, and it is the first change on the new develop version. It runs after consumer-refresh, once the release is tagged and published, so it can never affect the release itself. Pass --without-deps to skip it.

The stage brings the root checkout's develop up to date with origin/develop (the root checkout must be on develop), then runs the same pipeline as vrg-update-deps:

  1. Create the deps/update-<version> branch in a managed worktree, where <version> is the new develop version. If that branch already exists, its PR decides what happens; see An existing update branch. On --resume, if the update for this version already merged, the stage succeeds and its tracking-issue comment links the merged PR.
  2. Run each applicable updater, committing each one's changes separately. The built-in updaters and the per-repo hook are described in the dependency-update reference.
  3. If nothing changed, stop: no branch is pushed and no PR is opened. The tracking-issue comment says "No dependency changes; no PR opened."
  4. Otherwise run vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate once, push the branch, and open a PR to develop labelled dependency-update.
  5. If validation passed, wait for the PR's checks, merge it, and delete its branch on origin.

The stage's comment on the tracking issue always carries a Held back by declared bounds table: the dependencies whose newest release is outside the bounds the repo declares. These are reported, never bumped. A dependency on that list moves only when someone widens its bound deliberately.

docs.title: When the dependency update fails
docs.text:
A failed dependency update never fails the release, but it cannot be ignored. What it leaves behind depends on where it failed:

  • An updater or the repo hook failed (update), for example a lookup error, a non-zero hook exit, or a hook that committed: this happens before validation, so nothing is pushed and no PR is opened. A task titled "Fix failed dependency update for <version>" is still filed under the repo's ad-hoc epic. It stands on its own: it names the failing updater, carries the error and the command to reproduce it on develop, and is linked from the failure on the tracking issue and in the run summary. The worktree is removed. With no labelled PR, it does not gate the next release.
  • Validation failed (validation), or the PR's checks or merge failed (merge): the PR stays open with its dependency-update label, and a task titled "Fix failed dependency update for <version>" is filed under the repo's ad-hoc epic. The PR body gets a Fix task: <url> line and a failure section. For a validation failure, that section shows the output of the failing vrg-validate stage, or, when that stage cannot be isolated, a labelled tail of the raw output. It ends with the command to reproduce the failure.

If a fix task for the same version and failure kind is already open, for example after vrg-release --resume re-runs an update that failed on a transient error, no second task is filed: the new failure is added as a comment on the open task, which is linked as above.

Either way vrg-release exits 1, and the failure counts once in its summary: the update-deps stage fails, and publish-status repeats it as a warning. If a publish job also failed, publish-status fails with both.

To fix a failed update, work the fix task like any other task, but cut its branch from the failed update so it starts from those commits:

vrg-git fetch origin
vrg-git worktree add -b chore/<fix-issue>-dep-update-<version> \
  .worktrees/issue-<fix-issue>-dep-update origin/deps/update-<version>

Fix the cause, then hand off and merge as usual. When the fix PR merges and closes the fix task as completed, the next vrg-release closes the dependency-update PR for you.

An update failure pushed no deps/update-<version> branch, so cut that fix task's branch from origin/develop instead. Once the fix merges, the next vrg-update-deps run, or the next vrg-release, applies the update.

docs.title: The dependency-update gate
docs.text:
On a fresh start (not --resume), preflight lists the open PRs labelled dependency-update. For each one:

  • The PR's fix task is closed as completed. The update landed through the fix PR. A squash-merged fix PR never marks the deps PR as merged, so preflight comments on the deps PR, closes it, deletes its deps/update-<version> branch, and records it in the prepare comment on the tracking issue. GitHub's delete-on-merge setting never applies to a PR closed without merging, so preflight deletes the branch itself. If that delete fails, the PR stays closed and the gate still clears, but the release prints a warning and the prepare comment names the branch to delete by hand.
  • The fix task is still open, the PR has no fix task, or the fix task was closed without being completed. The PR blocks the release and preflight refuses, naming each PR and why it blocks. A fix task closed without being completed means the update did not land; whether to close the PR or fix it is a human decision.

Clear a blocking PR by landing its fix task, merging the PR, or closing it deliberately. For an urgent release, --allow-pending-deps lets the release go ahead anyway. The bypass is not silent: it prints a warning and the prepare comment lists the bypassed PRs.

If preflight cannot list the PRs or look up a fix task, it refuses to release rather than guess. Every fix task is looked up before any PR is closed, so a failed lookup changes nothing.

docs.title: The package re-publish check
docs.text:
For a repo with [package], a fresh start (not --resume) refuses to release when a package it would publish has the same name, full version, architecture and format as a package an earlier stable release of the repo already published. Package builds are not byte-reproducible, so the rebuilt file would differ from the published one. The shared package index refuses that, and because the index is built from every release of every repo, the refusal would fail every repo's index publish until the duplicate assets were removed by hand.

The check runs in preflight, before anything is branched, tagged or published. That is the earliest point that knows the full package versions: they follow from [package] (its version, its upstream-version joined with the release version, or the release version when neither is set) and the build matrix, without building anything. It runs before the dependency-update gate, so a refusal changes nothing. The refusal names each conflicting package and the release that first published it:

vergil-project/example@v1.2.0 would re-publish 4 package(s) at a version an earlier release already published:
  - example-server 2.0.0-1 amd64 (deb): already published by vergil-project/example@v1.1.0
  ...

To fix it, bump the package version in vergil.toml: a new upstream-version, or for a version override a new version. An upstream-version package's version ends in the repo version, so each new release is already a new package version. If the check cannot read the repo's releases, it refuses rather than skipping. CD runs the same check as a backstop; see the package reference.

docs.title: The main/develop divergence check
docs.text:
A completed release leaves main contained in develop: back-merge-bump branches release/post-<version> from main and merges it to develop with a merge commit. develop being ahead of main is normal. main having commits that develop lacks is not. It means an earlier release stopped between merge-release and back-merge-bump, or something landed on main directly. A new release on top of that would fail late, at merge-release.

So a fresh start (not --resume) fetches main and refuses, before any other fresh-start check, when origin/main has commits not on origin/develop. The refusal lists those commits. To recover:

  • If an earlier release stopped before its back-merge (its tracking issue is still open), finish it with vrg-release --resume. A resume skips this check, because a release between merge-release and back-merge-bump has main ahead of develop by design.
  • Otherwise, back-merge main into develop by hand:
git fetch origin
git switch -c release/back-merge-main origin/main
git push -u origin release/back-merge-main

Open a PR from release/back-merge-main to develop and merge it with a merge commit. A squash merge leaves main's commits off develop, and the check keeps refusing. Then re-run vrg-release.

If preflight cannot fetch main or compare the branches, it refuses rather than skipping.

docs.title: Documentation publication
docs.text:
The Documentation workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml) deploys the MkDocs site to GitHub Pages on every push to develop and main. It's container-based: the workflow runs inside dev-base:latest and uses vergil-project/vergil-actions/actions/docs-deploy.

The post-merge publish is awaited, not glanced at. The CD workflow (docker build/publish, docs, release) is dispatched asynchronously by the base-branch push the merge produces. To catch silent failures, vrg-finalize-pr blocks on the CD run this merge triggered — identified by the merge commit SHA, not "the latest run on the branch" — and waits for it to complete. If that run does not succeed, finalize prints the failure with a direct link to the log and exits non-zero, so you investigate before moving on. The wait is bounded by timeouts and --no-wait-cd opts out (issue #2753). The watch deadline defaults to 90 minutes and can be changed with VRG_CD_TIMEOUT (seconds). A run still going at the deadline is reported as "still in progress; result unknown", with the run URL and how to re-check it, not as a failed run. It still fails finalize (issue #3316).

For deeper investigation, view recent runs directly:

gh run list --repo vergil-project/vergil-tooling \
  --workflow="Documentation" --limit 5

docs.title: Release tracking artifacts
docs.text:
Each release has a tracking issue, release: <version>, which vrg-release creates in its prepare stage. Its body carries the stage checklist, and each tracked stage adds a comment when it completes or fails:

  • The prepare comment names the release branch, the release PR and the tracking issue. It also lists any dependency-update PRs the gate closed because their fix task completed, and any it let through with --allow-pending-deps.
  • Later comments record the merge, the tag and GitHub Release, the CD runs, the back-merge PR and next version, and the promotion.
  • The update-deps comment carries the held-back table and either the dependency-update PR or "No dependency changes; no PR opened." (or "Dependency update skipped (--without-deps)."). A failed update posts a failure comment with the same table and the failure section instead.

The close-finalize stage closes the issue with a summary, which happens before the last few stages run, so their comments land on the closed issue. It stays open when an earlier stage failed (so the release can be resumed) or a publish job was deferred. vrg-release --resume finds the open tracking issue and runs the pipeline again, adopting the branches, PRs and tag the earlier run already created.

Use the issue as well to capture the rationale for the release and any consumer coordination it needs, especially for minor and major bumps. Follow-ups move to their own issues.

docs.title: Security Boundaries
docs.text:
VERGIL lets powerful AI agents do real work by managing risk, not by pretending it away. The riskiest places are usually not inside one component. They are at the seams between systems (Vergil, GitHub, the agent VM and the agent harness), where one system's guarantees do not quite line up with the next system's.

This page is the register of those seams. Each entry records what the seam is, what can go wrong, what limits the risk today, and the fix we would want. The entries also serve as comparison criteria when looking at alternatives to GitHub or to the current harness: does the alternative have the same gap, or does it close it?

For the enforcement model these seams sit within, see Permission Model. For the identities involved, see Identity Architecture.

docs.title: Adding an entry
docs.text:
Add an entry whenever a new cross-system seam is found. Give each entry the same fields:

  • Seam: the two systems whose guarantees do not line up.
  • Risk: what an agent, or code acting through it, could do as a result.
  • Current mitigation: what limits the risk today. Record only mitigations that are actually in place.
  • Desired fix: the change that would close the seam.
  • Status: open or resolved. Keep resolved entries, and note what resolved them.
  • Tracking: the issue or PR where the fix is followed.

This page is ordinary documentation. Update it through a normal PR when a seam opens, changes or closes. It is not tracked as an open issue.

docs.title: Entries and security records
docs.text:
This page is public, so it follows the Security Records policy:

  • A seam an attacker could use gets a security record while it is open. Create one with vrg-security-record create. The details live in its private advisory, not here.
  • Its entry here stays neutral. Name the seam and point to the tracking issue, but give no detail of how to use the gap: no triggering steps, command shapes or bypass. Fill in the full account when the seam is resolved.
  • Platform limits that are already public stay as they are. A documented limit of GitHub or the harness (such as entry 1) tells an attacker nothing new, so its entry can describe it in full.

docs.title: 1. GitHub permissions are coarser than the agent model
docs.text:
GitHub's permission model cannot express exactly what an agent identity may and may not do. Granting one permission can bring a companion capability we did not want to grant, and there is no finer-grained control over agent capabilities at the level we would design for.

  • Seam: Vergil's least-privilege agent model and the permission shapes GitHub Apps can declare.
  • Risk: an identity can do more than its role should allow.
  • Current mitigation: each role is its own GitHub App (<username>-vergil-user, <username>-vergil-audit) with inverted permission shapes, and App installation scope is kept minimal. The vrg-git and vrg-gh wrappers narrow agent behaviour further, but they are client-side guardrails, not a boundary.
  • Desired fix: finer-grained GitHub App permissions. This needs an upstream change from GitHub that may never come.
  • Comparison criterion: does an alternative offer the granularity GitHub lacks?
  • Status: open.
  • Tracking: no open issue; this entry is the record. It was first logged in vergil-tooling#1369.

docs.title: 2. Repo-supplied provisioning ran as root in a credentialed VM
docs.text:
Per-repo VM profiles (vergil-vm#99) added a provision hook: a consuming repo could ship a shell script that the VM ran as root at provision time. The same VM later holds the identity's GitHub App private key. A hostile or compromised script, or a dependency it pulled, could read and exfiltrate that key. Host isolation protects the laptop; it does not protect a credential inside the VM.

  • Seam: the VM's host-isolation guarantee and the trust level of repo-supplied code running inside it, next to a live credential.
  • Risk: credential exfiltration, or a persistent backdoor planted at provision time.
  • Mitigation before the fix: a stated trust boundary (build a dedicated VM only for a repo you trust to run code as root), and the hook's content was part of the VM spec fingerprint, so any change to it forced a rebuild and a review checkpoint.
  • Fix: the provision hook was removed and replaced with declarative apt_repos, packages and vagrant_plugins keys in the repo's vergil.toml [vm] tables. The reviewed, versioned vergil-vm template owns how they are installed, so no repo-supplied code runs as root. These fields feed the VM spec fingerprint directly.
  • Status: resolved.
  • Tracking: vergil-vm#105 (fixed by vergil-vm#106).

docs.title: 3. A misfiring commit guard pushes agents to disable the sandbox
docs.text:
The vergil plugin's protected-branch hook (block-protected-branch-work.sh) decided which repo a command targeted from the Bash tool's starting directory, which the harness resets to the session root before every call. A vrg-commit in a feature worktree could then be denied as a commit to develop. Agents worked around the false deny by running the command with the sandbox disabled, which removes the whole sandbox boundary for that call.

  • Seam: the harness's pre-execution hook, which sees the reset starting directory, and the command, which runs after its own cd.
  • Risk: agents learn to treat a safety guard as noise and switch off the sandbox to get past it.
  • Mitigation before the fix: vrg-commit checks the real current branch when it runs and refuses commits to protected branches, so the bypass never let a vrg-commit land on develop or main.
  • Fix: the hook no longer matches vrg-commit. vrg-commit already checks the real branch it commits to when it runs, so that run-time check is the authoritative one, and the false deny that pushed agents to disable the sandbox is gone. Raw git commit stays guarded by the hook as before.
  • Status: resolved.
  • Tracking: vergil-claude-plugin#694 (fixed by vergil-claude-plugin#719).

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Permission Model: the enforcement layers and the boundaries agents cannot edit their way out of
  • Identity Architecture: the agent identities and their permission shapes
  • Credential Management: how credentials are minted and selected

docs.title: Security records
docs.text: A security finding never goes into a public issue. Each finding gets a security record: a private draft advisory that holds the details, paired with a neutral issue that drives the work. This guide covers the policy and how to work with a record. The command is vrg-security-record. The design is epic vergil-project/.github#517, extended to several advisories per issue by epic vergil-project/.github#573.

docs.title: The policy
docs.text:
• Every security finding gets one record. A record is one pair (an issue may name several advisories, one per finding; see The two reference lines):
  • a draft repository security advisory in <org>/.github, which holds the details;
  • a neutral security-labelled issue in the intake queue, which holds only a title, a body that says nothing about the problem, and a pointer to the advisory.
  • The same rule for every repo, public or private. Issues are always neutral, and the details always live in the advisory. A private repo gets no exception: its issues are written as if they were public.
  • Fix it within about a day. Security is a top priority. A record is meant to be short-lived: once it is captured, fixing it comes first, with a target of about a day. This target is policy. The tooling does not enforce it.
  • Advisories are secure notes, not a disclosure process. A record is never published and no CVE is requested. Nothing in the tooling stops a human from publishing one later, but that is a separate, deliberate decision.

Advisories complement issues. They don't replace them: the issue is what intake review routes, what a task's PR closes, and what the sweep follows.

docs.title: What counts as a security finding
docs.text:
The definition is paad's, used by every paad review skill:

a finding is security-related if reading it would help an attacker — any OWASP Top 10:2025 category, and anything in a payment, tenant-isolation, or secret-handling path; on the edge, treat it as security.

paad writes such findings only to its gitignored paad/security/ folder, which is local scratch: it lives on one machine and is lost to git clean -x or a deleted worktree. A security record is the durable, private home for them.

docs.title: Where a record lives
docs.text:
• The advisory is always in <org>/.github, whichever repo the finding is about. The affected repo is recorded as the advisory's package name (ecosystem other), so it stays queryable.
  • The issue is created in the affected repo's queue home, the same place vrg-intake-create files an item, and linked under its intake epic:
  • a public repo's queue home is <org>/.github;
  • a private repo keeps its own queues, so its issue stays in the private repo.

It is never created in a public code repo itself.

The org's .github repo must be public. GitHub documents repository security advisories for public repos only. When <org>/.github is not public, every vrg-security-record command refuses, the sweep fails, and vrg-intake-route and vrg-queue planning fail when they meet a security item. None of them falls back to an issue-only record. Orgs with a private .github, and repos owned by a user account rather than an org, are not supported.

docs.title: The two reference lines
docs.text:
Each half of a pair names the other with an exact line, alone on its line:

  • the issue body has one line per advisory it names: Security advisory: <org>/.github <GHSA-id>;
  • the advisory description has one line per issue it tracks: Tracking issue: <owner>/<repo>#<N>.

So the link is many-to-many. One advisory can track several issues (a finding fixed by more than one task), and one issue can name several advisories (one task that fixes more than one finding, or a planning issue that collected several). An issue keeps the security label while any of its advisory lines remains; the label goes only with the last one.

The GHSA ID reveals only that a record exists. Don't edit these lines by hand; vrg-security-record writes and moves them.

docs.title: The labels
docs.text: Label Meaning security Has a private security record in the org's .github advisories. The sweep checks every issue with this label. security-disclosed Past issue that disclosed a security problem publicly; fixed, no private record. The sweep ignores it.

docs.title: Writing a neutral issue
docs.text:
The tool cannot judge whether text is neutral. That is the caller's duty, whether the caller is a human or an agent. The issue title and body go to --title and --body-file; the details go to --details-file, which is sent only to the advisory.

A neutral issue:

  • names the affected area (a command, a module, a workflow) so that intake review can route it, and nothing more;
  • does not describe the weakness, how to trigger it, what an attacker gains, or which input, path, endpoint or secret is involved;
  • has no severity in its title or body (the severity is on the advisory);
  • carries no excerpts of code, logs, payloads or tool output that show the problem.

The same rule covers everything public that the work produces: comments, commit messages, PR titles and bodies, report-ready notes and the relay ref, and Actions logs. Say "fix the security record for <area>", or name the GHSA ID; never restate the finding.

The examples on this page use placeholder text, never a real finding. A neutral title is Test record: security-records API check, and a neutral body is Tracked privately; see the security advisory named below. The details file holds everything else, and its first line becomes the advisory summary unless --summary is given:

PROBE: security-records API check (no real finding)

Probe for epic #517. Not a vulnerability.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
An advisory's severity uses GitHub's terms: critical, high, medium or low. Map a paad severity to it with this table:

GitHub severity agentic-review agentic-owasp pushback, agentic-architecture critical Critical Critical n/a high Important High High medium Suggestion Medium Medium low n/a Low Low

A finding with no paad severity (one an agent or a human found directly) is given a severity by whoever records it.

docs.title: Recording a finding
docs.text:
vrg-security-record create --repo vergil-project/vergil-tooling \
  --title "Test record: security-records API check" \
  --body-file neutral-body.md \
  --details-file details.md \
  --severity low

create runs the steps in a fixed order: a duplicate check, the advisory, the issue, the link under the intake epic, then the advisory's Tracking issue: line. If a step fails after the advisory exists, it prints the exact command that finishes the pair and exits 1. Drafts can't be deleted, so never re-run the original command; run the printed one. See the CLI reference for attach mode (--issue) and resume (--resume).

docs.title: Managing a record through its issue
docs.text:
The issue drives the record. Work the issue like any other: route it, build the fix, close it with the PR. Never change an advisory's state by hand.

The scheduled sweep (vrg-epic-audit --close, run by the org's automation App) keeps each advisory's state in step with the issues it tracks:

  • the advisory is closed when every issue it tracks is closed, whether fixed or dropped as not planned;
  • it is a draft while any of them is open, so reopening an issue reopens its advisory.

A manual state change to a draft or closed advisory is overwritten on the next run. The sweep only moves an advisory between draft and closed. It never touches an advisory in any other state (published, withdrawn, or triage), and never touches an unpaired external report.

Each run also checks every pair and reports the broken ones, by GHSA ID and issue ref only. A pair is broken when:

  • a security issue has no Security advisory: line, or any of its lines names an advisory that does not exist or does not track it;
  • an advisory has no Tracking issue: lines, or tracks an issue that is not a security-labelled issue, or one that does not point back;
  • an advisory is not named by any security issue and is not an external report.

The sweep reports a broken pair and does not repair it; a human decides what to do. Broken pairs make vrg-epic-audit --close exit 1, after it has synced the rest. An org whose .github is private also makes it exit 1.

External reports. .github accepts private vulnerability reports from outside (see its SECURITY.md). GitHub marks such a report with the triage state or a submission. When no security issue names one, the sweep lists it as an unpaired external report, never treats it as broken, and never changes it. To work on one, attach it to an issue with vrg-security-record create --issue.

The sweep's output goes to the public Actions logs of .github, so it names only GHSA IDs, issue refs, labels and states, never advisory text.

docs.title: When the issue moves
docs.text:
A record's link moves only through vrg-security-record retarget, and vrg-intake-route calls it for you:

  • transfer (one-off into another repo): after the move, every advisory the issue names is retargeted, in body order, so each tracking line is rewritten to the issue's new number. If one fails, the move stands and the error names every advisory still not retargeted, with one retarget command for each, to run in order;
  • recreate (when GitHub refuses the transfer): every advisory the issue names is retargeted to the copy, in body order, before the original closes. If one fails, the original stays open, the copy stays unlinked, and the error names every advisory still not retargeted and how to finish;
  • split: an item naming one advisory has it retargeted to every task in --into before the original closes. If that fails, the route stops and the original stays open. The advisory then closes only once every task is closed.

An item naming several advisories is refused before anything changes, because which advisory goes to which task can't be inferred:

vrg-intake-route: <owner>/<repo>#<N> names several advisories (<GHSA-id>, <GHSA-id>); retarget each by hand with vrg-security-record retarget, then split

Retarget each advisory to the task or tasks that fix it, one at a time. The last retarget leaves the item with no advisory line and no security label, so the split that follows is an ordinary one.

An issue an advisory stops tracking loses that advisory's line, and gets the neutral comment Security record moved to <refs>. It loses its security label only when that was its last advisory line; while it still names another advisory, the label and the other lines stay.

docs.title: Security items in planning
docs.text:
A security item can go through planning like any other. Planning discusses the problem in general terms; the details stay in the advisory. A planning issue may name several advisories, and it keeps tracking each of them until the plan exists.

  • Hand each advisory to its fix. When epic-create files the tasks (its step 9), retarget each advisory the planning issue names from the planning issue to the task or tasks that fix it. Run one retarget per advisory, one after another, never in parallel: each retarget rewrites the planning issue's body, so two at once can write back a line the other removed. Post Tasks filed: yes only after every retarget has succeeded:
vrg-security-record retarget GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx \
  --to vergil-project/vergil-tooling#101 \
  --to vergil-project/vergil-tooling#102
vrg-security-record retarget GHSA-yyyy-yyyy-yyyy \
  --to vergil-project/vergil-tooling#103

From then on, the PRs that close those tasks are what close each advisory. - A finding the design itself resolves. A finding that the revised design resolves on its own, with no task implementing it (for example, the spec now removes the mechanism it was about), is retargeted to the epic's documentation task, whose PR publishes the revised spec. Do this only when the weakness exists only in the design and no shipped code has it. A finding about shipped behaviour always goes to a fix task that changes the code. - The guard. vrg-queue planning never shows a planning issue as ready-to-close while any advisory it names still tracks it. It shows it as in-progress with a note that counts the advisories still tracking it and names them by GHSA ID only:

held: 1 advisory still tracks this planning issue (GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx) — retarget each to the task or tasks that fix it with vrg-security-record retarget
held: 2 advisories still track this planning issue (GHSA-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx, GHSA-yyyy-yyyy-yyyy) — retarget each to the task or tasks that fix it with vrg-security-record retarget

After one of two retargets, the planning issue stays held by the other. Don't close the planning issue by hand before every retarget: that would close the remaining advisories with the fix unwritten.

docs.title: Recording findings from a review
docs.text:
A review can raise security findings while the work is still being designed or built. Two recipes cover the reviews that run inside the epic/task framework. Both use only create, retarget and vrg-intake-route. As everywhere on this page, the refs and GHSA IDs are placeholders, not a real finding.

Design review, during epic-create. The review runs against the spec while a planning issue tracks the work:

  • an accepted finding (the design will change, or a task will fix it) is recorded on the planning issue with attach mode, vrg-security-record create --issue <planning issue> …. Step 9 then hands it off to its fix like any other advisory the planning issue names (see Security items in planning);
  • a rejected or dropped finding is recorded with plain create, which gives it its own intake issue, so intake review decides what becomes of it.

Agentic review, during issue-implement. This review records each finding as it is collected, before anyone knows whether the branch will fix it:

  • at collection, record each new or repair security finding with plain create, which gives it its own intake issue (its record). A known finding already has a record, made in an earlier round of the same task, so it is not recorded again;
  • a finding fixed on the branch is handed to the task by splitting its record into it:
vrg-intake-route <record> split --into <task> \
  --reason "Fixed on the task's branch"

The split retargets the advisory to the task and closes the record, so the advisory closes when the task does. A known finding's record is split when the finding is fixed, unless an earlier round already split it; - a finding not fixed needs nothing more. Its record stays an ordinary intake item, with no pointer to the task.

Agentic review does not attach a finding to the task at collection, which is why it records with plain create. If it did, handing an unfixed finding off later would make retarget post the public comment Security record moved to <record> on the task, pointing from the shipped diff to the open record.

docs.title: Checking existing records after the several-advisories change
docs.text:
An issue naming one advisory is a valid case of the several-advisories form, so existing records need no converting and there is no migration code. To confirm an org's live records are consistent, check them by hand:

  • vrg-security-record list shows every advisory and the issues it tracks;
  • vrg-epic-audit (read-only) prints the sweep's pass as a preview, including its broken-pair report.

The sweep reports a broken pair and never repairs it, so a human repairs each one it reports, by hand.

docs.title: Before a private repo goes public
docs.text:
Because issues are neutral everywhere, a private repo's issues hold no security details, and nothing needs converting. Some places are outside the tooling's reach, though. Before you make a private repo public, check each of these by hand:

  • [ ] Git history and commit messages, on every branch and tag that will be published.
  • [ ] PR bodies and review comments, including closed PRs.
  • [ ] Wikis and Actions logs. Logs become public with the repo.
  • [ ] Issues written before this policy existed. Run the past-issues audit on the repo: attach a record to each unfixed one (vrg-security-record create --issue), and label each fixed one security-disclosed.

The repo's epics move separately; see Epic Home Visibility Flips.

docs.title: Accepted trade-offs
docs.text:
• Advisories are not next to their code. Every record is in <org>/.github, so every admin and security manager of .github can see every draft, including one about a private (for example, client) repo. Today those are the same people. The package-name field keeps the affected repo queryable.
  • A public issue shows that a problem exists. For a public repo the issue is public. Its security label and advisory line, together with a title that names the affected area, tell anyone that an unfixed security problem exists in that area. The issue never says what the problem is, and the record is meant to live about a day. This small, deliberate disclosure is accepted in exchange for a visible, queryable label.
  • Agents may manage advisories. Records are notes: the user agent creates, edits and retargets them, and the sweep closes and reopens them. There is no strong protection against an agent editing or closing one.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
vrg-security-record calls the advisories API directly, with the identity's App token or, in human mode, the human's own gh login. It does not go through vrg-gh api, which stays denied to the user agent.

Two Apps need Repository security advisories: Read and write:

  • every user App (<username>-vergil-user), for vrg-security-record and the hooks in vrg-intake-route and vrg-queue;
  • each org's automation App (<org>-automation), for the sweep.

The audit App does not get it; see Account Setup.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• vrg-security-record: the CLI reference
  • Account Setup: App permissions
  • Identity Architecture: the org automation Apps
  • GitHub Issues: the intake, planning and deferred queues

docs.title: Validation Matrix
docs.text: This page maps every validation check to the tool that runs it and where it runs. No git hooks are installed: every check runs inside a vrg-* tool, in the Claude Code hook guard, or in PR CI.

docs.title: Check Summary
docs.text:
Check Run by Local PR CI Raw git / gh blocked Claude Code hook guard (vrg-hook-guard) Agent sessions -- Branch name format at creation vrg-git Yes -- Worktree placement and naming vrg-git worktree add Yes -- Branch switch in the main worktree vrg-git checkout / switch Yes -- Branch and commit context vrg-commit Yes -- No auto-close keyword in the commit body vrg-commit Yes -- PR body issue linkage vrg-submit-pr Yes -- Repository profile vrg-repo-profile (common checks) Yes quality / common Versions resolve against the window; toolchain selection; language floor vrg-validate (config check, before any stage) Yes Every vrg-validate job Markdown, shell, YAML, Dockerfile, workflow and Ansible lint vrg-validate (common checks) Yes quality / common Lint and typecheck vrg-validate Yes (primary version) quality / lint / <version>, quality / typecheck / <version> Tests vrg-validate Yes (primary version; every version with --all-versions, Python only) test / unit / <version> Dependency audit vrg-validate Yes (primary version) audit / dependencies / <version> Custom validator vrg-validate (custom stage) Yes (primary version) quality / custom (once, primary version) Security scans (CodeQL, Trivy, Semgrep) ci-security.yml -- security / * Version bump ci-version-bump.yml -- version / version-bump

"Local" for vrg-validate means vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate, which runs one container on the resolved primary version. PR CI runs the same commands through the vergil-actions reusable workflows on every resolved version (see Version resolution). See CI Architecture for the jobs and the required checks.

The config check runs on every vrg-validate invocation, whatever --check selects. It fails when the repo's versions do not resolve against the published window (a pin outside the window, an app pin of more than one version, an unreadable window) or when a file selects the toolchain behind Vergil's back (for Python, .python-version). A declared floor that falls below the window's oldest version, or an upper bound that excludes its newest (for Python, requires-python), is printed as a warning and does not fail. See Python version management.

docs.title: Claude Code hook guard
docs.text:
Trigger: every Bash tool call in a Claude Code session, in a repository that has a vergil.toml.

.claude/hooks/guard.sh, wired in .claude/settings.json, calls vrg-hook-guard. It blocks raw git and gh commands and lets vrg-git, vrg-gh and the other vrg-* tools through. See the Claude Code Hook Guard reference.

docs.title: vrg-git
docs.text:
Trigger: every vrg-git command.

  • vrg-git worktree add must create the worktree as a direct child of <project-root>/.worktrees/. When -b creates a feature/, bugfix/, hotfix/ or chore/ branch, the branch must be <type>/<N>-<slug> and the directory must be issue-<N>-<slug>.
  • vrg-git checkout -b and vrg-git switch -c apply the same branch name format.
  • On all three creation paths, issue <N> must be open and must not be labelled epic or archive. A failed issue read refuses the branch.
  • When .worktrees/ exists, switching branches in the main worktree is blocked, except to a protected branch.

docs.title: vrg-commit
docs.text:
Trigger: every vrg-commit.

Check Error message Fix Detached HEAD detached HEAD is not allowed for commits Create a branch Protected branch (develop, release, main) direct commits to protected branches are forbidden Create a feature branch Prefix not allowed by [project].branching-model branch name must use ... Rename the branch Missing issue number branch name must include a repo issue number Rename to <type>/<N>-<slug> Work-branch commit from the main worktree when .worktrees/ exists feature-branch commits from the main worktree are forbidden Commit from the worktree Auto-close keyword in --body commit body contains a GitHub auto-close keyword Remove it; linkage goes on the PR

vrg-commit also refuses a commit on a branch frozen by vrg-pr-workflow report-ready, and a commit with nothing staged unless --allow-empty is given. The Git Workflow guide covers the branching models and the per-change cycle.

docs.title: vrg-submit-pr
docs.text:
Trigger: PR creation.

PR body issue linkage is checked when vrg-submit-pr builds the body. Ref #N and Closes #N are accepted; Fixes and Resolves are banned. There is no separate CI check for it.

docs.title: vrg-validate Checks
docs.text: Trigger: vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate locally, and the reusable CI workflows on every pull request.

docs.title: Common checks
docs.text:
vrg-validate --check common runs, in order:

  1. vrg-repo-profile: vergil.toml is present and valid, and README.md follows the structural conventions. See the vrg-repo-profile reference.
  2. markdownlint on docs/site/**/*.md and README.md, with the canonical config bundled in vergil-tooling, then on epics/ with a config that relaxes line length. See the Markdown Validation reference.
  3. shellcheck on shell scripts under scripts/.
  4. yamllint on YAML under .github/ and docs/, with the bundled config.
  5. hadolint on Dockerfile* at the repository root.
  6. actionlint on .github/workflows/.
  7. ansible-lint, when the repository has Ansible content.

The first failing check stops the run. In CI the common checks run once, as quality / common.

docs.title: Language checks
docs.text: vrg-validate then runs the lint, typecheck, test and audit commands for [project].primary-language. Pass --check lint, typecheck, test or audit to run one stage.

docs.title: Custom validator
docs.text:
Last, vrg-validate runs the repository's custom validator, when it has one: scripts/bin/validate-custom or a vrg-validate-custom on PATH. --check custom runs only that stage, after the language's install stage so the validator sees the dev dependencies. With no custom validator it prints custom: no custom validator (scripts/bin/validate-custom or vrg-validate-custom) — nothing to run and exits 0. A validator that is present but not an executable regular file fails the stage. --check custom --all-versions is a usage error.

PR CI runs the same stage once per run, as quality / custom, on the primary-version image that quality / common uses. Its transcript is quality-custom.log in the ci-evidence-quality artifact, and the quality / evidence gate needs the job, so a failed or skipped custom stage fails that gate. quality / custom is not a required check of its own, but every repository requires quality / evidence (see CI gates), so a failing custom validator blocks the merge whatever the repository's language. A repository's custom validator therefore runs both locally and in PR CI.

docs.title: All versions (Python)
docs.text:
vrg-validate --all-versions adds one test (python X.Y) stage per resolved CI version after the test stage, so the --cov-branch --cov-fail-under=100 gate runs on every interpreter PR-CI tests, not only the dev container's. Combine it with --check test to run only the tests. Each stage has uv install the version as a managed interpreter and sync the dev group into its own environment under the container's temp directory, so the project .venv is untouched. The container interpreter's own version is skipped: the plain test stage already covers it. Its coverage and JUnit reports go beside that environment, so the workspace's coverage.xml and junit.xml stay the container interpreter's.

It needs network access to download the interpreters, and it costs one extra suite run per extra version: on a Lima VM a full vrg-container-run -- vrg-validate --all-versions for this repo's four versions takes about 1.5 minutes, against about 20 seconds without it. The default vrg-validate is unchanged. Other languages are refused: their toolchains are not uv-managed, and their PR-CI matrix stays CI-only.

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
Every tool above exits 0 on success and non-zero when a check fails. vrg-repo-profile distinguishes the two failure cases:

Code Meaning 0 vergil.toml and README.md are valid 1 vergil.toml is invalid, or README.md breaks the structural conventions 2 vergil.toml not found

docs.title: Script Reference
docs.text: Vergil-tooling provides Python CLI tools installed as vrg-* console scripts, plus git hooks. For the full audit of every tool's runtime preconditions, host-vs-container classification, and failure modes, see the CLI Tools Overview.

docs.title: Host tools
docs.text:
Run on the developer's machine. Installed via uv tool install or the dev-tree override venv.

Tool Purpose vrg-commit Standards-compliant commit wrapper vrg-submit-pr Standards-compliant PR submission wrapper vrg-release Run the full release workflow, ending with the dependency update vrg-update-deps Update dependencies within their declared bounds and merge the result vrg-finalize-pr Merge a PR and run post-merge cleanup vrg-ensure-label Ensure GitHub labels exist vrg-github-repo-config Audit/reconcile a repo against canonical config vrg-dependabot-audit Fail on any open Dependabot alert vrg-github-repo-init Bootstrap a new managed repository vrg-container-run Run commands inside a dev container vrg-container-test Run test suite inside a dev container vrg-container-docs Preview/build MkDocs in a dev container vrg-container-build-command Print the declared [container].build-command (CI consumption) vrg-container-system-packages Print the declared [container].system-packages (CI consumption) vrg-container-cache Manage the per-branch cached dev image vrg-generate-commands Generate MQSC command methods vrg-host Report, upgrade and pin the macOS host dependencies

docs.title: Container tools
docs.text:
Run inside dev containers launched by vrg-container-run.

Tool Purpose vrg-validate Unified validation driver (common + language-specific checks) vrg-repo-profile Repository profile attribute validation vrg-package Build, install-test and index binary OS packages from [package] vrg-sarif-filter Drop accepted-suppressed results from a SARIF file before upload Markdown validation Markdownlint with bundled canonical config

docs.title: Claude Code Hooks
docs.text: Hook Purpose Claude Code Hook Guard PreToolUse guard that blocks raw git and gh; also documents the vrg-commit branch checks

docs.title: CLI Tools Overview
docs.text: Every CLI command provided by this package, organized by runtime context. Each entry documents the tool's purpose, where it runs, what it assumes, and how it fails when those assumptions are violated.

docs.title: Host tools
docs.text: Host tools run on the developer's machine (outside any container). They drive git, gh, SSH, and Docker operations. Installed via uv tool install or the dev-tree override venv.

docs.title: vrg-commit
docs.text:
Construct standards-compliant conventional commits (no AI co-author trailer; see #3200). Performs five branch/context checks before committing (detached HEAD, protected branch, branch prefix, issue number, worktree convention).

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_commit Args --type (required), --scope (required), --message (required), --body, --allow-empty Preconditions Git repo, staged changes, not detached HEAD, not on protected branch, branch prefix matches branching model, issue number in branch name, not main worktree when .worktrees/ present Failure mode SystemExit with diagnostic on stderr for each check Exit codes 0 success, 1 rejection or error Status Active

docs.title: vrg-submit-pr
docs.text:
Create standards-compliant pull requests. Template mode pushes the current branch and opens a PR from .vergil/pr-workflow.json. Relay branch mode (positional <branch> [<branch> …]) opens PRs worktree-free for branches already on origin — the Mac side of the cloud→Mac handoff: each branch's ready-state comes from a local worktree's pr-workflow.json when present, else the relay ref refs/vergil/pr-workflow/<branch>; origin's tip is checked against the recorded head_sha and the PR opens with --head without pushing. It refuses an issue whose native parent is an intake, planning or deferred epic (see vrg-pr-workflow).

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_submit_pr Args positional branches (relay mode); or --issue (required), --summary (required), --linkage (default: Ref; vrg-submit-pr auto-selects Closes for a managed task — Fixes/Resolves are banned), --notes, --title, --dry-run Preconditions Git repo, gh CLI on PATH; relay mode: named branches on origin with a resolvable ready-state and matching head_sha Failure mode Subprocess error from git push or gh pr create; relay mode: loud failure on a missing ready-state or head_sha drift Exit codes 0 success Status Active

docs.title: vrg-pr-fix-body
docs.text:
Repair a PR's body by regenerating it from corrected fields through the same validated builder as vrg-submit-pr, then push an empty commit to re-trigger CI. The agent-safe fix path for body-level standards failures during the pr-watch reconcile loop (denied to the audit identity; the user identity may only fix its own PR).

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_pr_fix_body Args pr (positional, required), --issue (required), --summary (required), --linkage (default: Ref), --notes, --dry-run, --no-retrigger Preconditions Git repo, gh CLI on PATH, PR open, agent identities on the PR's head branch Failure mode SystemExit/diagnostic on identity, scope, or state rejection Exit codes 0 success, 1 rejection or error Status Active

docs.title: vrg-pr-workflow
docs.text:
Record and manage the PR handoff state in .vergil/pr-workflow.json — the oracle vrg-submit-pr reads. report-ready writes the PR metadata (--issue/--title/--summary/--notes, optional --linkage) and marks the branch ready; it is idempotent — re-running overwrites the recorded prose (correcting the title/summary/notes is always allowed). report-ready always also mirrors the ready-state onto the reserved relay ref refs/vergil/pr-workflow/<branch> (unconditional — no config, no off-platform detection), so a cloud VM's report-ready reaches the Mac that later runs vrg-submit-pr <branch> even though the two never share a disk. The relay push is a pure ref write built with git plumbing; it never advances the branch, so it stays freeze-neutral. A push failure is loud on stderr but never rolls back the durable local file. Because the ref is world-readable on a public repo, keep secrets out of --title/--summary/--notes. Reaching ready freezes the branch: vrg-commit and the vrg-git push path then refuse further commits/pushes, because a task is exactly one PR and more work is a new follow-up issue (epic #146). report-ready pushes the branch itself, to origin/<branch> with upstream set, before recording anything (#3602), so no separate push is needed; a branch already on origin at that commit is a no-op push. When the delta touches .github/workflows/** GitHub refuses the agent push: report-ready reports that as expected, records the state anyway, and the human's vrg-submit-pr pushes the branch. Any other push failure fails report-ready with no local state and no relay ref written. A re-run on a frozen branch whose HEAD has drifted past the reported commit is refused before any push. An explicit vrg-git push [-u] origin <branch> also stays allowed while HEAD is exactly the reported commit — it publishes, not advances, the branch (issue #3071). unfreeze is the only sanctioned way to reopen a still-unsubmitted branch — it drops the state back to implementing while keeping the metadata; an already-submitted branch cannot be unfrozen. status prints the current state. report-ready (like vrg-submit-pr) refuses an issue whose native parent is an intake, planning or deferred epic: a queue item is not buildable until intake review routes it, epic-create expands it, or deferred review revives it (epics vergil-project/.github#176 and #508).

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_pr_workflow Args report-ready (--issue, --title, --summary, --notes required; --linkage default Ref), unfreeze, status; global --base (default: origin/develop) Preconditions Git repo; run from the worktree whose branch is being staged Failure mode WorkflowError on stderr (e.g. unfreeze after submit, or nothing to unfreeze) Exit codes 0 success, 1 error Status Active

docs.title: vrg-release
docs.text:
Run the full release workflow from develop to main: tracking issue, changelog, release PR and merge, CD confirmation, back-merge and version bump, rolling-tag promotion, cleanup, consumer refresh, and finally the update-deps stage, which runs the dependency update on the new develop version. On a fresh start, preflight refuses while an open PR carries the dependency-update label, after first closing any whose fix task completed. Human-only. See the vrg-release reference and the Releasing guide.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_release Args minor/major (optional positional), --no-promote, --without-deps, --allow-pending-deps, --install, --resume [X.Y.Z], --skip-audit, --output-window, --output-format Preconditions Human identity; on develop, clean working tree, local develop matches origin/develop; gh authenticated and git-cliff on PATH Failure mode Fail-fast stages stop the run; deferred stages (including update-deps) record the failure, let later stages run, and are summarized at the end Exit codes 0 success, 1 any failure or refusal, 130 interrupted Status Active

docs.title: vrg-update-deps
docs.text:
Update the repo's dependencies to the newest versions their declared bounds allow, in a deps/update-<version> managed worktree: run the applicable updaters (python, vergil, images, then the repo hook), validate once, open a dependency-update-labelled PR, and merge it. A no-op run opens no PR. A validation or merge failure leaves the PR open and files a fix task; an updater or hook failure opens no PR but still files a fix task. Every run prints the held-back report. vrg-release runs the same pipeline as its update-deps stage. Human-only. See the vrg-update-deps reference and the dependency-update reference.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_update_deps Args --only NAME[,NAME], --skip NAME[,NAME], --vergil X.Y (mutually exclusive), --output-window, --output-format Preconditions Human identity; on develop, clean working tree, local develop matches origin/develop; gh authenticated; no existing deps/update-<version> branch Failure mode Updater, validation and merge failures are recorded, the worktree is cleaned up, then the run exits non-zero Exit codes 0 success or no-op, 1 failure or refusal, 130 interrupted Status Active

docs.title: vrg-upstream-refresh
docs.text:
Run the repo's [upstream-refresh].hook on a clean checkout of the base branch, then open, refresh or close the single upstream-refresh PR. A no-change run closes any stale refresh PR, or exits quietly when there is none. It never merges, and never runs dependency updaters, validation or a release. It runs from the scheduled ops-upstream-refresh workflow, or by hand as a human. See the upstream-refresh reference.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_upstream_refresh Args --repo OWNER/NAME (default: $GITHUB_REPOSITORY, then origin), --base BRANCH (default: the repo's default branch), --dry-run Preconditions Not an agent identity; [upstream-refresh] in vergil.toml; clean working tree with HEAD at origin/<base>; gh authenticated with contents and pull-requests write Failure mode A hook failure or untracked files left by the hook stop the run before any push; errors on stderr Exit codes 0 any outcome (nothing, closed, opened, refreshed, unchanged), 1 error or refusal Status Active

docs.title: vrg-finalize-pr
docs.text:
Finalize a pull request. Given a PR, runs the provenance check, merges it, then cleans up; with no PR, runs cleanup only. Cleanup switches to the target branch, fast-forward pulls, deletes merged local branches (auto-removing worktrees inside .worktrees/ when necessary), deletes each merged branch's PR-workflow relay ref (refs/vergil/pr-workflow/<branch>) and sweeps any orphaned relay ref whose branch is gone (issue #2369), prunes remotes, runs validation, and checks the CD workflow status. It also removes each merged branch's cached dev images and sweeps cached images whose branch is live in no repo of the platform repo set, as vrg-container-cache prune decides it (skipped on the physical host, which has no default repo set); a failed image removal is reported as a warning, never a failed finalize (issue #3566). A merged/closed worktree the sweep cannot remove — a dirty tree, or a reused branch name with unmerged commits (issue #1719) — is surfaced prominently after the pipeline rather than buried in the stage log; --clean-dirty opt-in clears one whose only dirt is untracked build/validation output, after showing the paths and confirming (issue #2348).

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_finalize_pr Args PR (optional), --target-branch (default: develop), --strategy (default: squash), --allow-provenance-violation, --clean-dirty, --dry-run Preconditions Must run from the main worktree, vrg-container-run on PATH Failure mode Provenance violations, a dirty working tree, validation failures, or a failed CD run all return exit 1 Exit codes 0 success, 1 provenance/worktree/validation/CD failure or unrecognized branching model Status Active

docs.title: vrg-branch-sweep
docs.text:
Report, or with --apply delete, a repo's finished remote branches: the newest PR is merged or closed, none is open, and the branch tip still equals that PR's head. The safety net behind the delete-on-merge repo setting and the delete-on-close rule (issue #3332). Never deletes the default branch, develop, main, gh-pages, a protected branch (branch protection or any ruleset rule), a branch with no PR, or a branch whose name was reused (issue #1719). See vrg-branch-sweep.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_branch_sweep Args --repo OWNER/NAME (default: the current repo), --apply (default: dry run) Preconditions gh authenticated with read access (delete access for --apply) to the target repo Failure mode A per-branch gh error is reported on that branch's line, the rest are processed, then exit 1 Exit codes 0 success, 1 any branch error, listing failure or auth failure, 2 bad arguments Status Active

docs.title: vrg-intake-create
docs.text:
Capture an uncurated item — a bug, an idea, an investigation, a one-line "don't forget X" — into the intake queue (epic vergil-project/.github#176). The issue is filed in the current repo's queue home (<org>/.github for a public repo, the repo itself for a self-homed private one) and linked under that home's Epic (intake): <name> as it is created, so there is no unlinked path. It carries no kind label. The intake epic is resolved (created if absent) before the issue is created; if linking the created issue fails, the tool exits 1 naming its URL and the vrg-epic-move command that links it. Used by the intake-capture skill. See Intake, planning and deferred queues.

vrg-triage-create is a deprecated alias kept for one release: it warns on stderr, ignores --kind (intake has no kind label), and forwards every other argument to vrg-intake-create.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_intake_create (alias: vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_triage_create) Args --title (required), --body / --body-file, --label (repeatable), --assignee (repeatable), --repo OWNER/NAME (default: the current repo's queue home) Preconditions Run inside a repo in the target org, or pass --repo; GitHub App credentials for that org Failure mode An extra --label missing from the registry is refused before anything is created; a failed link after creation exits 1 naming the created issue Exit codes 0 created and linked, 1 error Status Active

docs.title: vrg-intake-route
docs.text:
Route one item between the container epics — intake, planning, ad hoc and deferred — applying one queue-review decision. Owns the routing mechanics — transfer-or-recreate, reparent, re-link, close with a pointer, record a deferral — so no review skill hand-rolls them. Routes:

  • drop --reason TEXT — comment the reason, naming the queue it was dropped from (Dropped in <queue> review: …), and close (not planned).
  • defer --reason TEXT --revisit-when TEXT [--date YYYY-MM-DD] — move the item into its queue home's deferred epic and post the deferral record:
Deferred <YYYY-MM-DD>: <reason>
Revisit when: <conditions>
Deferred from: <owner>/<repo>#<N>

--date stamps an original deferral date instead of today. The item is linked before the record is posted, and a planning item's in-progress label is removed. On an item already deferred, defer is a refresh: a new record, no move, and no Deferred from: line. If the record fails after the move, the command fails loudly and prints the full intended comment to post by hand. - intake — reparent a deferred item back onto its home's intake epic. - one-off --repo OWNER/REPO [--epic REF] — move the item into the target repo (transfer, or recreate with a link back when GitHub refuses the transfer) and link it under that repo's ad-hoc epic (default adhoc) or the named epic. - planning — reparent the item onto the planning epic of the same queue home. - split --into REF [--into REF …] --reason TEXT — comment links to the replacement tasks (already created with vrg-issue-create) and close.

Which routes an item allows depends on the container epic it is in:

Item is in Allowed routes intake drop, defer, one-off, planning, split planning defer, drop — both refused once an Epic: marker is recorded ad hoc defer — refused while an open PR would close the item deferred defer (refresh), intake, planning, one-off, drop, split no parent planning (the epic-create free-text path) a development epic, or anything else none — refused, naming the parent Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_intake_route (mechanics and route table: lib/intake_route.py) Args <issue-ref> (owner/repo#N, or #N in the current repo), then a route: drop, defer, intake, one-off, planning, split Preconditions The item is a child of a container epic that allows the route (planning also accepts an unparented issue); GitHub App credentials for the item's org Failure mode A refused route — not allowed from the item's container, a development-epic task, a planning item with an Epic: marker, an ad-hoc item with an open closing PR, a cross-org target, or a private item headed to a public repo or epic — exits 1 with the reason on stderr. A route half-applied by a failure raises with the state it left and how to fix it Exit codes 0 routed, 1 refused or error, 2 bad arguments (including a missing --revisit-when or a malformed --date) Status Active

A security item keeps its advisory links. A recreate retargets every advisory the item names before the original closes, and a transfer retargets every one after the move; on a failure, either names every advisory still not retargeted. A split retargets an item's one advisory before the original closes. A split of an item naming several advisories is refused before any change, because which advisory goes to which task can't be inferred:

vrg-intake-route: <owner>/<repo>#<N> names several advisories (<GHSA-id>, <GHSA-id>); retarget each by hand with vrg-security-record retarget, then split

See Security Records.

docs.title: vrg-security-record
docs.text:
Record a security finding as a private draft advisory in <org>/.github paired with a neutral security-labelled intake issue (epic vergil-project/.github#517). create makes the pair (or attaches an advisory to an existing issue, or resumes an unfinished pair), list and show read records, and retarget moves an advisory's tracking to new issues. Advisory text is printed only by show and list --details. See vrg-security-record and Security Records.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_security_record (library: lib/security_records.py) Args create --repo --title --body-file --details-file --severity [--summary] [--issue] [--resume]; list [--repo] [--state draft\|closed\|all] [--details]; show GHSA-ID\|OWNER/REPO#N; retarget GHSA-ID --to REF [--to REF …] Preconditions The org's .github is public; Repository security advisories: Read and write on the identity's App (or a human gh login with access) Failure mode A partial pair exits 1 naming what exists and the exact --resume command that finishes it; a private .github, a duplicate draft, or --details under VRG_EPIC_SWEEP is refused Exit codes 0 success, 1 refused or error, 2 bad arguments Status Active

docs.title: vrg-queue
docs.text:
Read-only view of a standing queue. vrg-queue intake lists the open items under the intake epic, oldest first. vrg-queue planning lists the open items under the planning epic with their state: waiting (no in-progress label), in-progress (labelled, with its latest progress note), or ready-to-close (labelled, the Epic: / Docs task: / Tasks filed: yes markers present, and the docs task closed). A planning item that any security advisory it names still tracks is held at in-progress until every such advisory is retargeted to the task or tasks that fix it, with a note that counts them and names them by GHSA ID only (held: <k> advisory still tracks this planning issue (<GHSA-id>) — … for one, held: <k> advisories still track this planning issue (<GHSA-id>, …) — … for more; see Security Records). vrg-queue deferred lists the open items under the deferred epic, all waiting, least recently deferred first; each item's note is its latest deferral (Deferred <day>: <reason> | Revisit when: <conditions>), and an item with no deferral comment sorts first with an empty note. A bare vrg-queue lists all three queues in that order (intake, planning, deferred). Used by the collect step of the three review skills (intake-review, planning-review, deferred-review) and by epic-create's no-argument summary.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_queue (views: lib/queue_view.py) Args {intake,planning,deferred} (optional; default: all three); --repo OWNER/NAME (that repo's queue home; default: the current org's .github queues); --json (a list of items; with no queue named, an object keyed by queue, null for a missing one) Preconditions GitHub App credentials for the target org Failure mode A named queue whose home has no live queue epic exits 1 naming the missing epic; with no queue named, a missing queue prints <queue> queue for <name> in <home>: no queue yet and the run exits 0. Nothing is created Exit codes 0 success, 1 error, 2 bad arguments Status Active

docs.title: vrg-epic-audit
docs.text:
Report epic/task drift and invariant violations for an org, as Markdown on stdout. It is read-only by default. Drift is a task still open although the merged PR that Refs it landed within the last --window-days days, and an open finite epic whose children are all closed. The invariant checks are the compliance invariants: epics outside .github, stray .github issues, a closed epic with an open child, orphans, retired kind labels, body-only Parent: links, self-homed queues in a now-public repo, and private work under a public epic. It also lists open epics with operational tasks still pending, and closed operational tasks with no Outcome: SUCCESS. The report previews, without writing, the ad-hoc and queue-epic drains and the security-records pass that --close would run.

The org comes from the current repo's origin remote (there is no --org flag). --repo OWNER/NAME audits that repo's resolved epic home instead of the org's .github, so a private repo that self-homes its epics can be audited; the home-scoped checks (epic drift, stray issues, operation-pending epics, and the --close drift closes) then target it. --epic REF is a separate read-only mode: it prints one epic's children as JSON ({"epic": <slug>, "children": [{repo, number, title, state}, …]}) and skips the drift audit. A bare #N resolves against the current repo's epic home.

--close applies the fixes, in order:

  1. Close the drifted tasks and rolled-up epics, and reopen each epic closed while a child was still open, with an explanatory comment on each.
  2. Drain the closed children of the ad-hoc, intake, planning and deferred epics into per-quarter archives, and close past archives (see Ad-hoc epic archiving).
  3. Run the orphan pass: nativize body-only Parent: links, strip the retired kind labels, move a now-public repo's queue items under .github, and attach every orphan to its home's intake epic.
  4. Run the security-records pass, even when the orphan pass failed: each paired draft advisory in the org's .github is set to closed once every issue it tracks is closed, and back to draft while any is open; broken pairs are reported, not repaired. Its output names only GHSA IDs, issue refs and states, never advisory text (see Security Records).

--close is a human action, or the scheduled ops-epic-sweep workflow, which sets VRG_EPIC_SWEEP=1. Other invariant violations stay report-only.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_epic_audit (checks and passes: lib/epic_audit.py; security pass: lib/security_records.py) Args --window-days N (positive; default 30), --repo OWNER/NAME, --epic REF, --close Preconditions Run inside a repo in the target org; GitHub App credentials for that org. --close needs a human identity or VRG_EPIC_SWEEP=1. The security-records pass needs Repository security advisories: Read and write Failure mode --close in an agent session is refused before any network call; a --repo without /, an org that cannot be detected, or an org with no .github home exits 1. A full intake epic stops the orphan pass, listing what it did not attach; a broken security pair or a failed security pass exits 1 after the rest of the run. With --epic, a ref that is not an epic exits 1 Exit codes 0 success (the read-only report exits 0 even when it finds drift), 1 refused, a pass failed, or error, 2 bad arguments Status Active

docs.title: vrg-worktree-status
docs.text:
Show every worktree git knows about in the current repo, grouped by kind, so nothing with code on disk goes unseen (issue #3386). Read-only — cleanup stays vrg-finalize-pr's job, and finalize and sweep still act only on development worktrees. Local branches with no worktree are not shown. The sections, in order:

  1. Main checkout — always shown. Its STATUS is ok, or PROBLEM: followed by each issue found: not on the integration branch, dirty, or mid-rebase. The integration branch comes from the branching-model in vergil.toml (every current model integrates on develop); without a vergil.toml it defaults to develop and a note says so. A malformed vergil.toml is an error (exit 1).
  2. Development — issue-branch worktrees under .worktrees/: a feature/, bugfix/, hotfix/ or chore/ branch carrying an issue number (<type>/<N>-<slug>), including the chore/<N>-dep-update-* fix branch vrg-update-deps asks for. An issue prefix without an issue number, or an unknown prefix, goes to Other / unknown. A mid-rebase worktree is placed by the branch recovered from the paused rebase or its issue-<N>-<slug> directory name.
  3. Release and dependency machinery — release/*, release/post-* and deps/update-* worktrees. These are meant to be single-run, so each row shows age, PR state and dirty state and a leftover stands out.
  4. Other / unknown — any other branch, a detached HEAD, or a worktree outside .worktrees/ (shown by its full path).

Empty sections are omitted; the summary line counts every section, including the empty ones. A branch that was deleted on its remote is still listed, with (branch gone) after its name. That check queries each remote once; if it fails, a note gives the reason.

The worktree sections share one table. PR state is queried from GitHub per worktree; a failed lookup shows as unknown with the reason rather than being silently downgraded. The development summary counts fall into disjoint buckets — active, needs-attention, stalled (no-pr), and cruft (removable). A finished-but-stuck worktree (merged/closed but not removable: dirty, or a reused branch name whose merged verdict was withheld, issue #1719) is counted under needs-attention with an actionable note, never miscounted as active behind a "0 cruft" message (issue #2347). A merged release or deps worktree shows as merged in its own section but is not counted as vrg-finalize-pr cruft.

Main checkout (integration branch: develop)
CHECKOUT               BRANCH   DIRTY  LAST COMMIT  STATUS
mq-gateway-replay-lab  develop  -      23d ago      ok

Development
WORKTREE                      BRANCH                          PR  STATE  WORKFLOW  AHEAD  DIRTY  LAST COMMIT  LAST MODIFIED
issue-315-deps-security-bump  feature/315-deps-security-bump  -   no-pr  ready     1      -      1h ago       1h ago

Other / unknown
WORKTREE         BRANCH      PR  STATE     WORKFLOW  AHEAD  DIRTY  LAST COMMIT  LAST MODIFIED
tmp-wheel-build  (detached)  -   detached  -         0      -      82d ago      82d ago
  note: tmp-wheel-build (detached): detached HEAD — no branch checked out; check out a branch to resume work

3 worktrees: main checkout (ok), 1 development, 0 release and dependency machinery, 1 other / unknown.
Development: 0 active, 0 needs-attention, 1 stalled (no-pr), 0 cruft (removable). 1 PR prepared.
Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_worktree_status Args --target-branch (default: develop) — the branch AHEAD is measured against Preconditions Git repo; gh CLI on PATH for PR state Failure mode None for classification — a failed PR lookup is reported as an unknown row and a failed branch-gone check as a note, never a crash. A malformed vergil.toml exits 1 with the reason Exit codes 0 success, 1 malformed vergil.toml Status Active

docs.title: vrg-ensure-label
docs.text:
Ensure GitHub labels exist. Three modes: single-label (create/update one label), sync (provision all labels from the canonical registry, and delete the registry's delete list and the retired triage, idea and research labels where present), and project (discover repos via a GitHub Project and sync each). The registry is src/vergil_tooling/data/labels.json; the labels it defines are listed in GitHub Issue Standards.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_ensure_label Args --repo, --label, --color, --description, --sync, --owner, --project Preconditions gh CLI on PATH Failure mode argparse validation for incompatible flag combinations; subprocess error from gh Exit codes 0 success Status Active

docs.title: vrg-github-repo-config
docs.text:
Audit a managed repo against the canonical Vergil configuration, and in apply mode reconcile the GitHub half. Combines local filesystem checks (vergil.toml, CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json, hook-guard shim, workflow pins, .gitignore managed fence, canonical dependabot.yml, ops.yml wiring) with GitHub-API checks (repo settings, rulesets, required-check set). Runs nightly from each repo's ops.yml via the reusable ops-github-config.yml workflow, where drift is fatal. See the GitHub Config Audit reference.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_github_repo_config Args audit | diff | apply; --repo OWNER/REPO, --config PATH Preconditions Local checks require the repo's own checkout as CWD; GitHub checks require gh credentials Failure mode DiffItem list on drift; clean diagnostic on unreachable GitHub state Exit codes 0 compliant, 1 non-compliant (drift), 2 audit could not complete Status Active

docs.title: vrg-dependabot-audit
docs.text:
Fail on any open Dependabot alert, at any severity: the gate for the fleet's report-only Dependabot posture. Private repos get an itemized report; public repos (and any repo whose visibility cannot be resolved) get counts by severity and the Security-tab link only. See the Dependabot Alert Audit reference.

Attribute Value Source vergil_tooling.bin.vrg_dependabot_audit Args --repo OWNER/REPO (required) Preconditions A token with "Dependabot alerts: Read" on the repo; alerts enabled on the repo Failure mode One vrg-dependabot-audit: diagnostic on stderr when the alerts cannot be read Exit codes 0 no open alerts, 1 at least one open alert, 2 could not check Status Active

docs.title: vrg-github-repo-init
docs.text:
Interactive (or --non-interactive) wizard that bootstraps a new managed repository: creates and clones the repo, generates vergil.toml, scaffolds config files (CLAUDE.md, hook-guard shim, the managed .gitignore fence, the canonical report-only .github/dependabot.yml), scaffolds the language skeleton (born-green — see below), generates CI/CD/epic-rollup/ops.yml workflows, the docs site, branch structure, GitHub config, and Pages. The scaffolded base + <language> .gitignore fence, canonical dependabot.yml and staggered-cron ops.yml make a new repo pass the config audit's checks for those files from day one.

The vergil series a new repo uses comes from the installed vergil-tooling: [dependencies].vergil defaults to its vX.Y, and the generated workflows pin the vergil-actions reusable workflows to that series. A new repo therefore starts on the series that created it.

Born-green language skeleton. A dedicated scaffolding step (step 5, lib/lang_scaffold.py) renders the language's packaged skeleton templates (src/vergil_tooling/data/skeletons/<lang>/) into the fresh checkout, stamping only files that are missing so it never clobbers existing content.
