Not with version noarch boolean false Architecture-independent: one build cell on amd64, emitting deb all / rpm noarch exclude list of globs [] Targets to drop from the default set targets list of globs (unset) Explicit subset replacing the default set native list of globs [] Selected targets that get their own build cell inside their own OS

docs.title: [package.python]
docs.text:
Valid only with builder = "python", and optional there.

Key Type Default Semantics runtime string derived Exact-patch pin (3.Y.Z) on the vergil-python runtime. Absent, the runtime is derived (see below) commands list of strings all of [project.scripts] The commands to shim into /usr/bin; each must be in [project.scripts]

vergil-python publishes one package per CPython series it lists, vergil-python<X.Y>, as one [[package]] entry each. Every vergil-python release publishes every listed series. The version is the entry's upstream-version joined with the vergil-python release, <cpython>+<pbs-tag>.<release> (for example 3.15.1+20261021.1.0.4); releases before v1.0.4 are <cpython>+<pbs-tag> alone. Its patch floats: each release replaces the previous patch. A package always builds against, installs and depends on the per-series package, at /opt/vergil/python/<X.Y>.

With no runtime, the series is derived: it is the newest resolved version whose window entry marks the runtime published (epic vergil-project/.github#407, spec §7). The build takes whatever patch the series package serves. This is the recommended setting.

A runtime pin keeps its X.Y in the window and builds on vergil-python<X.Y>, never the legacy per-patch vergil-python<X.Y.Z>. It is exact: after installing the series package, the build checks that the CPython part of the installed version equals the pinned X.Y.Z. If the repository serves any other patch, the build fails with the served version and a fix: remove the pin, or update it to the served patch. A pin cannot hold the build on an older patch, because the series package no longer serves it. The pin governs the build only. The built package depends on vergil-python<X.Y> (>= <installed version>), so consumers still take later patches of the series.

docs.title: [package.staged]
docs.text:
Valid only with builder = "staged".

Key Type Default Semantics build-command string (unset) Command that populates $VRG_STAGING_ROOT (an empty directory standing in for /) for $VRG_TARGET_ARCH. A non-zero exit is a hard error

A staged package needs a build-command, overlay contents, or both. A staging root that ends up empty is a build-time error.

The build-command runs from the repo root via bash -c, with these variables set:

Variable Value VRG_STAGING_ROOT The empty staging directory, standing in for / VRG_TARGET_ARCH The build cell's architecture (amd64 or arm64) VRG_PACKAGE_NAME The package being built (its name), so one script can serve several [[package]] entries VRG_PACKAGE_VERSION The package's full version: <upstream-version>.<repo version>, the version override, or the repo version

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
Supported targets live in a registry in vergil-tooling (src/vergil_tooling/lib/package/targets.py). Each target is <distro>/<version>/<arch>, and the distro implies the format:

Target Format Suite glibc Install-test image ubuntu/24.04/{amd64,arm64} .deb noble 2.39 ubuntu:24.04 ubuntu/26.04/{amd64,arm64} .deb resolute 2.43 ubuntu:26.04 rhel/9/{amd64,arm64} .rpm el9 2.34 registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi rhel/10/{amd64,arm64} .rpm el10 2.39 registry.access.redhat.com/ubi10/ubi

Adding a target, such as Ubuntu 28.04, is a registry change and a vergil-tooling release. No workflow changes.

docs.title: Matrix resolution and the 2×2 default
docs.text:
vrg-package matrix turns the config into explicit JSON lists of build cells and test cells. The workflows consume only that JSON.

  • Every non-native selected target on an architecture shares one build cell (shared-amd64, shared-arm64). It builds in ubuntu:24.04 and emits every format its targets need.
  • Each native target gets its own build cell (native-<distro>-<version>-<arch>) inside a container of that OS.
  • A noarch package has exactly one build cell, shared-noarch, on amd64.
  • Every selected target gets its own test cell (test-<distro>-<version>-<arch>).
  • With several [[package]] entries, each entry resolves its own cells, and every id is qualified with its package name as <name>--<id>, for example vergil-python3.15--shared-amd64 or vergil-python3.15--test-rhel-9-arm64. The double dash never occurs in an unqualified id, so per-cell artifact names never collide. A single package keeps the unqualified ids above.

Every cell in the JSON carries its package name.

With the defaults (2 distros × 2 versions × 2 architectures, no native) this gives 2 build cells, 4 artifacts (a .deb and an .rpm per architecture) and 8 test cells. Runners are ubuntu-24.04 for amd64 and ubuntu-24.04-arm for arm64.

docs.title: Tiers: full and reduced
docs.text:
vrg-package matrix --tier {full,reduced} picks how much of the matrix runs. The default is full: every build cell and every test cell, as above.

reduced is the cheaper gate for feature PRs (the full matrix runs on release PRs). It keeps every build cell, because build breaks are cheap to catch and common, and one test cell per format present (per package, with several [[package]] entries):

  • the oldest selected release of that format (compared numerically, so RHEL 9 before RHEL 10), on amd64, else on arm64. The oldest release is the strictest compatibility case: lowest glibc, oldest rpm/dnf and systemd. A package that installs there nearly always installs on newer releases, which the full tier still covers on release PRs;
  • drawn from the shared targets; a native target is chosen only when the format has no shared target.

With the defaults, reduced gives the same 2 build cells and 2 test cells: test-rhel-9-amd64 and test-ubuntu-24.04-amd64. A deb-only product (targets = ["ubuntu/*/*"]) gets one, test-ubuntu-24.04-amd64.

The printed JSON carries "tier", and --github-output writes a tier= line after enabled, build and test. --manifest is unaffected: the build cells, and so the release artifact manifest, are the same in both tiers.

docs.title: The release manifest
docs.text:
vrg-package matrix --manifest PATH writes packages-manifest.json, which the release attaches and the index reads:

{
  "artifacts": [
    {"fmt": "deb", "arch": "amd64", "suite": null, "name": "vergil-python3.14"},
    {"fmt": "deb", "arch": "amd64", "suite": null, "name": "vergil-python3.15"}
  ],
  "runtimes": {"vergil-python3.14": null, "vergil-python3.15": null}
}
  • artifacts lists one (fmt, arch, suite) per artifact built. With several packages, each one also names its package as name. A single package's artifact list has no name key and is exactly what it always was.
  • runtimes maps each package name to the vergil-python runtime its release resolved, or null for a non-python package.
  • A single package with a runtime also keeps the top-level runtime, the shape that older readers check.

The index pairs each manifest entry with exactly one attached file. A named entry matches only files of that exact package name, so two packages built for the same (fmt, arch, suite) each claim their own file, and a package named foo never claims foo-bar's files. An entry without name (a single package, or any release from before multi-package repos) matches as it always did. A manifest that names some artifacts but not others is rejected.

Because a shared cell builds on Ubuntu 24.04 for every target, the python builder applies a glibc floor guard: any ELF object in the venv that needs a GLIBC_x.y symbol newer than the lowest glibc among the cell's targets is a hard error. Trip it, and the fix is to mark the affected targets native.

The package revision is 1 for shared builds, and 1~<suite> (deb) or 1.<suite> (rpm) for native builds.

docs.title: python
docs.text:
In each build cell, as root:

  1. Enable the vergil package repository and install vergil-python<X.Y> with the OS package manager, as a consumer would. With a runtime pin, check that it serves the pinned patch.
  2. Create the venv at its final path, /opt/<vendor>/<name>/venv, against /opt/vergil/python/<X.Y>/bin/python<X.Y>.
  3. Install from uv.lock only (uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-editable --compile-bytecode). uv.lock must exist next to vergil.toml.
  4. Apply the glibc floor guard.
  5. Add /usr/bin/<cmd> symlinks to venv/bin/<cmd> for each shimmed command.

The package depends on the runtime it was built against: vergil-python<X.Y> (>= <installed-version>) (deb) or vergil-python<X.Y> >= <installed-version> (rpm).

docs.title: staged
docs.text: Runs the optional build-command, merges the overlay's files over the staging root, and packages the result. Used for vergil-python itself and for the <org>-archive-keyring package.

docs.title: Install layout
docs.text:
/opt/<vendor>/python/<X.Y>/        runtime (vergil-python)
/opt/<vendor>/<name>/venv/         product venv
/usr/bin/<cmd>  -> venv/bin/<cmd>  command shims
/etc/<vendor>/<name>/              config (overlay, noreplace)
/var/lib/<vendor>/<name>/          state

A package owns every directory strictly below /opt/<vendor>, never /opt/<vendor> itself, which is shared.

docs.title: The overlay contract
docs.text:
Files beyond the builder's output (systemd units, /etc config, maintainer scripts) go in an optional packaging/nfpm.overlay.yaml, merged over the nFPM config the tooling generates. nFPM's schema is not re-encoded in TOML.

The tooling owns the package's identity (name, version, release, arch and so on). The overlay may set only these top-level keys:

Key Meaning contents Extra files: mappings with a string dst (relative src paths resolve against the repo root) scripts Maintainer scripts: script name → repo-relative path overrides Per-format settings under deb / rpm: depends, contents, scripts, and the relationship keys provides, conflicts, replaces, recommends, suggests Relationships: lists of strings

depends is not allowed at the top level, because deb and rpm spell dependencies differently. Put it under overrides.deb.depends and overrides.rpm.depends.

docs.title: Systemd units: the helper-macro rule
docs.text:
Install tests run in plain containers without systemd as PID 1, so:

  • Maintainer scripts that enable or start units must use the standard helpers, which do nothing when systemd is not running: deb-systemd-helper / deb-systemd-invoke on Ubuntu, and /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-update-helper (the %systemd_post / %systemd_preun equivalent) on RHEL.
  • A raw systemctl call (bare or by path) in any overlay maintainer script is a hard error at package build time. Comments are ignored.
  • The install test checks that each shipped unit file is installed and passes systemd-analyze verify. Whether the service actually starts and works is proven in a lab, not in CI.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
vrg-validate treats each of these as a hard error, never a warning:

  • a target glob in targets, exclude or native that matches nothing (native must match a selected target);
  • exclude and targets both set;
  • a selection that resolves to zero targets;
  • native combined with noarch = true;
  • a [package.python].runtime that is not an exact 3.Y.Z patch;
  • a missing uv.lock for the python builder;
  • builder = "staged" without name, or with neither a build-command nor overlay contents;
  • [package.python] with builder = "staged", or [package.staged] with builder = "python";
  • an overlay that is not a YAML mapping or that sets a key outside the list above;
  • with several [[package]] entries, a missing or duplicate name, entries with different vendors, or a packaging/nfpm.overlay.yaml (see Several packages).

Unrecognized keys are the exception: an unknown key in [package], [package.python] or [package.staged] only prints an unrecognized key warning on stderr, and validation still passes.

vrg-validate checks the overlay's shape only, because nFPM is not in the dev container. nFPM's own config check runs at build time in CI.

docs.title: PR CI
docs.text:
Add a package job to .github/workflows/ci.yml that calls the reusable workflow:

  package:
    uses: vergil-project/vergil-actions/.github/workflows/ci-package.yml@v2.1

It runs matrix, then one build job per build cell (unsigned artifacts), then one install-test job per test cell. Each install test:

  1. for python products, enables the vergil repository as a consumer would, so the runtime resolves from the live repository (staged products install standalone);
  2. installs the artifact and verifies any shipped systemd units;
  3. runs smoke and resolves each shim under a sanitized environment (env -i with a system-only PATH), so only the packaged binaries are found, never the uv copy of vergil-tooling that drives the test;
  4. removes the package and asserts nothing remains under /opt/<vendor>/<name> or in the shims.

All legs roll up into the single package / evidence gate. Like the other evidence gates it is required only where it applies: the per-repo ruleset adds package / evidence for repos whose vergil.toml has [package]. After adding [package], re-apply the repo's GitHub configuration so the gate becomes required.

docs.title: CD
docs.text:
A release builds the same cells, then a separate package-sign job signs every .rpm and attests every artifact before the release is tagged. Any failure is fatal before tagging. The caller has two requirements:

  • A package-signing environment, restricted to main, holding PACKAGE_SIGNING_KEY and PACKAGE_SIGNING_PASSPHRASE. Only package-sign uses it, so repos without [package] never reference it.
  • secrets: inherit on the cd-release caller. Environment secrets reach a job in a cross-repo reusable workflow only with inherit; an explicit secrets map leaves package-sign with an empty key (proven by vergil-project/packages#6). Semgrep flags secrets: inherit, so suppress it inline with a justification:
  release:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    uses: vergil-project/vergil-actions/.github/workflows/cd-release.yml@v2.1
    with:
      language: python
    # `inherit` is required: environment secrets reach a job in a cross-repo
    # reusable workflow only with `secrets: inherit`. The callee is first-party.
    secrets: inherit  # nosemgrep: yaml.github-actions.security.secrets-inherit.secrets-inherit

After the release is tagged, cd-release dispatches to the org's packages repository with the org's GitHub App token (APP_CLIENT_ID / APP_PRIVATE_KEY, also reached through inherit), which indexes the new packages. A dispatch failure is deferred: it does not fail the release.

docs.title: The re-publish check
docs.text:
A package's identity is its name, full version (<version>-<revision>), architecture and format. Builds are not byte-reproducible, so a release that rebuilds an identity an earlier release already published ships different bytes under the same identity. The package index refuses that (the same identity must be byte-identical), and since the index is built from every release of every repo, the refusal fails every repo's index publish. The index refusal stays as the last line of defence, but two earlier checks stop such a release before it publishes:

  1. vrg-release preflight, on a fresh start, before anything is tagged. This is the earliest point that knows the full versions: the package name, the package version (see version and upstream-version) and the revision of every artifact in the release manifest are all known without building. See Releasing.
  2. vrg-package check-unpublished, for the CD packaging path to run before it builds, as a backstop for a release that did not go through vrg-release:
vrg-package check-unpublished --version "$(vrg-version show)"

--repo defaults to $GITHUB_REPOSITORY. It needs gh with read access to the repo's releases.

Both compare the identities the release would publish against those attached to every earlier stable release that carries a packages-manifest.json, which are the releases the index collects. The published identities are read from the attached file names, which nFPM derives from the same metadata the index reads. The release's own tag is never counted as an earlier release. Any failure to read the releases refuses the release; the check never skips. A repo without [package] passes.

To fix a refusal, bump the package version. For an upstream-version package, set a new upstream-version, or cut a new repo release: the package version ends in the repo version, so a new release is a new version. For a version override, set a new version. The revision (-1) is set by the tooling and cannot be configured.

docs.title: One runtime per package
docs.text:
Each python package of a release must depend on one runtime on every architecture. Build cells run in parallel and at slightly different times, so if each cell read the version window itself, a window change mid-release could give each architecture a different runtime. This happened to vergil-tooling 2.1.258: amd64 got vergil-python3.15 and arm64 got vergil-python3.14 (vergil-project/vergil-tooling#3478).

To prevent it, the runtime is resolved once:

  1. vrg-package matrix resolves the runtime of each python package: the runtime pin, or the derived series. It records the result as runtime on every build cell of that package and in the manifest's runtimes map, and prints it on stderr. Other builders record no runtime (null).
  2. vrg-package build --runtime <runtime> builds against the recorded value and never re-reads the window. Pass the cell's runtime unchanged. An empty value counts as none recorded, so the same line works for every builder. A value that differs from a runtime pin is an error. Without --runtime, as in a local build, the build resolves the runtime itself. Either way it prints the runtime it chose and where that came from.
  3. vrg-package check-runtime fails the release if any package disagrees. Run it where every cell's packages are together, before anything is published:
vrg-package check-runtime --manifest packages-manifest.json --artifacts dist/packages

Every .deb and .rpm of a python package must depend on exactly the vergil-python<X.Y> recorded for that package, and on no other runtime series. Each mismatch is listed. A python package with no files fails, and so does a file whose package the manifest does not list. Packages recorded with a null runtime are not checked, so a release of only non-python packages passes. A manifest from before the runtimes map is checked against its top-level runtime, as one package.

docs.title: The package index (packages.toml)
docs.text:
The org's package repository lists the products it indexes in packages.toml, which vrg-package index reads. Retention is optional:

vendor = "vergil"
products = ["vergil-project/packages", "vergil-project/vergil-tooling"]

[retention]
keep = 3                          # releases kept per major.minor line (default 3)
lines = 2                         # newest major.minor lines kept per product (default 2)
retire = ["vergil-python3.14.8"]  # exact package names to drop (default: none)

The index is rebuilt from scratch on every run. For each product it keeps the newest keep releases in each of the newest lines major.minor lines, then adds the newest provider of every dependency of a kept package, so everything indexed is installable.

retire drops packages by exact name, for every format (deb and rpm) and architecture, whichever release ships them. A retired package is dropped before dependencies are resolved, so it keeps none of its own dependencies in the index. Each entry must be a non-empty string, listed once. If a package the index keeps still depends on a retired name, the index build fails rather than publishing a package that cannot be installed. To fix it, remove the name from retire or make sure retention no longer keeps the dependent release. Omitting retire, or setting it to [], retires nothing.

Every retire entry must name a package that some collected release ships, in any format or architecture. The check runs against everything collected before retention drops anything, so a name found only in releases that retention would evict still counts. An entry that matches nothing fails the index build. It is either a typo, which would otherwise leave the package published, or a package whose releases are gone; either way, remove it from packages.toml.

docs.title: Checking packages.toml without building
docs.text:
vrg-package index --check-config --config packages.toml

validates packages.toml and exits without building anything. It applies every check the index build makes on the file itself: known keys only, a non-empty vendor, well-formed and unique products, positive integer keep and lines, and well-formed and unique retire entries. It uses no network, signing keys or output directory, so --keys and --out are not needed. On success it prints vrg-package: packages.toml: ok. On any invalid value it prints the error and exits non-zero, so a repo's validation can catch a typo before publish time. Checks that need the collected releases, such as a retire entry that matches no package, still run only in the full index build.

docs.title: Inspecting the matrix
docs.text:
vrg-container-run -- vrg-package matrix

prints the resolved build and test cells as JSON without building anything. Add --tier reduced to see the reduced feature-PR matrix.

docs.title: Test Config Reference ([test])
docs.text: A repo tunes how its test stage runs under vrg-validate through the [test] section of its vergil.toml. The section is optional; every key defaults so that a repo which omits [test] gets the fleet-wide default behavior.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
[test]
parallel = false   # opt out of parallel test execution (default: true)
workers = "auto"   # xdist worker count: "auto" or a positive integer

[test.local-vm]    # override for one validation context (see below)
workers = 12

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Type Default Semantics parallel boolean true Whether the Python validation gate runs tests in parallel via pytest-xdist. On by default fleet-wide; set false to force serial execution workers "auto" or positive integer "auto" The pytest-xdist worker count (-n) when the gate runs in parallel [test.<context>].workers "auto" or positive integer (none) The worker count for one validation context: ci, local-vm, cloud-vm, or physical-host. Wins over workers in that context. A context subtable must set workers

A non-boolean parallel is rejected rather than silently coerced, so a mistyped opt-out (for example parallel = "no") fails loudly at config-parse time instead of quietly leaving parallelism on. A workers that is not "auto" or a positive integer (for example 0, -2, true, or "many") is rejected the same way.

docs.title: parallel
docs.text: Parallelism is on by default for every Python repo. When vrg-validate runs the Python test stage, the shared command (languages.py) appends pytest-xdist's work-stealing flags — -n <workers> --dist worksteal — to the base coverage-gate argv, so the suite fans out across workers (one per reported CPU at the default auto; see workers). On this repo's own suite that lever alone took the test stage from ~23.5 s to ~7.4 s (≈3.2× faster; see epics/333-python-test-perf/evidence/baseline.md), and it was landed fleet-wide as the new default (epic vergil-project/.github#333).

docs.title: How the flag is computed
docs.text:
The Python TEST command is computed, not stored as a fixed list. The shared command derives the final argv from three inputs:

  • [test].parallel — the repo's declared intent (this knob).
  • xdist availability — a live probe of the project's test environment, run when the test stage starts (after the install stage has populated .venv). It asks the Python interpreter next to the pytest on PATH — the same pytest the command runs, with .venv/bin first — whether xdist is importable. It deliberately does not consult vrg-validate's own interpreter: that is usually a uv tool venv without pytest-xdist, which once left every consumer repo running serially (#3322).
  • The resolved worker count — see workers.

-n <workers> --dist worksteal is appended iff xdist_available and parallel. The order that produces:

  • Default (parallel = true) with pytest-xdist in the project environment → parallel run. This is the fleet default: every Python repo carries pytest-xdist in its dev group.
  • parallel = false → serial run, no error, and the probe does not run. This is the per-repo opt-out.
  • pytest-xdist not installed in the project environment → serial run, no error. Availability is a probe, never a hard requirement.
  • The probe itself fails (no pytest on PATH, no interpreter beside it, or the interpreter errors) → the test stage fails loudly. A broken probe is never read as "not installed".

The stage prints its decision — for example Test parallelism: -n 12 (from [test.local-vm].workers, context local-vm) — so the run log always shows whether, and how widely, the suite ran in parallel.

The coverage gate (--cov-branch --cov-fail-under=100) is part of the base argv and is therefore present in every computed command — serial or parallel, opted-in or opted-out. Parallelism changes only how fast the suite runs, never what the coverage gate measures.

docs.title: When to opt out
docs.text: Set parallel = false only when the suite is order-dependent or otherwise unsafe to distribute across workers (shared mutable fixtures, hard-coded ports, tests that assume single-process execution). The knob exists so that no repo is ever left known-broken by the fleet-wide default — but the goal is a suite that runs correctly in parallel, so treat an opt-out as a bug to fix, not a resting state.

docs.title: workers
docs.text:
auto gives one xdist worker per CPU the machine reports. That is the right default on a GitHub runner or a physical host, but it can be badly wrong in a VM whose vCPUs exceed the host's real cores, or that shares them with other VMs: the workers contend and most of the speed-up disappears. One measurement (#3322) on a 24-vCPU Lima VM on an 18-core Mac:

Workers Wall clock serial 196 s 8 48–52 s 12 42 s 16 56 s auto (= 24) 136–162 s

The optimum depends on both the suite and the machine, so it has to be measured, and it can be set at three levels:

[test]
workers = "auto"     # repo default — anything not listed below

[test.local-vm]
workers = 12         # this repo's Lima VM (measured)

docs.title: Validation contexts
docs.text:
A context names where validation runs:

Context Means ci A GitHub Actions runner (GITHUB_ACTIONS=true) local-vm A Lima agent VM (vrg-whoami --platform) cloud-vm An off-platform cloud agent VM, or any VM not positively confirmed local (vrg-whoami --platform, fail-closed) physical-host The developer's Mac itself (vrg-whoami --platform)

vrg-container-run resolves the context outside the container, where the platform is observable, and forwards it into the container as VRG_TEST_CONTEXT. Setting VRG_TEST_CONTEXT yourself overrides that detection. When vrg-validate runs without vrg-container-run, a GitHub Actions runner is still recognized as ci; any other run has no context and uses [test].workers. A VRG_TEST_CONTEXT that names no known context is an error.

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
Highest first:

  1. VRG_TEST_WORKERS — an environment override for one machine (for example a second Mac whose VM measured differently). vrg-container-run forwards it into the container. It takes the same values as workers, and an invalid value fails the run.
  2. [test.<context>].workers — the repo's tuned count for the current context.
  3. [test].workers — the repo default.
  4. "auto".

Because the tuned value lives in the repo's vergil.toml, retuning is a commit. No VM rebuild or vrg-vm update is needed.

docs.title: Levers evaluated and dropped
docs.text:
Two other test-stage levers were evaluated during epic vergil-project/.github#333 and deliberately not adopted. They are recorded here so they are not mistaken for available knobs:

  • COVERAGE_CORE=sysmon (the sys.monitoring coverage backend) — inert under this fleet's inviolate --cov-branch gate. coverage.py cannot measure branches with sys.monitoring in the shipped coverage version and silently falls back to the C tracer, so setting it was misleading, not a speedup. See baseline.md Finding 1.
  • --import-mode=importlib — no measured speedup and not fleet-safe (it broke a real import in this repo's own suite). See baseline.md Finding 2.

Neither is emitted by the shared command; parallelism via pytest-xdist is the one universal lever that shipped.

docs.title: Upstream Refresh Reference ([upstream-refresh])
docs.text:
vrg-upstream-refresh keeps a repo's upstream inputs current. The repo supplies the logic in a hook, and the command supplies the mechanics: it runs the hook, then opens, refreshes or closes one PR. A human reviews and merges that PR; nothing auto-merges.

The design is epic vergil-project/.github#472 (spec epics/472-multi-series-runtime/spec.md, section 5.6).

docs.title: How it differs from a dependency update
docs.text:
An upstream refresh and a dependency update are separate pipelines with separate hooks:

Upstream refresh Dependency update Command vrg-upstream-refresh vrg-update-deps, and the update-deps stage of vrg-release Config [upstream-refresh].hook [dependency-update].hook What changes Inputs the repo pins from upstream, such as a runtime build or a tool version Dependencies within their declared bounds Branch upstream-refresh (one, fixed) deps/update-<version> Validation None; the PR's own CI checks it One vrg-validate run before the PR Merge Never; a human merges Merged when green Who runs it A scheduled ops workflow, or a human A human

Neither command runs the other's hook. vrg-upstream-refresh never runs dependency updaters, validation or a release.

docs.title: [upstream-refresh]
docs.text:
[upstream-refresh]
hook = "scripts/dev/upstream-refresh.sh"
Key Type Default Description hook string (required) Command that refreshes the repo's upstream inputs. Must be non-empty

The table is optional, but vrg-upstream-refresh refuses to run without it (vergil.toml has no [upstream-refresh] section). When the table is present, hook is required, and any other key is an error.

docs.title: The hook contract
docs.text:
The command runs the hook as bash -c "<hook>" from the repo root, on a clean checkout of the base branch. The hook:

  • Edits tracked files only. It must not commit, and it must not leave new untracked files. If it does, the command fails and names them (hook left untracked files: <paths>), and nothing is pushed. Files the repo's .gitignore ignores are allowed and never committed.
  • May write notes to the file named in $VRG_UPSTREAM_REPORT, one note per line. Each non-empty line becomes a bullet under ## Notes in the PR body. The format of each line is the repo's choice.
  • Fails with a non-zero exit. The command then stops with [upstream-refresh].hook failed (exit <n>): <hook>, and nothing is pushed.

docs.title: What the command does
docs.text:
vrg-upstream-refresh first fetches origin/<base> and requires a clean working tree with HEAD at origin/<base>. It then runs the hook and asks git what changed. Every run ends in one of these outcomes:

Outcome When What happens nothing No change and no open refresh PR Exits quietly; no GitHub writes closed No change, but a refresh PR is open Closes it with Nothing to refresh on <base>; closing. and deletes its branch opened A change and no open refresh PR Pushes one commit to upstream-refresh and opens the PR refreshed A change that differs from the open PR Force-pushes the new commit, updates the PR body and adds one comment unchanged A change identical to the open PR's tree Pushes nothing and comments nothing, so the PR does not churn

The refresh commit is chore(upstream): refresh upstream inputs, built directly on top of origin/<base>. Every run recomputes it from scratch, so the PR always holds a full snapshot rather than an increment. Its title is the commit subject, and its body lists the changed files and the hook's notes. The commit is built with git plumbing, so no local branch moves and no commit hook runs. Pushes use --force-with-lease, so a branch someone else moved is never overwritten.

A refresh PR is an open PR against the base whose head is upstream-refresh or upstream-refresh-<anything> (a manual re-create). When more than one is open, the oldest is kept and refreshed. The others are closed with a comment naming it, and their branches are deleted.

The command works from a shallow, depth-1 checkout, such as the default actions/checkout. It fetches the refs it needs itself, at depth 1 when the checkout is shallow, so it never deepens the clone.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
vrg-upstream-refresh [--repo OWNER/NAME] [--base BRANCH] [--dry-run]
Option Default Description --repo $GITHUB_REPOSITORY, then the origin remote Repository that owns the refresh PR --base The repository's default branch Base branch to refresh against --dry-run off Run the hook and print the PR body; push nothing and change no PR

It exits 0 on every outcome above, and 1 on any error or refusal.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: The command opens PRs, so agent identity modes (user and audit) are refused with vrg-upstream-refresh opens PRs and is not run by agents. It runs from a scheduled ops workflow under the per-org automation App token, or by hand as a human. It needs contents and pull-requests write on its own repo.

docs.title: The scheduled workflow
docs.text: The reusable vergil-actions workflow ops-upstream-refresh.yml runs the command on a schedule. It mints a repo-scoped App token, checks out with it so pushes are App-authored and trigger CI, and runs vrg-upstream-refresh --base <ref> in the prod-base image. Each consuming repo calls it from its own ops.yml on its own schedule. A failed run shows as a red scheduled run.

docs.title: VM Spec Reference ([vm])
docs.text:
A repo declares the VM it needs in the [vm] section of its vergil.toml. vrg-vm composes that declaration with the identity's base footprint and any host override into the effective spec for each (identity, repo) pair, then builds a dedicated VM whenever the repo customizes anything.

The composition model and rationale live in the per-repo VM profiles design spec (vergil-vm docs/specs/2026-06-04-per-repo-vm-profiles-design.md); this page is the key-by-key reference.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
[vm]                      # applies to every identity
packages = ["qemu-system-x86", "libvirt-clients"]

[[vm.apt_repos]]          # extra apt repositories (list of tables)
name = "hashicorp"
key_url = "https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com/gpg"
uri = "https://apt.releases.hashicorp.com"
suite = "noble"
components = "main"

[vm.vergil-user]          # role overlay: only the vergil-user identity
cpus = 12
memory = "64GiB"
disk = "300GiB"
stale_days = 7
vagrant_plugins = ["vagrant-libvirt"]
port_forwards = ["3000|10.50.0.2:3000"]   # local VM port | nested target
nested = true

docs.title: Precedence
docs.text:
Five tiers, later wins:

  1. Built-in base footprint
  2. Identity footprint (identities.toml)
  3. Repo [vm] (all identities)
  4. Repo [vm.<role>] (one identity)
  5. Host override (identities.toml per-repo override; scalars pushed below the repo-declared floor are flagged loudly)

Scalars are last-wins; list keys (packages, apt_repos, vagrant_plugins, port_forwards) accumulate across tiers. Declaring any [vm] key marks the spec customized, which gives the repo a dedicated VM.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Type Default Semantics cpus int identity/base footprint vCPUs (last-wins scalar) memory string "<N>GiB" identity/base footprint RAM (last-wins scalar) disk string "<N>GiB" identity/base footprint Disk size (last-wins scalar) stale_days int 3 Age threshold before vrg-vm prompts to rebuild packages list of strings [] Extra apt packages (accumulates) apt_repos list of tables [] Extra apt repositories — name, key_url, uri, suite, components (accumulates) vagrant_plugins list of strings [] Vagrant plugins to install (accumulates) port_forwards list of strings [] "<port>\|<host:port>" relay records — bind <port> in the VM and proxy to <host:port> (accumulates; see below) nested bool false Nested virtualization (last-wins scalar; see below) shared_from string "org/repo" (none) Borrow another repo's VM instead of declaring one. Mutually exclusive with every other [vm] key (see below) backend string "local" VM backend: "local" (Lima) or "off-platform" (remote cloud). Last-wins scalar; selects the driver (see below) provider string (none) Cloud provider when backend = "off-platform" (e.g. "gcp", "azure") — selects the OpenTofu module (see below) region string (none) Provider-native region when off-platform (e.g. "us-central1") instance string (none) Provider-native, nested-virt-capable instance type when off-platform (e.g. "n2-standard-16") volume string "<N>GiB" (none) Persistent block-volume size when off-platform — created once, reused, outlives the VM. Does not fall back to disk boot_disk string "<N>GiB" (module default, ~30 GiB) Ephemeral boot/root-disk size when off-platform. Optional — unset keeps the image default. Sizes the disk that holds scratch data living outside volume boot_disk_type string (module default) Ephemeral boot/root-disk type when off-platform, provider-native (GCP "pd-ssd", Azure "Premium_LRS"). Optional; checked against the provider's allowed set (see below)

The vergil-vm template owns how declarative installs happen — repos never supply scripts.

docs.title: Nested virtualization (nested)
docs.text:
nested = true requests /dev/kvm inside the VM (vergil-project/vergil-vm#131). At create time vrg-vm applies both halves together:

  • --set='.nestedVirtualization = true' — the Lima config knob
  • --set='.param.NESTED_VIRT = "true"' — turns on the template's in-guest verification, which fails the build loudly when /dev/kvm did not appear

Three-layer defense, outermost first:

  1. Host preflight — vrg-vm create/rebuild abort before any build (and before the destroy half of a rebuild) unless the host is macOS 15+ on M3-or-later Apple silicon.
  2. Lima — rejects nestedVirtualization on unsupported hosts.
  3. In-guest check — the template verifies /dev/kvm exists and fails the build rather than degrading silently to TCG emulation.

docs.title: Borrowing a VM (shared_from)
docs.text:
A repo with no VM of its own can run its sessions inside another repo's dedicated VM:

[vm]
shared_from = "logical-minds-foundry/mq-resiliency-lab"

vrg-vm session <org>/<borrower> then shells into the lender's box and cds into the borrower's checkout. On a local (Lima) box both checkouts are already present because the whole projects directory is mounted into every VM. A cloud (off-platform) box has no such mount, so the borrower's checkout does not exist until the session creates it: the session clones-or-fetches the borrower onto the box's persistent volume before homing on it (idempotent and self-healing — no rebuild, and the lender's checkout and running services are untouched).

  • The value must be a fully-qualified org/repo.
  • shared_from is the only key allowed under [vm] — combining it with a footprint/package key or a [vm.<role>] overlay is a config error. A repo either describes a VM or borrows one.
  • The borrower may use the shared box (session, start) but not manage it: create, stop, restart, update, destroy, and rebuild on the borrower are refused and point at the lender repo, which owns the box.
  • One hop only — the lender may not itself declare shared_from.

docs.title: Off-platform (cloud) backend
docs.text:
By default a repo's VM is a local macOS Lima box (backend = "local"). Setting backend = "off-platform" switches it to a remote native-x86 cloud host driven by OpenTofu — for repos that genuinely need native x86 (nested KVM, not TCG emulation). The backend, modules, and provisioning live in vergil-vm (#199); the design spec is vergil-vm docs/specs/2026-06-19-off-platform-vm-backend-design.md.

[vm.vergil-user]
backend   = "off-platform"
provider  = "gcp"              # selects the OpenTofu module
region    = "us-central1"      # provider-native region
instance  = "n2-standard-16"   # provider-native, nested-virt-capable
volume    = "300GiB"           # PERSISTENT volume — outlives the VM
boot_disk = "100GiB"           # EPHEMERAL boot disk — optional; dies with the VM
boot_disk_type = "pd-ssd"      # its disk type — optional; provider-native
nested    = true               # /dev/kvm in the cloud box too
cpus      = 12                 # request / under-provision intent (see below)
memory    = "64GiB"
  • The five keys are last-wins scalars that ride the same five-tier cascade as the footprint keys. Declaring any of them dedicates the box. Because the cascade is resolved before validation, you may split them across tiers (e.g. backend in [vm], instance in [vm.<role>]).
  • backend = "off-platform" requires provider, region, instance, and volume. A missing key is a loud config error — no silent default. volume must be "<N>GiB" and never falls back to disk.
  • provider/region/instance are opaque provider-native strings — the tooling does not enumerate them, so adding a provider is a vergil-vm module change with no tooling change.
  • disk is ignored off-platform. On cloud there are two disks with opposite lifecycles: the ephemeral VM boot disk and the persistent volume declared above. The Lima disk knob drives neither — use volume for the persistent disk and boot_disk for the ephemeral one.
  • boot_disk sizes the ephemeral boot/root disk (optional). Unset, the boot disk inherits the cloud image's default (~30 GiB); set it ("<N>GiB") to grow the disk for workloads whose scratch data lives outside the persistent volume — e.g. a nested-virt image pool and qcow2 overlays, which belong on the wipe-on-rebuild boot disk rather than the never-wiped volume. Unlike volume it is not required off-platform, and it never enters the local (Lima) spec.
  • boot_disk_type picks the ephemeral boot disk's type (optional). Unset, the key is not passed and the vergil-vm module default holds: on GCP, GCE picks the default type for the machine series; on Azure, StandardSSD_LRS. Set it when the boot disk carries I/O-heavy scratch data (e.g. a nested-virt image pool). Unlike provider/region/instance, the value is checked at composition, before any cloud call, against the provider's allowed set. That set mirrors the vergil-vm vm module's own validation (vergil-vm#312):
provider Allowed boot_disk_type gcp pd-standard, pd-balanced, pd-ssd, hyperdisk-balanced azure Standard_LRS, StandardSSD_LRS, Premium_LRS, StandardSSD_ZRS, Premium_ZRS

An unknown value is a loud config error. Values are never mapped across providers: pd-ssd on an Azure profile is rejected, not translated to a SKU. Like boot_disk, it is ignored on a local (Lima) profile, so it can sit on a named cloud instance ([vm.<role>.instances.<name>]) or on the role with the instance inheriting it. - boot_disk_type needs vergil-vm v2.1.42 or later. The modules are fetched by the host's module tag (vergil-vm in identities.toml, else vergil, or --tag), not by this tooling's version. OpenTofu only warns about an undeclared variable in a var file, so an older module would silently build the default disk type. vrg-vm create/rebuild therefore check that the fetched module declares boot_disk_type and fail loudly, naming the tag, if it does not. rebuild runs this check before it destroys the old VM. The moving v2.1 tag picks up v2.1.42 once it is released; a host pinned to an older exact tag must move the pin. - instance is authoritative over cpus/memory on cloud. They stay in the spec as human-readable intent; a session-time under-provisioning warning (instance smaller than the declared cpus/memory) is part of the backend dispatcher, not this schema layer (it needs the provider's instance specs).

docs.title: Lifecycle and access (off-platform)
docs.text:
The same vrg-vm verbs work, dispatched on the resolved backend:

  • create — tofu applys the persistent volume (idempotent — a no-op if it already exists), then the ephemeral VM pinned to that volume's zone, blocks until cloud-init provisioning is done, injects GitHub App + Claude credentials over the tunnel, and clones the repo onto the volume (first time) or fetches (reattach). Refuses to stand up a second VM for a repo that already has one running.
  • session — opens the session over the tunnel into /vergil/projects/<org>/<repo> on the volume.
  • destroy — tears down the ephemeral VM only. The persistent volume (the repo checkout and .claude session history) survives. This is the routine end-of-day teardown.
  • rebuild — destroy + recreate the VM against the existing volume; the data reattaches intact. This is the path for changing boot_disk or boot_disk_type on an existing box: either change replaces the ephemeral boot disk, which means a new instance. list flags the box NEEDS-REBUILD until you do.
  • destroy-volume — the only command that deletes the persistent volume. Guarded: retype org/repo to confirm, or pass --yes.
  • update — refreshes vergil-tooling (see vergil-tooling inside the VM) and Claude plugins in place over the IAP tunnel on a running box (seconds, non-disruptive), exactly like a Lima box. rebuild is reserved for what genuinely needs a fresh image (a new base image or changed provision scripts), not a tooling bump. update --all includes off-platform boxes and updates each running one in place; a non-running box is skipped and reported. Two boxes that share an org/repo (one per identity) stay distinct by their identity.
  • stop / start / restart — not supported. Off-platform VMs are ephemeral; use destroy / create.
  • list — gains a BACKEND column (local for Lima rows, the provider for cloud rows). Cloud rows carry their box's IDENTITY so two boxes sharing an org/repo (one per identity) stay distinct. Without cloud credentials a cloud row's status degrades to unknown (no <provider> creds) rather than erroring or hiding the row.
  • volumes — enumerates the persistent volumes (the long-lived, billable, quota-consuming disks that outlive each ephemeral VM) from local tofu state: IDENTITY, ORG/REPO, DISK NAME, SIZE, ZONE, REGION, all read from each disk's stamped labels/attributes with no network call. --live adds a LIVE column that cross-checks each disk against the provider — a disk deleted out of band shows MISSING; an unauthed/unreachable provider degrades to unknown. This is how you identify which volume to destroy-volume and track SSD quota usage.

Access is via the provider's identity-aware tunnel (GCP IAP) — there is no public IP and no operator-IP allow-list; authentication is the operator's existing cloud IAM/ADC. Host prerequisites are therefore OpenTofu (≥ 1.8.0) and the provider CLI (gcloud, with ADC); cloud verbs preflight both and fail with a clear remediation. On a macOS host, vrg-host tracks both tools' versions and checks that the interpreter gcloud runs on can import NumPy, without which every IAP tunnel session warns and runs slower (vrg-host status --fix installs it). The in-guest login user defaults to the cloud image's default user and can be overridden with VRG_OFF_PLATFORM_SSH_USER.

docs.title: Port forwards (port_forwards)
docs.text:
Each record is "<port>|<host:port>". The vergil-vm template (vergil-project/vergil-vm#170) provisions a systemd-socket-proxyd relay per record: it binds 0.0.0.0:<port> inside the VM and proxies to <host:port> — typically a nested libvirt guest. The 0.0.0.0 bind is auto-forwarded by Lima to the Mac's localhost:<port> with no extra config. The relay is boot-persistent; the build fails loudly if the port is already bound.

vrg-vm joins the accumulated records with ; and passes them as --set='.param.PORT_FORWARDS = "<records>"' — the template splits on ; then |. Repos never supply a script; the template owns the relay.

docs.title: Fingerprint and NEEDS-REBUILD
docs.text:
The composed spec is fingerprinted (SHA-256 over the declaration) and stamped into the VM at create time. vrg-vm list compares the stored fingerprint against the freshly composed one and shows NEEDS-REBUILD on any drift. Editing any declarative key — including toggling nested — flips the fingerprint. nested and port_forwards enter the fingerprint payload only when set (true / non-empty), so profiles that never declare them kept their fingerprints when the knobs were introduced.

The off-platform keys (backend, provider, region, instance, volume) follow the same rule: they enter the payload only when backend = "off-platform", and on that path disk is dropped from the payload (it is not a cloud knob). A local profile therefore keeps its byte-for-byte fingerprint from before these keys existed — existing Lima VMs never falsely read NEEDS-REBUILD — while flipping a repo Lima→cloud, or resizing the instance/volume, trips NEEDS-REBUILD as expected. boot_disk enters the off-platform payload only when set, so cloud VMs created before the knob existed keep their fingerprints; declaring or resizing it trips NEEDS-REBUILD like volume. boot_disk_type follows the same rule: it enters the payload only when set, and declaring or changing it trips NEEDS-REBUILD.

docs.title: vergil-tooling inside the VM
docs.text:
Lima and cloud VMs install vergil-tooling from the vergil package repository (https://vergil-project.github.io/packages) with apt, not with uv tool install. The macOS host, the dev container cache and this repo's dev-tree .venv are unchanged and still use uv.

Which version. The version is the identity's resolved vergil version: the per-identity vergil setting in identities.toml, else the config-level vergil. The repo's vergil.toml plays no part. A vrg-vm update --tag <ref> overrides it for that one update and is not remembered.

Packaged install (any release version):

  • vX.Y (a release line) pins vergil-tooling to X.Y.* in /etc/apt/preferences.d/vergil-tooling and installs the newest package on that line.
  • vX.Y.Z (an exact release) pins X.Y.Z-1 and installs vergil-tooling=X.Y.Z-1.
  • Before anything is written to the apt sources, vrg-vm downloads the org signing key and checks its fingerprint against the one pinned in vergil-tooling. It then installs vergil-archive-keyring, which owns the key and the source entry from then on.
  • Every apt call vrg-vm makes, both the repository setup and the apt-get update and apt-get install of vergil-tooling, runs with Acquire::Retries=3 and 20-second Acquire::http::Timeout/Acquire::https::Timeout, so a dead mirror connection fails or retries in seconds rather than hanging. It also sets Acquire::Retries::Delay=false, because apt 2.4–2.8 can deadlock on mirror failover when retries are delayed (Launchpad #2003851), and DPkg::Lock::Timeout=60, so a dpkg lock held by unattended-upgrades or apt-daily on a freshly booted VM is waited out for up to 60 seconds instead of failing provisioning at once.
  • The VM's Ubuntu codename must be a published suite (noble or resolute). Any other codename fails provisioning.
  • If the repository has no package matching the version, for example a new line before its first packaged release, provisioning fails and names the version and the repository URL. It never falls back to another version or to a uv install.
  • vrg-vm update re-runs the same steps, which upgrades the VM within the pin.
  • Once the apt install has succeeded, any uv-installed copy (a legacy install or an earlier dev install) is removed, because the copy in ~/.local/bin would shadow /usr/bin. A failed packaged install leaves the existing tooling in place.
  • After that, obsolete vergil-python* runtimes are purged, so a runtime move (for example from vergil-python3.14 to vergil-python3.15) does not leave the old runtime and its /opt/vergil/python/<…> tree behind. A runtime is obsolete only when it is auto-installed (apt-mark showauto) and apt would autoremove it (apt-get -s autoremove, a simulation), so a runtime that an installed package still needs, or one installed by hand, is kept. The obsolete runtimes are named in one explicit apt-get purge -y <names> and printed. vrg-vm never runs a blanket apt-get autoremove, which could remove unrelated orphaned OS packages. A failed purge fails the update, and a failed install purges nothing.
  • This applies to apt only. Agent VMs are always Ubuntu (noble or resolute), so there are no dnf VMs to clean up.

Dev install (explicit, for a git ref that is not a release version, such as develop or a feature branch):

vrg-vm update --tag develop
  • This runs uv tool install from git into ~/.local/bin, which takes precedence over the packaged /usr/bin copy on the VM user's PATH, and records the ref in ~/.config/vergil/tooling-dev-ref.
  • You only get a dev install by passing a dev ref. A failed packaged install never falls back to one.
  • While it is in place, every vrg-vm command that touches the VM (create, rebuild, start, update, session) prints DEV tooling (ref <ref>) — not the packaged install.
  • A plain vrg-vm update (no --tag) returns the VM to the packaged install and removes the dev copy.

docs.title: Cache image prune on update
docs.text:
After the reinstall, vrg-vm update (and each box of update --all) runs the VM's own, freshly installed vrg-container-cache prune --apply inside the VM. It removes cached dev images whose branch is finished and prints what it removed. Pass --no-prune to skip it.

  • An off-platform box prunes against its default repo set, /vergil/projects. A Lima box is given its identity's projects_dir as --root. That path is mounted at the same location in the VM, and the in-VM command does not run from a checkout, so it cannot work out the default on its own.
  • A failed prune is printed as an ERROR with the command's output and exit status, but it does not fail the update.
  • If the VM's vergil-tooling has no prune subcommand yet, or no vrg-container-cache at all, the prune is skipped with a warning that says so.

docs.title: vrg-branch-sweep
docs.text:
Installed as: vrg-branch-sweep (Python console script)

Source: src/vergil_tooling/bin/vrg_branch_sweep.py (rules in src/vergil_tooling/lib/branch_sweep.py)

Finds the branches on a GitHub repo whose pull-request work is finished and, with --apply, deletes them.

Finished branches are normally removed automatically, by two mechanisms:

  • the delete-on-merge repo setting (Automatically delete head branches), which removes a branch when its PR merges;
  • the delete-on-close rule (issue #3332), which removes a branch when its PR is closed without merging. GitHub never does this on its own.

vrg-branch-sweep is the safety net behind both. GitHub sometimes skips its after-merge processing, and a merge can then fire no push event and leave its branch behind. A PR can also be closed before the delete-on-close rule existed, or outside it. Leftover branches are not harmless: tools that treat a branch's existence as "work in flight" stall on them, and they hide the dropped events that should get someone's attention (issue #3333).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
vrg-branch-sweep [--repo OWNER/NAME] [--apply]
  • --repo OWNER/NAME: the repo to sweep. Defaults to the current directory's repo. Every lookup goes through the GitHub API, so the target does not need to be checked out.
  • --apply: delete the finished branches. Without it the command is a dry run: it reports what it would delete and changes nothing.

docs.title: What counts as finished
docs.text:
A branch is finished, and deleted under --apply, when all of these hold:

  1. it has at least one PR from the same repo (fork PRs that share the branch name are ignored);
  2. none of its PRs is open;
  3. its newest PR (the highest number) is merged or closed;
  4. its current tip equals that PR's headRefOid.

When the tip differs, the branch name was reused after the PR finished (issue #1719) and holds new work, so it is kept.

docs.title: What it never deletes
docs.text:
• The repo's default branch, develop, main and gh-pages.
  • A protected branch. A branch counts as protected when the branches API reports protected, which covers classic branch protection and rulesets. Before deleting, the sweep also asks the rules-for-a-branch endpoint (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rules/branches/{branch}) and keeps the branch if any active ruleset rule applies to it.
  • A branch with no PR. An agent pushes its branch before vrg-pr-workflow report-ready, and that branch has no PR until the human runs vrg-submit-pr.

Under --apply, the tip is read again just before each delete. If the branch moved after the listing, it is kept.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
One line per branch, sorted by name: the branch, its newest PR, that PR's state, and the action with its reason. A summary line follows.

Sweeping finished branches in acme/widgets (dry run)
develop            -       -       kept (default branch)
feature/12-done    #40     MERGED  would delete (PR #40 merged)
feature/13-wip     #41     OPEN    kept (open PR #41)
feature/14-new     -       -       kept (no PR)
feature/9-reused   #30     MERGED  kept (reused branch name: tip 1a2b3c4d5e6f is not PR #30's head 9f8e7d6c5b4a)
release/2.0.55     #31     CLOSED  would delete (PR #31 closed)

acme/widgets: 6 branches, 2 would delete, 4 kept, 0 errors (dry run; pass --apply to delete)

Actions are kept, would delete (dry run), deleted (--apply) and error.

docs.title: Failure handling
docs.text: No branch is skipped quietly. When a gh call fails for one branch, the command reports an error line with the cause, finishes the remaining branches, and then exits 1. A failure to read the repo's default branch or branch list stops the sweep at once with exit 1, since nothing can be decided without them. Missing or invalid GitHub credentials end the run with the standard authentication message.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Every branch was processed without error 1 At least one branch failed, the branch list could not be read, or authentication failed 2 Invalid arguments

docs.title: vrg-commit
docs.text:
Installed as: vrg-commit (Python console script)

Source: src/vergil_tooling/bin/vrg_commit.py

Wrapper that constructs standards-compliant commit messages in Conventional Commits format.

Required for AI agents

AI agents must use this tool instead of raw git commit.

No AI co-author trailer

Commits carry no AI Co-Authored-By trailer. AI co-author attribution was dropped, and Claude Code's own attribution is turned off in each repo's checked-in .claude/settings.json ("attribution": { "commit": "", "pr": "" }; see #3200).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
vrg-commit \
  --type TYPE --scope SCOPE --message MESSAGE [options]

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Required Description --type Yes Conventional commit type --scope Yes Conventional commit scope --message Yes Commit description --body No Detailed commit body --allow-empty No Allow a commit with no staged changes (e.g. to re-trigger CI)

docs.title: Allowed Types
docs.text: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore, ci, build, revert

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Feature with scope
vrg-commit \
  --type feat --scope lint \
  --message "add new check"

# Documentation with body
vrg-commit \
  --type docs --scope readme --message "update README" \
  --body "Expanded usage section"

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
1. Reads [project].branching-model from vergil.toml.
  2. Validates the branch context: no detached HEAD, not a protected branch, branch prefix matches the branching model, issue number in the branch name, not the main worktree when .worktrees/ is present.
  3. Refuses the commit when the branch has been reported ready (vrg-pr-workflow report-ready) and is frozen.
  4. Rejects a body containing a GitHub auto-close keyword.
  5. Verifies staged changes exist (unless --allow-empty).
  6. Constructs the commit message in a temporary file and runs git commit --file.

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Commit created successfully 1 Validation failure or error

docs.title: vrg-finalize-pr
docs.text:
Installed as: vrg-finalize-pr (Python console script)

Source: src/vergil_tooling/bin/vrg_finalize_pr.py

Finalizes a pull request and reconciles local state afterwards. Has three modes:

  • vrg-finalize-pr <PR> — runs the pre-merge provenance check, waits for checks to go green, merges the PR (or confirms it is already merged), then runs the cleanup below. This replaces a manual web merge followed by a separate cleanup step.
  • vrg-finalize-pr (no PR) — interactive: infers the PR from the .worktrees/ worktrees and always confirms before acting (see Choosing the PR below). With no candidates, cleanup-only after confirmation: switch to the target branch, fast-forward pull, delete merged local branches, and prune stale remote-tracking references.
  • vrg-finalize-pr --cleanup-only — non-interactive release path: skips inference and merge entirely, never reads stdin, and runs only the cleanup. This is what vrg-release invokes during its close-finalize phase (issue #1448). Mutually exclusive with a PR argument.

Must be run from the main worktree — the cleanup removes worktrees, which is unsafe when the calling shell's CWD is inside one.

docs.title: Choosing the PR
docs.text:
• vrg-finalize-pr <pr-url-or-number> — no prompts; the explicit argument is the confirmation. This is the scriptable path (vrg-submit-pr prints the URL to pass here).
  • vrg-finalize-pr (no arguments) — infers candidates by mapping each .worktrees/ worktree's branch to its open PR, and always confirms before acting: one candidate asks Finalize PR #N?; several present a menu; none asks before running cleanup-only. Worktrees without an open PR are listed with the reason they were skipped. Inference mode requires an interactive terminal and fails fast unless both stdin and stdout are TTYs — a captured stdout would make the prompts invisible (issue #1448).
  • vrg-finalize-pr --cleanup-only — no prompts and no merge; the scriptable path for callers (like vrg-release) that only want the cleanup.

docs.title: Waiting for green
docs.text:
When the PR's checks are not finished, vrg-finalize-pr waits for them and merges automatically once everything is green and current. The wait is bounded by a deadline — it never blocks forever — and it never merges past a non-terminal check. Doomed outcomes abort immediately rather than after the wait: a draft PR, merge conflicts, a failed check (named in the error), or a branch still behind after five update attempts. A branch that is merely behind the target is updated automatically and the wait restarts.

Orphaned check-runs. GitHub occasionally leaves a check-run non-terminal (queued/in_progress) even though the workflow run that owns it has already completed — an orphan that would never go green on its own. The waiter detects this while waiting, not only at the deadline (issue #3358). About every 30 seconds it checks the backing run (gh run view) of each pending Actions check. Once a run has completed, its check gets a one-minute grace period to turn terminal. If the check is still pending after that, the backing job's own conclusion decides (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/jobs/{job_id}):

  • The job succeeded and the check is not required: the check is treated as passed and a warning names it ('test / matrix' check-run stale; backing job succeeded), so the merge goes ahead instead of waiting out the deadline. Checks that really failed are still caught by the failed-checks gate.
  • The job succeeded but the check is one of the target branch's required status checks: the check is a suspected orphan (issue #3379). GitHub keeps blocking the merge on a required check it reports as pending, so passing it would only move the wait to the merge step. If it is still pending when the grace period below runs out, the error names the check, says GitHub will block the merge until it settles, and gives the same close-and-reopen guidance.
  • The job succeeded but the required checks could not be read (see Required checks below): a suspected orphan for the same reason, because finalize cannot tell whether GitHub will block on the stale check. The error, if the grace runs out, says the required-check lookup failed. Without a stale check, a failed lookup still only warns and waits on registered checks.
  • The job did not succeed, has no conclusion, or its conclusion cannot be read: a suspected orphan. If the grace runs out, finalize aborts with recovery guidance: close and reopen the PR to re-run the gate, then re-run vrg-finalize-pr. The error names each such check, its job's outcome and its job link.

Grace period for suspected orphans. During a GitHub Actions incident, GitHub can write job results back minutes late, and at the moment of checking that looks exactly like an orphan (issue #3431). Closing and reopening the PR then would throw away results that are on their way. So a suspected orphan is not declared at once. The waiter prints a warning naming the suspects (… have a completed run but no result yet … GitHub may be delayed; re-checking for up to 5m00s …) and keeps polling, re-reading each suspect's job about every 30 seconds. A result that arrives in time lets the wait finish normally. Only a check still pending when the grace runs out is declared orphaned, and the error says how long each check waited. The grace defaults to 5 minutes from when the backing run was first seen completed. Set VRG_ORPHAN_GRACE (seconds, a positive whole number) to change it; a malformed value is an error. vrg-pr-await applies the same grace before it settles with orphaned_check.

The deadline is the backstop. When it elapses with checks still pending, each one is checked against its backing run again, and a non-terminal check over a completed run aborts with the same guidance. Genuinely still-running checks are waited on as normal; if the deadline elapses with nothing orphaned (for example an app-posted status that is legitimately slow), finalize fails with a timeout error that names every still-pending check and its run/job link, with the recovery path: re-run the stuck job, then re-run the waiting command (vrg-finalize-pr, or vrg-release --resume).

Deadline. The deadline defaults to 30 minutes (about four times the longest legitimate CI run, 5–8 minutes) and is shared by every merge wait: vrg-finalize-pr, vrg-release (merge-release, back-merge-bump), vrg-update-deps and vrg-wait-until-green. Set VRG_CHECKS_TIMEOUT (seconds, a positive whole number) to change it; a malformed value is an error, and the deadline cannot be disabled. While waiting, the waiter prints each pending check with how long it has been pending, re-reporting whenever the pending set changes and at least once a minute.

Stale check-runs. GitHub occasionally sets a check-run's conclusion and completedAt but leaves its status at IN_PROGRESS. gh pr checks derives its state from status, so it reports such a check as pending indefinitely. The waiter checks each pending check's conclusion in the PR's statusCheckRollup. A check that has a conclusion is terminal and is classified by that conclusion, so a stale success passes and a stale failure fails. A warning names the inconsistent check (issue #3170).

Required checks. "Green" includes the target branch's required status checks, read from both classic branch protection (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/branches/{branch}) and repository rulesets (GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/rules/branches/{branch}). CI aggregator jobs such as test / evidence only register as checks once their dependencies finish, so every registered check can be done while a required one does not exist yet. Finalize keeps waiting until each required check is registered and terminal, printing what it awaits (for example Awaiting required checks: test / evidence (not registered)). If the merge is still refused with "the base branch policy prohibits the merge" and no check has failed, finalize treats it as not ready: it polls and re-attempts within the same deadline, then fails naming the outstanding required checks. A policy block that waiting cannot clear, such as a required review (reviewDecision=REVIEW_REQUIRED), aborts at once. If the required checks cannot be read (permissions or an API error), finalize prints a warning and falls back to waiting on registered checks only (issue #3061).

After the merge, the PR's own branch and worktree are cleaned up explicitly (a squash merge hides them from git branch --merged), followed by the usual sweep, pull, and prune.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
vrg-finalize-pr [PR | --cleanup-only] [--target-branch BRANCH]
                [--strategy {merge,squash,rebase}]
                [--allow-provenance-violation] [--clean-dirty] [--dry-run]
                [--no-wait-cd]

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Argument Description PR PR number or URL to merge and finalize. Omit to infer interactively. --cleanup-only Skip PR inference and merge; run cleanup without prompting or reading stdin (non-interactive release path). Mutually exclusive with PR. --target-branch Branch to switch to (default: develop) --strategy Merge strategy when a PR is given (default: squash) --allow-provenance-violation Proceed despite provenance violations (conscious human override) --clean-dirty Opt-in: clear a merged/closed worktree whose only dirt is untracked build/validation output, after showing what will be deleted and confirming. Never touches modified tracked files or a reused-branch straggler with unmerged commits (issue #2348). --dry-run Show what would be done without making changes --no-wait-cd Do not block on the CD workflow run the merge triggers. Blocking (and failing on a non-success run) is the default (issue #2753); this is the conscious opt-out.

docs.title: 1. Provenance Check, Wait, and Merge (PR mode only)
docs.text: Runs the pre-merge provenance check first, so violations surface before any waiting. Advisories are printed but do not block. Violations abort the merge unless --allow-provenance-violation is given. If the PR is already merged, the merge step is skipped and finalize proceeds straight to cleanup. Otherwise the wait-for-green loop runs (see Waiting for green) and the PR is merged with the selected strategy. --dry-run skips the wait and prints what it would do.

docs.title: 1a. Explicit-Target Cleanup (PR mode only)
docs.text: The just-merged PR branch and its .worktrees/ worktree are deleted by name. The default squash strategy rewrites history onto the target, so the branch is never an ancestor and the merged-branch sweep below cannot see it. The branch's PR-workflow relay ref (refs/vergil/pr-workflow/<branch>, pushed by report-ready) is deleted alongside it, so a cloud-handoff ref never outlives its branch (issue #2369). Deleting a relay ref that was never pushed is a no-op.

docs.title: 2. Switch to Target Branch
docs.text: Checks out the target branch (default: develop).

docs.title: 3. Fast-Forward Pull
docs.text: Fetches (--tags --force) and fast-forward merges origin/{target}.

docs.title: 4. Delete Merged Branches and Worktrees
docs.text:
Deletes local branches merged into the target branch. If a merged branch is still checked out in a canonical .worktrees/ worktree, that worktree is removed first (skipped if it has uncommitted changes). Cached container images for the branch are cleaned.

Two guards keep this sweep from racing parallel agent sessions in their creation-to-first-commit window (issue #1445), since git branch --merged classifies a branch just created from the target's tip as merged:

  • Zero-commit branches are skipped. A branch whose tip equals the target's tip carries no merged work, so deleting it saves nothing — and it is exactly what an in-flight issue branch looks like before its first commit.
  • Merge evidence is required. A branch is only swept when a closed or merged PR exists for its head; ancestry alone cannot distinguish a merged branch from one created off an older target tip. Branches skipped for lack of evidence are listed with the reason and left for manual cleanup.

Both guards gate the worktree removal as strictly as the branch deletion. The explicit-target cleanup (step 1a) is unaffected — the just-merged PR branch has merge evidence by construction.

docs.title: Stuck merged worktrees are surfaced, not buried
docs.text: A merged/closed worktree the sweep cannot remove — its tree is dirty, or its branch name was reused after a same-named PR merged (issue #1719) — is neither live work nor removable cruft. Rather than leaving the skip reason inside the collapsed progress-stage log (where a clean ✓ cleanup summary hides it), finalize reports every such worktree prominently after the pipeline, with the reason, so finishing with stuck worktrees is impossible to miss (issue #2348).

docs.title: --clean-dirty: guarded clear of untracked-only dirt
docs.text:
The common Mac case is a merged worktree whose only "dirt" is un-gitignored build or validation output. --clean-dirty offers an opt-in path to clear exactly that, after the pipeline, on real stdio:

  • Only a merged/closed worktree whose every uncommitted path is untracked is a candidate. A reused-branch straggler classifies as no-pr/draft (its merged verdict withheld, issue #1719), so it is never in a clearable state and its unmerged commits are never at risk.
  • A worktree with modified tracked files is refused — those are never discarded — and left surfaced as needing attention.
  • Each removal shows exactly what will be deleted (the untracked paths) and requires confirmation before git worktree remove --force discards the output and deletes the branch.

The default guards are unchanged: without --clean-dirty, anything with tracked modifications or unmerged commits is protected, as before.

Tip: the cleaner fix is to gitignore your validation output so the worktree is never dirtied in the first place — then it sweeps automatically with no --clean-dirty needed. That is repo-specific configuration, out of scope for finalize itself.

Eternal branches are protected based on the branching_model:

Branching Model Protected Branches docs-single-branch develop, gh-pages library-release develop, main, gh-pages application-promotion develop, release, main, gh-pages

docs.title: 5. Prune Remote References
docs.text: Runs git remote prune origin to clean up stale remote-tracking branches. As a swept safety net, any PR-workflow relay ref (refs/vergil/pr-workflow/*) whose branch no longer exists on origin is pruned too, so a relay ref stranded by a branch deleted outside finalize (or by an earlier failed run) is never left behind (issue #2369).

docs.title: 6. Working-Tree Cleanliness Gate
docs.text: Fails if the target branch's working tree is not clean, so leftover files are cleaned up before the next issue.

docs.title: 7. Post-Finalization Validation
docs.text: Runs canonical validation via vrg-container-run to catch problems on the target branch before the next PR is created.

docs.title: 8. CD Workflow Wait
docs.text:
Blocks on the CD workflow run this merge triggered — identified by the merge commit SHA, not "the latest run on the branch" — and fails if that run does not succeed (issue #2753). The base-branch push a merge produces dispatches CD asynchronously (docker build/publish, docs, release), so finalize polls for the run to register (bounded by a dispatch timeout), watches it to completion (bounded by a watch timeout), and surfaces the failing run's URL so a post-merge publish failure is caught here rather than discovered later. --no-wait-cd is the conscious opt-out from blocking. When the repo has no CD workflow, or no run is dispatched for the merge within the dispatch window (a change CD legitimately skips), finalize does not block.

Watch deadline. The watch defaults to 90 minutes (5400 seconds), about twice the longest known CD: vergil-containers' CD routinely takes around 43 minutes, because its rust image jobs alone take about 40. Set VRG_CD_TIMEOUT (seconds, a positive whole number) to change it. It mirrors VRG_CHECKS_TIMEOUT: a malformed value is an error rather than a silent fallback, and the deadline cannot be disabled.

Timeout is not failure. A run that concludes non-success fails the stage with "the CD workflow run triggered by this merge did not succeed". A run still going at the deadline gets a different headline: "CD run still in progress after Ns; result unknown". It comes with the run URL, a gh run view <id> command to re-check it, and a pointer to vrg-finalize-pr --cleanup-only to re-confirm once the run has finished. It still fails the stage, because an unknown result is not a pass, but it never claims the run failed (issue #3316).

docs.title: Batch mode (comma-list / --all)
docs.text:
A comma-separated PR argument (vrg-finalize-pr 123,124,125) or --all (every open PR in .worktrees/) finalizes several PRs as a single serialized batch (issue #1673). Each item runs vrg-finalize-pr <pr> --skip-post-checks (merge + cleanup, deferring the post-merge checks); after every item merges, one end-of-batch vrg-finalize-pr --cleanup-only runs validation and the CD check, then — with --release/--install — a single vrg-release.

The batch summary reports that end-of-batch step as post-checks. Its exit code cannot say which of the two checks failed, so a failure reads "end-of-batch post-checks (validation + CD check) exited N" and never blames validation alone. The --cleanup-only stage summary printed just above it names the failing stage (issue #3316).

Unlike vrg-submit-pr's batch, these PRs are already open, so each one that lands behind another will update-branch and re-run its gate (the normal serialized-merge cost). For zero-waste CI, submit the batch with vrg-submit-pr --all --finalize instead, which rebases each branch before opening its PR.

The batch asks one confirmation up front (skipped with --yes) and is fail-fast: the first failure stops it and prints a merged / failed / not started summary. The single-PR modes are unchanged.

The --skip-post-checks flag (used internally by the batch) finalizes a PR but skips the validation and CD-check stages and never chains a release — the batch runs those once at the end.

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Finalization complete, or declined at a confirmation prompt 1 Provenance violation, unmergeable PR (draft, conflicts, failed checks, stuck behind, orphaned check-run, or wait timeout), not run from main worktree, non-TTY stdin or stdout in inference mode, dirty working tree, failed validation, failed CD run, CD watch timeout (result unknown), or a batch item failed

docs.title: vrg-host
docs.text:
Installed as: vrg-host (Python console script)

Source: src/vergil_tooling/bin/vrg_host.py (libraries: src/vergil_tooling/lib/host_deps.py, host_methods.py, host_pins.py, host_status.py, host_versions.py)

Observes and manages the tools Vergil development needs on the macOS host itself — the ones that cannot live in a dev container or an agent VM, such as gh, git, uv, gcloud, Lima, Docker Desktop and the Xcode Command Line Tools. It reports how far each one has drifted from its latest release, upgrades the ones it is allowed to upgrade, and records deliberate pins as tracked technical debt rather than silent freezes.

vrg-host is a host tool: run it on the Mac, not inside vrg-container-run. It runs as the ordinary user and never prompts for a password (see No privilege escalation).
